body:
McClelland's Iceberg Model Explained

David McClelland (1917–1998) was an American psychologist, academic, and scientist. He became famous for his theory of motivation. What motivates people? Which needs are learned? According to him, regardless of age, gender, or culture, everyone deals with motivation, which in turn is directly linked to needs. Linked to his theory of motivation, he developed the Iceberg Model. In this world-famous model, the client is compared to an iceberg. Above the waterline, you see the tip of the iceberg. Below the waterline, however, lies the largest part—the part that is not visible. The model encourages reflection. What are your strengths? What do you want to achieve? How do you plan to achieve this?

Would you like to discover the underlying motivations of your employees?

Discover our Motivational Test for deeper insights into motivation

You can read more about the meaning behind this on this page.

The Structure of the Iceberg Model

The Iceberg Model consists of two main parts that together describe the entirety of human functioning:
Level Visibility Components Developability
Above the Waterline Visible Behavior, skills, knowledge Easy to train
Below the waterline Invisible Values, beliefs, motives Difficult to change

Above the waterline

Above the water’s surface, you see the tip of the mountain. Here, McClelland identifies people’s observable behavior, skills, and knowledge. Action is central here. These elements are: - Observable by others - Measurable and tangible - Relatively easy to develop through training - Directly applicable in work situations

Below the waterline

The largest part of an iceberg lies hidden below the waterline. This symbolizes people’s unconscious and invisible beliefs, norms, values, traits, and motives. This hidden part often contains the unspoken thoughts and desires that drive visible behavior.

Want to map out personality and motivations?

The Big Five personality test helps you understand the underlying factors

Invisible Factors

Here, we’ll take a moment to consider the invisible components below the waterline:
Factor Definition Impact on behavior
Beliefs Strong opinions about yourself and others Determines patterns of thought and behavior
Norms & Values What is considered good or bad Guides choices and decisions
Personal traits Introverted/extroverted, sociable/shy Influences interaction style
Motives Underlying motivations and needs Source of energy for performance
Beliefs are strong opinions or views about yourself, others, or a situation. They are shaped by your upbringing and environmental factors. This also includes self-doubt. Norms and values are what people come to regard as good or bad. A certain action is taken—or not taken—because an underlying norm or value influences it. For example, you might not want to bother a coworker because they’re too busy. Personal traits also influence behavior. People can be introverted or extroverted. One person is sociable, while another is shy. Motives are the basis for taking action. You’re motivated to achieve your goal. Otherwise, it will be difficult if you aren’t convinced yourself.

The Iceberg Model Within an Organization

Within an organization, it’s important to understand what motivates employees and their teams.

Why the Iceberg Model is important for HR:

• 80% of behavior is driven by invisible factors

• Sustainable change begins below the waterline

• Better team dynamics through an understanding of underlying motivations

• More effective coaching by focusing on intrinsic motivation

You can bring about behavioral changes based on the iceberg theory. Often, the focus within teams is on what you see—the concrete, tangible elements that are addressed. On the one hand, it’s important to establish clear guidelines, work within a structure, solidify agreements, or provide feedback. But it’s also important to consider what employees are experiencing internally. The characteristics below the waterline of the iceberg model have a significant impact on visible behavior. They can either reinforce or hinder progress. The abstract part below the waterline must not be overlooked. Here, the emphasis is on feelings. When people are guided from this deeper level, change arises from within.

Practical Application in HR

HR Process Focus Above the Waterline Focus Below the Waterline Tools
Selection Resume, degrees, experience Motivations, values, fit Motivations Test
Development Skills training Personality, beliefs Big Five Test
Coaching Behavioral Feedback Internal Barriers Conversation Techniques
Team Building Roles and Responsibilities Underlying Tensions 360° feedback

Frequently Asked Questions:

How can organizations effectively uncover the underlying motivations and values of employees that aren’t immediately apparent? Organizations can gain deeper insight through confidential conversations, psychometric tests , and regular feedback sessions. Creating an open culture where employees can share their beliefs and values can also help.
What are the best practices for integrating insights from the iceberg model into day-to-day management and team dynamics? Best practices may include: regular team meetings to discuss underlying values and norms, adapting management styles to employees’ individual needs, and using coaching to address subconscious motivations.
How can organizations ensure that behavioral changes among employees, influenced by the iceberg model, are sustainable in the long term? Sustainable change can be fostered through regular follow-ups, setting measurable goals, and ongoing support and training to ensure that new behaviors become ingrained in daily practice.
Which assessments are most effective for measuring factors below the waterline? The Motivational Test is highly effective for measuring motivations and drive. For personality traits, the Big Five personality test offers in-depth insights.

Start with the Iceberg Model in your organization

Would you like to gain more insight into what drives your employees? What their motivations are? What their personalities are like?

Discover what lies beneath the surface

Motivation Test: Measure underlying motivations

Big Five: Map out personality

Both assessments provide you with comprehensive insights into the Iceberg Model

body:
Many organizations want leaders who can guide their teams through change, justify decisions, and communicate clearly. Yet in practice, it turns out that new team leaders or managers often struggle with self-awareness, behavioral flexibility, and guidance. Leadership development based on assessment data provides insight into behavior, motivations, and potential. This enables you to make better decisions and accelerate growth.

Key points of this article

  • Leadership development begins with insight into behavior and motivations
  • A leadership assessment makes leadership potential measurable
  • Cognitive skills predict success in complex roles
  • Training is more effective when it aligns with assessment results
  • Continuous development strengthens teams and drives organizational growth

What is leadership development?

Leadership development is about expanding the behavioral repertoire of leaders. It’s not about a specific personality type, but about behavior that aligns with a role, a team, and an organization’s goals. HR professionals are increasingly using online assessments to gain objective insights into leadership competencies, motivators, and cognitive skills. With a leadership assessment, you can predict behaviors relevant to daily managerial tasks such as decision-making, providing direction, giving feedback, and handling resistance.

How does leadership development work with assessments?

1. Mapping Behavior

A personality assessment reveals the behavioral preferences a person exhibits under pressure, when collaborating, or when being managed.

2. Identifying motivators

Motivators explain why someone exhibits certain behaviors. This sheds light on motivation, energy boosters and drainers, and engagement.

3. Measuring cognitive skills

The Ability Scan shows how quickly someone makes connections, processes information, and solves complex problems. This is particularly relevant in changing environments.

4. Align development with the job profile

Determine which competencies are required for the role: coaching, planning, providing direction, analyzing, delegating, and collaborating.

5. Targeting Training Effectively

Leadership development training is only truly effective when it aligns with individual assessment results. This gives individuals insight into learning areas that directly impact the team.

Leadership Development Training: What Really Works?

Many training programs focus on general leadership models . These are useful, but insufficient if you don’t know who you’re dealing with and what someone needs to continue growing. The most effective approach:
  1. Start with a leadership test → gain insight into behavioral styles
  2. Combine it with a competency test or Ability Scan → insight into cognitive abilities
  3. Link insights to the context and role → what does the team need?
  4. Plan customized training and coaching → focused on specific situations
  5. Use an ongoing feedback cycle → make growth visible
View the recommended assessment here: hrmforce leadership test

How do you identify leadership potential with an online test?

A leadership test provides insight into three key factors:

1. Behavioral preferences

For example, how someone handles conflicts, takes initiative, or provides direction to a team.

2. Motivators

Motivators reveal why someone exhibits certain behaviors and what kind of environment suits them best.

3. Cognitive abilities

Particularly relevant for teams facing frequent changes, complex challenges, or high levels of responsibility.

Framework: The 5-Factor Model for Leadership Growth

Use this model to develop leadership:
  1. Self-awareness – Understand your own behavior, motivators, and pitfalls.
  2. Environmental Awareness – Understand what the team needs.
  3. Behavioral Flexibility – Be able to switch between directing and coaching behaviors.
  4. Decision-making – Working with information, risks, and priorities.
  5. Communication & Relationship Building – Be honest, clear, and attentive to others.
The assessment highlights the areas where a person already excels and where there is room for growth.

FAQ – Frequently Asked Questions About Leadership Development

1. What does a leadership test measure? Behavior, motivations, and cognitive skills that predict how someone leads. 2. Can leadership development be learned? Yes. Leadership is behavior, and behavior can be developed through an understanding of patterns. 3. How long does leadership development take? Usually six to twelve months when working with feedback, assessments, and specific learning objectives. 4. What training is suitable for new managers? Training that focuses on communication, feedback, self-awareness, and basic management skills. 5. How do you recognize leadership potential? Through a combination of behavioral profile, motivators, and cognitive skills. 6. Why use assessments? They provide objective information that goes beyond observations, beliefs, or a resume. 7. When should you opt for a leadership test? During selection, development, internal promotion, or when there are doubts about leadership fit. 8. Does every leadership style fit every role? No. A coaching style works differently from a directive style and isn’t equally suitable for every situation.

In conclusion: steps to start leadership development right away

  1. Start with the hrmforce Leadership Test
  2. Link results to job profiles and team goals
  3. Set three to five specific behavioral goals
  4. Choose training that aligns with the assessment data
  5. Evaluate progress through the performance review cycle

body:
In the modern workplace, employees continue to learn and develop—both professionally and personally, with a focus on their behavior and competencies. We were already aware of the importance of this, and the COVID-19 crisis has significantly reinforced this understanding. Yet implementation often stalls when it comes to putting these concepts into practice on the job. This is despite the fact that encouraging learning and development—or even behavioral change—among employees is entirely possible. We’ve listed seven closely interrelated success factors.

The seven success factors at a glance:

  1. Increase and facilitate self-direction
  2. Strengthen self-awareness
  3. Consider 360-degree feedback
  4. Watch out for fear of failure!
  5. Adapt to different conversation styles
  6. Provide appropriate learning opportunities
  7. Give employees a meaningful purpose

From wanting to actually doing

Many employers and employees are now familiar with the benefits. When employees remain actively engaged in learning and their professional development, it leads to greater job satisfaction, job security, and career opportunities. Numerous studies also show that these employees are more loyal, motivated, and productive. Moreover, it is a key prerequisite for, for example, enhancing long-term employability.
📊 Impact of COVID-19 on learning Before COVID-19 After the pandemic
CEOs who see value in lifelong learning 29% 70%
So the will is there, but creating a “learning organization” doesn’t always turn out to be easy in practice. Often, high workloads act as a barrier, preventing employees from “ever getting around to” a learning program, or they aren’t sufficiently encouraged and supported to continue developing. How can this be achieved? These success factors can help right away.

1. Increase and facilitate self-direction

In practice, fostering self-direction among employees has proven to be the crucial factor for companies that have successfully become learning organizations. However, this arises from an interaction between employer and employee. It’s not just a matter of placing responsibility on employees, but also of providing them with adequate support.

✅ Practical approach:

  • Start by raising awareness
  • Implement a robust feedback cycle
  • Provide accessible development opportunities
  • Communicate from the employees’ perspective
  • Focus on what they gain from it (not what they’re required to do)

2. Strengthen self-awareness

Employers can effectively facilitate employees’ awareness and self-management with practical, accessible tools. In addition to providing greater self-awareness regarding their current situation, online tools can, for example, help employees gain a clearer picture of their long-term development path.
💡 Tip: Most organizations nowadays use online assessments to support the development needs of employees or teams.

3. Consider 360-Degree Feedback

A concrete example of a powerful tool for increasing self-awareness is implementing 360-Degree Feedback. After all, good feedback is extremely valuable for fostering self-awareness and employee development.
Feedback Provider Valuable insights about
Colleagues Collaboration, team dynamics, communication
Manager Performance, potential, areas for development
(Internal) customers Service orientation, results orientation
Subordinates Leadership style, coaching, inspiration
 

4. Watch out for fear of failure!

When organizational changes require different learning or development behaviors, it’s important to be aware of a major pitfall. It lies within our brains.

🧠 Neurological fact:

"Our brains primarily view change—even positive change—as a loss. This triggers thoughts of mortality, because death is the ultimate loss."

— Prof. James R. Bailey, George Washington University

But you can also put these principles to work:
  • Inform and prepare employees well in advance
  • Let people acclimate safely first
  • Connect changes to people’s deepest motivations (the WHY)
  • Focus on WHY someone actually does something

5. Adapt to different conversation styles

To facilitate effective conversations between employees and managers during changes or learning and development processes, it’s important to keep the different conversation cycles in mind.

📅 Full conversation cycle:

Bila+ conversations: Short, frequent check-ins → Development discussions: Focus on growth and learning → Annual reviews: Evaluation and planning

6. Provide appropriate learning opportunities

It may sound obvious at first, but be sure to provide appropriate learning opportunities when it comes to actually facilitating learning and development.
Learning format Suitable for Advantages
E-learning Individual knowledge acquisition Flexible, scalable, self-paced
Classroom-based Practitioners, team learning Interaction, immediately applicable
Peer learning Knowledge sharing, best practices Accessible, context-rich
Webinars Updates, inspiration Efficient, wide reach

7. Give employees a meaningful purpose

In a thriving “learning organization,” many of the success factors just mentioned—ideally—are closely intertwined. After all, there can be no self-direction without self-awareness. And there can be no enriching learning journey without appropriate learning opportunities.

🎯 The golden formula:

Organizational goal + Professional goal + Personal goal = Meaningful goal

Align talents, motivations, and interests with organizational goals

 Frequently Asked Questions:

❓ How can companies evaluate the effectiveness of their development programs?
Companies can evaluate effectiveness through periodic feedback sessions, monitoring performance improvements, and analyzing development-related KPIs. In addition, an annual review of learning goals and outcomes can provide insight into the long-term impact.
❓ What challenges are associated with remote or hybrid work?
In a remote or hybrid environment, challenges such as reduced engagement, communication barriers, and a lack of access to resources may arise. It is important to address these with tailored tools and strategies.
❓ How can companies set priorities when resources are limited?
Companies can prioritize by focusing on essential skills that directly contribute to business goals. Implementing short, targeted learning programs and encouraging peer learning can also be effective when resources are limited.
 

Ready to become a learning organization?

Start implementing these success factors today!

```
title: 7 Tips for Encouraging Employee Learning and Development

Talent management for your organization.

Based on your organization’s vision and goals, hrmforce can help you effectively manage the recruitment, development, and flow of talent. We do this by analyzing the various processes and tools. Where necessary, we implement improvements to achieve the very best results.

Strategic Talent Management

When applying the 80-20 rule to recruitment, it turns out that 20% of the candidates hired account for 80% of the results. More than ever, companies are focusing on recruiting these top talents. However, given the current economic conditions, it is also essential to identify and leverage talent within the organization. This talent must be managed, motivated, and retained for the organization. Talent management involves analyzing and fully utilizing the talents of employees and managers. Taking a critical look at how the organization, together with its employees and managers, can continue to realize its strategy and ambitions. Thinking innovatively about career policies based on healthy, mature collaboration and trust. Not a “quick win,” but a sustainable solution that connects individual and collective ambitions.

The strategic talent management planning process at hrmforce consists of three phases:

  1. Identifying talent
  2. Developing talent
  3. Retaining talent

Identifying talent

Talent is often taken for granted. Employees are frequently unaware of their talents and do not know how they can contribute to the organization’s success. If you want to make the most of the talent in your organization, you first need to know what talent you have on hand. To help you identify these talents, hrmforce offers a variety of assessment tools.

Talent Development

Talents stem, among other things, from an employee’s personality, intelligence, and work style. Recognizing talent is no guarantee that it will be developed. To give your organization a boost, you can actively develop that talent through talent development. HRMforce uses various tools for this purpose, such as a development center, training, and individual career counseling. The program is always tailored to your organization’s needs by our consultants.

Retaining Talent

Once talent has been identified and developed, the next question is how to ensure that talent remains within your organization. One solution is to optimize the alignment between an employee’s skills and the challenges at work. After all, this is when an employee is most productive, and their qualities are fully utilized. Talent management involves creating a specific plan tailored to your organization to retain talent both now and in the future.

Organizations that have gone before you

Request talent management services

Do you have any questions or need advice? Please contact one of our consultants. Our consultants are available Monday through Friday from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.

body:
The term “CanMEDS” is commonly used in nursing. It is also referred to as CanMEDS roles or competencies. The CanMEDS roles are primarily used by paramedical professions, but nowadays they are also applied to the Nurse Specialist Registry, the Long-Term Care Quality Registry, and the Healthcare Professionals Registry. Of course, the question remains: what exactly are these CanMEDS roles, and what is their purpose? [caption id="attachment_8414" align="aligncenter" width="300"] Source: Royal College of Nursing, Canada[/caption]  

What are CanMEDS roles?

The CanMEDS roles were developed by the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada. The term itself is an acronym for “Canadian Medical Education Directives for Specialists.” The CanMEDS framework is used internationally to describe the roles of various healthcare professionals. Generally, a distinction is made between seven different roles, each with its own set of competencies or skills.

The provider of accredited education assigns points across a maximum of three CanMEDS competencies. As a nurse practitioner, you must specify this distribution yourself when you submit a test or register other professional development activities in the Nurse Practitioner Registry. Caregivers, care coordinators, and registered nurses are not required to do this.

The Development of the CanMEDS Competencies: The 7 Roles

In any case, it is important to know which topics such an activity should cover in order to develop specific competencies. An overview of these competencies and a few examples is therefore in order here:
  1. Professional Practice—Have I acquired knowledge about caring for clients or patients?
Examples include physiology, anatomy, disabilities and clinical pictures, diagnostics, pharmacology, self-management, support and guidance, intervention, prevention, psychology and psychiatry, assistive devices, nursing techniques, care plans, and so on.
  1. Communication—Have I acquired knowledge regarding interaction with clients or patients?
Examples include conversation techniques, influencing behavior, empowerment, use of ICT, social media, motivation, theoretical communication, and so on.
  1. Collaboration - Have I acquired knowledge about collaborating with healthcare providers, as well as patients and clients, and healthcare institutions?
Examples include reporting, integrated care, handoffs, multidisciplinary collaboration, group dynamics, and so on.
  1. Science and Knowledge - Have I learned more, enabling me to reflect on my professionalism and the reasons behind my actions?
Examples include the application of science, evidence-based practice, research methodology, feedback, and so on.
  1. Socially Responsible Action - Have I learned more about social contexts and health-promoting measures?
Examples include prevention, cultural backgrounds, health education, intervention-based care, lifestyle promotion, epidemiology, and so on.
  1. Organization—Have I gained more knowledge about how care can be organized?
Examples include small-scale living arrangements, the affordability of care, care needs assessment, remote care, patient safety, work environment, organizational management, and so on.
  1. Quality and Professionalism - Have I learned more about professional standards and quality assurance?
Examples include the professional code of ethics, professional profiles, guidelines and standards, professional associations and reputation, quality registration and systems, laws and regulations regarding care, and so on.  

The Importance of CanMeds Competencies in Nursing

It goes without saying that the healthcare sector is one of great social value, both for healthcare institutions and providers, as well as for the patients themselves. The CanMeds aim to further refine the competencies that are crucial for the development of an improved healthcare sector, so that the care provided to those who need it is of higher quality and more professional. In addition, CanMEDS provide insight into the current state of healthcare providers’ competencies, enabling all necessary improvements to be implemented.  

CanMEDS Competencies Within Your Organization

By using a 360-degree feedback CanMEDS questionnaire, your employees receive better feedback, allowing them to develop more quickly and improve the quality of care. Additionally, you can better assess your employees’ performance.

CanMEDS in 2025: More Relevant Than Ever?

By 2025, the CanMEDS competencies will have gained an even more prominent position in the healthcare sector. The seven roles now form the foundation for virtually all quality systems and educational programs, such as higher professional education (HBO V).

Due to the increasing digitization and personalization of healthcare, the roles of Communication and Social Engagement, in particular, have expanded further. Healthcare professionals must now be skilled in both physical and digital communication, regularly switching between different platforms.

The integration of artificial intelligence into diagnosis and treatment plans has transformed the “Science and Knowledge” competency. Critical thinking and digital literacy have become essential for effectively utilizing technological tools without losing sight of the human element.

The experience of the pandemic has led to a renewed appreciation for the “Collaboration and Organization” competencies. Healthcare professionals now collaborate much more flexibly in changing teams, both within and outside the traditional healthcare setting.

The Quality Registry has also adapted. Higher standards are now set for the distribution of accreditation points across the various competency areas, with special attention given to the integration of these skills into daily practice.

As a result, the CanMEDS roles have not only remained relevant but have taken on an even more central role in 2025.
title: What are CanMEDS roles?

body:
It’s difficult to recognize burnout in employees if you rely solely on visible behavior. It’s precisely the employee who always delivers, meets deadlines, and never complains who is at the greatest risk. That may sound counterintuitive, but assessment data from HRMForce confirms this picture. In this article, we’ll show you which personality profile is associated with an increased risk of burnout, how to recognize that profile early on, and what you—as an HR professional or manager—can do before an employee actually takes time off.

The Numbers: What Does Assessment Data Show?

Data from HRMForce, based on Big Fifty personality assessments, reveals a striking pattern among employees who take leave due to burnout within twelve months:
  • Stress resilience: −31% compared to colleagues who remain sustainably employable
  • Discipline: +24% compared to that same group
  • Reliability: +27% compared to that same group
This means that employees with the highest risk of burnout are not the ones who drop out, complain, or underperform. Rather, they are the people everyone relies on—disciplined, reliable, and dedicated to their duties. But they have significantly lower resilience when work pressure increases.

Why Traditional Warning Signs Fall Short

Most articles on recognizing burnout focus on behavioral changes: taking more sick days, cynicism, reduced productivity, and irritability. These are valuable signs, but they only appear once the problem is already well advanced. For top performers, there’s an additional complication. They mask their symptoms—not intentionally, but because their behavioral profile is precisely tailored to do so. A high level of discipline ensures that they keep performing, even when they’re running on fumes. A high level of reliability means they don’t readily say no or turn down work. And low stress tolerance means they’re under intense internal pressure, while outwardly they still function normally. By the time the classic warning signs become apparent, it’s often already too late to change course without a prolonged absence from work.

Understanding the Risk Profile Through the Big Five

The Big Five personality traits form the scientific foundation of HRMForce’s Big Fifty assessment. This model describes personality based on five main dimensions: Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness. Stress resilience falls within the Neuroticism dimension. A low score means that a person becomes overwhelmed more easily, worries more, and recovers more slowly after periods of intense activity. Discipline and reliability fall under Conscientiousness, the dimension that describes how organized, goal-oriented, and responsible a person is. The combination of high Conscientiousness and low stress resilience is precisely what makes this risk profile so insidious. The drive maintains performance levels, while the lower resilience undermines recovery. It’s as if someone with a smaller gas tank is pressing harder on the accelerator.

What this means for HR and managers

Don’t wait for someone to burn out

The most important lesson from this data: don’t wait until an employee burns out. Behavioral patterns indicating a risk of burnout are visible in personality data months in advance. This calls for a shift from reactive to preventive action. Organizations that want to prevent work-related stress would be wise to look not only at workload and engagement but also at employees’ personality profiles. Not to screen for stress resilience, but to provide targeted support where the risk is highest.

Actively engage with high performers

It’s particularly tempting not to ask further questions of employees who are performing well—after all, they’re delivering results. But the data shows that high performance and high risk can go hand in hand. Schedule regular work experience check-ins with your top performers. Don’t just ask, “How’s work going?” but also: “How do you recover after a busy period?” and “What’s taking the most energy out of you right now?” These kinds of questions break the pattern of just plowing through without reflection.

Discussing stress resilience in talent reviews

Stress resilience belongs in talent reviews. Not as a weakness or a reason to assign someone else to the task, but as a risk factor that deserves attention. It’s similar to how you take injury susceptibility into account with an athlete. A Sustainable Employability Scan can provide an objective starting point here. By periodically assessing the state of employees’ employability, you prevent warning signs from surfacing only after absenteeism has already begun.

From Individual Risk to Organizational Policy

Burnout prevention is not just an individual issue. Data from HRMForce makes it possible to analyze risk profiles at the group level. This provides insights that go beyond the individual conversation. Suppose that within a particular team or department, a strikingly high number of employees exhibit a risk profile characterized by high discipline and low stress resilience. In that case, there is a good chance that the work culture or the distribution of tasks within that team constitutes a risk factor. In that case, adjusting work processes is more effective than providing individual coaching to employees. Organizations that want to retain staff for longer can use this approach to build a structural prevention strategy rather than putting out fires after the fact.

Practical Step-by-Step Plan: Recognizing Burnout with Data

As an HR professional or manager, do you want to start identifying burnout risk early on? Here’s a practical step-by-step plan: Step 1: Assess the personality profile. Use a validated personality assessment, such as the Big Fifty Personality Test, to assess scores for stress resilience, discipline, and reliability. Step 2: Identify the risk profile. Pay particular attention to the combination of high discipline and reliability with low stress resilience. This is the profile that is statistically most strongly associated with burnout-related absenteeism. Step 3: Conduct preventive conversations. Engage in conversations with employees who exhibit the risk profile. Do so not out of alarm, but out of concern. Discuss workload, opportunities for recovery, and boundaries. Step 4: Monitor periodically. Burnout risk is not a fixed factor. It changes with work pressure, personal circumstances, and the extent to which someone recovers. Periodic assessments provide insight into trends and shifts. Step 5: Translate findings into policy. Use the data not only at the individual level but also to evaluate team composition, task distribution, and work culture.

Burnout among top performers is no surprise. It is a pattern.

The employee who takes a leave of absence due to burnout was often already visible in the data for months. High discipline, high reliability, low stress resilience. It is a recognizable profile that recurs in assessment data from thousands of measurements. This also means that organizations are not powerless. With the right measurement tools and a preventive approach, the risk of burnout can be identified early on—not by waiting until someone collapses, but by looking at the patterns that precede it.
This article is based on anonymous, aggregated assessment data from the HRMForce platform. The percentages cited are derived from comparative analyses of employee profiles.
title: Recognizing Burnout in Top Performers: What Assessment Data Reveals

In today’s competitive job market, it is essential for organizations to place the right people in the right positions. Personality assessments, such as the PAPI 3 questionnaire, play a crucial role in identifying individuals’ unique characteristics and understanding how these characteristics influence their job performance. In this article, we take an in-depth look at the PAPI 3 questionnaire, its theoretical basis, the seven main domains it measures, and how organizations can effectively use the test for recruitment, career development, and team building.

Introduction to the PAPI 3 Questionnaire

The PAPI 3, or “Personality and Preference Inventory,” is a psychometric test developed by Talogy, formerly Cubiks, an international HR consulting firm. The questionnaire is based on the normative model, which means that an individual’s results are compared to those of a norm group. The PAPI 3 measures 20 personality traits grouped into seven main domains: influence, relationships, thinking style, structure, motivation, resilience, and decision-making.

Why do more than 5,000 organizations choose PAPI 3?

• Scientifically validated normative model

• 20 detailed personality traits

• Direct link to job performance

• Internationally recognized by Talogy

The seven main domains of the PAPI 3

  1. Influence measures the extent to which a person likes to exert influence on others, their environment, and outcomes. This is important for roles that require negotiation, persuasion, and leadership.
  2. Relationships, measures the extent to which a person enjoys collaborating with others and maintaining social connections. This can influence how effective a person is as part of a team and how well they build relationships with colleagues and clients.
  3. Thinking Style measures an individual’s preferences for analytical and conceptual thinking, as well as how they process information and make decisions. This is important for roles that require problem-solving, strategic thinking, and data analysis.
  4. Structure measures the extent to which a person prefers order, planning, and following rules and procedures. This can indicate how organized and disciplined a person is in their work.
  5. Motivation measures the extent to which a person is motivated by challenges, achievement, power, and recognition. This can influence a person’s ambition, perseverance, and focus on performance.
  6. Resilience measures the extent to which a person copes with pressure, stress, and change. This is crucial for roles with high demands and changing circumstances.
  7. Decision-making: an individual’s preferences for making decisions, such as speed, thoroughness, and involving others. This can impact how effective someone is at making decisions and managing projects.

PRESS RELEASE Amsterdam, October 2021 – hrmforce, a provider of online psychometric questionnaires and solutions, and Pearson Talentlens, a provider of online tests and assessments, have established an integration. As a result, Pearson’s most relevant assessments are now directly available on the hrmforce platform. Organizations can now send various Pearson tests to their applicants and employees directly from the hrmforce portal. The key benefits include time savings, process optimization, and a better understanding of a candidate’s qualities thanks to the additional features.

Making Better Decisions

The demand for this integration comes from the market, where a number of organizations use both Pearson and hrmforce questionnaires.  “hrmforce has about 40 questionnaires available, but on specific topics, Pearson’s questionnaires can still provide additional information to help make better selection and development decisions,” said Floor Hendriks, Managing Partner at hrmforce. “The process of requesting and returning the results, as well as the administrative processing, takes place entirely within the hrmforce platform. The integration saves time and results in an optimal experience for the candidate.”  

A Complete Offering from a Single Source

Martin Hoogland of Pearson notes: “With their questionnaires, hrmforce also complements our portfolio. When you look at our combined offering now, we can answer virtually any question regarding the selection or development of employees. It’s also very convenient for the client that everything can be managed from a single central location.  

The Power of Collaboration

Hendriks is enthusiastic about the partnership. “Pearson is a solid and professional company, and its questionnaires are based on sound scientific principles. The TD-12 (which assesses the risk of dysfunctional behavior) and the Watson-Glaser (critical thinking) are examples of questionnaires that greatly enhance the hrmforce portfolio. These tools enable organizations to make better-informed selection and development decisions. In addition, it’s a pleasure to work with the Pearson team to develop the most suitable joint solution for an organization.”  

About Pearson TalentLens

  TalentLens (www.talentlens.com/nl) is part of Pearson Benelux BV. For more than 60 years, this international network of test publishers has been a recognized leader in the publication and distribution of scientifically validated psychological assessment tools for people of all ages and cultures. TalentLens helps organizations select and develop talent through a high-quality portfolio of assessment centers, tests, training, and consulting services.

About hrmforce

hrmforce was founded in 2009 and specializes in online talent management using assessment tools and solutions. With an innovative approach, hrmforce develops solutions for human resources management, ranging from a single personality or intelligence questionnaire to a comprehensive tool for enhancing development and improving performance. hrmforce supports all key HRM processes, such as recruitment and selection, development, workforce readiness, and HR analytics. hrmforce is also active outside the Netherlands (through distributors) in countries such as Belgium, France, Romania, Spain, and India. body:
Recruiting the right staff can make all the difference for an organization. Organizations are also more focused than ever on retaining their top talent. Recruitment is a profession in its own right. We regularly receive questions about the recruitment process. For example: What recruitment methods do you use, and which ones yield the best results? For example, what do you do with a 38-year-old prospective employee who was unemployed for over a year during the economic crisis, comes across as somewhat headstrong, but scored the highest of all applicants on an intelligence test? In this article:
  • The Resume
  • The First Interview
  • Structured interview
  • Predictive validity
 

1. At the Start of the Selection Process—The Resume

[ps2id id='the-resume' target=''/] The curriculum vitae (resume) has traditionally been the first screening tool recruiters use to separate the wheat from the chaff. However, things often go wrong right at the start of the selection process. Recruiters are sometimes more easily swayed by a photo or a candidate’s name than by the relevant information on the resume. A study by CVster shows that attractive applicants are invited for an interview much more often than less attractive ones. By sending out about 300 nearly identical resumes from two fictional (attractive and less attractive) male and female applicants, the study found that 43% of the attractive applicants received a positive response, compared to 15% of the less attractive ones. A similar study was conducted regarding the applicants’ backgrounds. A total of 480 nearly identical cover letters were sent to companies in various industries. Of the four senders, three had names that did not sound Dutch. Email tracking software was used to determine whether the emails were opened and whether they received a response. It turned out that emails from applicants with Dutch-sounding names were opened more often and received positive responses more frequently. While the resume may serve as the applicant’s calling card, whether it is also a reliable tool for selecting new employees is a matter of debate.

2. A cup of coffee? The first interview

[ps2id id='first-interview' target=''/] Would you like a cup of coffee? How many times has that question been asked at the start of a job interview? It’s an ideal icebreaker and is meant to put the candidate at ease. As the inventors of the concept of “gezellig” (coziness), we in the Netherlands generally consider the “gezellig” factor an important part of the hiring process. In many organizations, interviewers therefore see it primarily as their task to put candidates at ease and have a “gezellig” conversation over coffee that focuses on personal questions. The fact that “a cup of coffee, tea, or something else?” is an important topic is also evident from how frequently it appears on websites that offer advice to job seekers. “Say no to coffee” is the first of 10 tips the site Hi-Re gives its readers. The Monsterboard website also addresses the topic of “drinking coffee.” The advice is that water is the safest option. “You can burn your mouth on coffee or tea, and when you’re nervous, there’s a high chance of spilling it.”

Candidate experience

Incidentally, there’s absolutely nothing wrong with creating a friendly atmosphere during a job interview. Whether or not the applicant turns out to be the right candidate, it can’t hurt if they feel positive about the hiring process. Negative experiences among applicants can have unexpected consequences. They tell friends and family, complain about the potential employer on social media, and—more than once—decide to stop purchasing products or services from the company they applied to. This happened to a major organization like Virgin. The negative experiences of job applicants cost the company about 5 million in revenue!

Optimal Job Application Experience

Recruitment management took action and established a “gold standard interview program.” From then on, candidates could count on an optimal job application experience. Among other things, this meant that the interviewer had to approach the applicant in a positive manner. From then on, everyone was also given a constructive explanation of why they were not a good fit for a particular position. In addition, rejected candidates received free advice on how they could improve certain aspects of their application. This transformation in the candidate experience quickly paid off. Not only did it result in significantly more satisfied candidates, but it also led to a reduction in recruitment and selection costs and an increase in the number of clients.

Freestyling During an Unstructured Job Interview

The job interview is undoubtedly one of the most commonly used selection methods when recruiting new staff. During a traditional interview, candidates often “freestyle.” The term “freestyling” comes from hip-hop and refers to the way rappers spontaneously complement (or contradict) each other and come up with lyrics on the spot. In an unstructured interview—as it’s called in professional jargon—the process is actually quite similar. The direction the conversation will take isn’t determined in advance. There’s hardly any structure to speak of. The conversation develops primarily based on the candidate’s answers. The interviewer builds on these responses. If you have five candidates visiting, this often results in five different conversations. How do you determine who the best candidate is based on such interviews? Do you rely purely on intuition, experience, or biases, or do rational considerations and measurable factors also play a role?

Insight into the person

Of course, an interview like this—which takes place in a seemingly informal atmosphere and focuses primarily on personal questions—has its advantages. After all, when you’re hiring a new employee, you want to know what kind of person you’re bringing on board, what motivates them, and whether they’ll be a good fit for the organization. Precisely because of the relaxed atmosphere, there’s a good chance the candidate will reveal more about themselves. You get a better sense of their personality. At least, that’s what you’d expect.

Reliability

“Tell me a little about yourself” is therefore a commonly used opening question. Of course, that question isn’t meant to find out why the candidate loves coffee so much, is an Ajax fan, or spends their free time in nature. Above all, you want to know more about their motivation and why this applicant believes they’re the right person for the open position. Most applicants—provided they’ve prepared well—know that when asked such a question, they should enthusiastically talk about their passions and talents and weave this into their answer in a way that makes it perfectly clear why they’re a great fit for the job. One of the sites mentioned earlier even advises: “Don’t talk about yourself.” With a question like this, you can go in any direction—it offers plenty of opportunities—and you should take advantage of that by using your knowledge and experiences to immediately make it clear why the position is a perfect fit for you. In short, how reliable is the answer? How do you see through the smooth talk?

Assessments: Personality Tests

In addition to the personal interview, a personality test can provide organizations with greater clarity on how the candidate’s personality profile translates into their knowledge, skills, and behavior. In such a test, candidates are presented with a list of about 150 questions. The test bases the candidate’s scores on openness, extraversion, neuroticism, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. Together, these form the five most important personality factors for behavior in work situations. Competencies such as leadership, entrepreneurship, customer-friendliness, or helpfulness can be better assessed using such a personality test.

3. Structured Interview

[ps2id id='interview' target=''/] In a structured job interview, the direction of the interview is determined in advance. The interviewer has carefully considered the criteria against which a candidate will be evaluated. The candidate must fit a predefined job profile. Knowledge, expertise, and professional competence are qualities that can be measured against specific standards. Standards and scores are therefore established for all questions. This prevents misunderstandings about who receives a positive or negative evaluation. All candidates are evaluated based on the same questions, criteria, and standards. This significantly reduces the likelihood of subjective judgments—such as first impressions, the halo effect—where you’re “charmed” by a single positive trait of the candidate—or the opposite, the horn effect—where a single negative trait ruins the potential employee’s chances—will play a decisive role in selecting the right candidate.

Higher predictive value

In other words, the reliability of a structured interview is significantly higher than that of the unstructured version and is a better method for predicting job performance. This is also confirmed by the study “Personnel Selection in the Netherlands,” conducted by the staffing agency Yacht in collaboration with the University of Amsterdam.

Characteristics of a Good Interview

In practice, organizations often underestimate the impact of well-prepared and structured interviews. The “coffee chat” is still a widely used method, even though its results are significantly less effective when it comes to selecting the right person for the right position. Only 25 to 38% of hired employees are still performing successfully and to the employer’s satisfaction after one year. With structured interviews, that figure rises to 50% of new employees. According to the study, interviews are therefore only a useful selection tool when they meet four key criteria.
  • Well-prepared and targeted questions regarding the most important job requirements
  • Specific questions about concrete behavior in the past, present, and future, designed to ensure that a candidate cannot get away with just smooth talk.
  • The same questions for everyone
  • The use of a scoring method
 

The right selection method is important

The study confirms, as we also saw in the Virgin example, that choosing the right selection methods influences the ability to attract quality staff. When applicants are treated unfairly, unpleasantly, or indifferently, it has a negative impact on the pool of new applicants. The study further shows that, in addition to structured interviews—in which the questions are SMART (specific, measurable, acceptable, realistic, and time-bound)—aptitude tests and demonstrable work performance also have a higher predictive value.

Effectiveness of Staff Selection Rarely Measured

Only 20 percent of Dutch organizations measure the effectiveness of their recruitment process, according to the University of Amsterdam (UVA) study. Fifty percent of organizations do provide feedback and ask applicants what they thought of the selection process. However, this feedback can only be partially trusted because it is unclear to what extent applicants are being completely honest. Recruiters often rely on their gut feeling and, in many cases, on unstructured interviews. In doing so, they overlook the added value of a structured selection process in which candidates are compared based on an objective scoring system.

Greater Focus on Mental Capacity and Broader Versatility

One of the recommendations emerging from the study is that recruiters should pay more attention to a candidate’s mental capacity and broader versatility. According to the researchers, too much emphasis is placed on specific knowledge and skills. While this is undoubtedly useful for well-defined roles, it is less effective in a dynamic work environment where knowledge and skills must be continuously developed. The researchers believe that the selection methods used in the United States—which place much greater emphasis on a candidate’s personality and intelligence—should serve as a model.

4. Predictive Validity - Schmidt & Hunter

[ps2id id='validity' target=''/] To predict whether you are hiring the right employee—one who will not only perform satisfactorily but will also still be with your organization a year from now—interviews (whether structured or not) are usually insufficient. There are other selection methods that influence the prediction of employees’ future performance. An economic factor also plays a role in attracting the best employees. For example, in their 1998 study “The Validity and Utility of Selection Methods in Personnel Psychology,” Schmidt & Hunter demonstrated that the level of employee performance can vary quite significantly. For example, an average employee might perform up to 40% worse than a high-performing employee. Carefully selecting potential employees can therefore yield significant economic benefits for a company. Schmidt and Hunter analyzed 85 years of research on selection methods. In their meta-analysis, the concept of predictive validity plays a key role. It describes the extent to which you can predict something. This applies not only to future events (prediction) but also to the present or past.

Combining Testing Methods

Schmidt and Hunter believe that assessments such as intelligence tests—also known as cognitive ability tests—are a reliable means of predicting job performance. It scores 0.51 on a scale from 0 to 1. However, when intelligence testing is combined with a structured interview, the predictive value increases to 0.63. Even unstructured interviews, which score relatively low, benefit from being combined with an intelligence or ability test. The predictive validity increases significantly from 0.38 to 0.55. The predictive validity also increases when combined with a work trial or practical simulation. It is precisely by combining different selection methods that the best results are achieved.

What do we do with that 38-year-old, headstrong candidate?

“What do you do with a 38-year-old potential employee who was unemployed for over a year during the economic crisis, comes across as somewhat headstrong, but scores the highest on an intelligence test out of all the applicants?” we asked ourselves at the beginning of this article. Let’s take a closer look at his hiring process as we wrap up. During the traditional, unstructured interview, this person had to contend with an interviewer who had already raised concerns beforehand about the fact that the candidate had been out of the workforce for over a year. The interviewer was also put off by the candidate’s tone, even though the candidate excelled at giving smart, well-thought-out answers. This is a classic example of the Horn effect.

Added Value of an Intelligence Test

This candidate would have had no chance from the outset if the hiring process had consisted solely of an interview. However, by scoring the highest on the intelligence test, it caught the interviewer’s attention. Various studies show that the reliability and predictive power of intelligence tests are high. The test revealed that this person possesses many cognitive skills, which are very important today and usually provide organizations with economic added value. This person is able to process information quickly and knows how to immediately link it to existing knowledge. The intelligent employee can analyze and solve problems and does not shy away from complexity. This benefits productivity. A complex, dynamic environment where quick adaptation is a requirement calls for an employee with a broad range of cognitive skills. Thanks to the added value of a selection tool such as the intelligence test, this person could be properly assessed and hired as an employee.

Frequently Asked Questions:

  • As an HR manager, how can you strike a balance between structured and unstructured interviews to achieve the best results?
    • Combining both interview methods can be effective by supplementing structured questions with informal conversations, ensuring that both objective criteria and personal insights are taken into account.
  • What specific tools or software can improve the accuracy of the selection process?
    • There are advanced HR software packages available that use AI and data analysis to improve the accuracy and efficiency of the selection process. Examples include applicant tracking systems (ATS) and assessment tools.
  • How can you address potential biases in the selection process, especially when using traditional methods?
    • Implementing training on unbiased hiring, using anonymous resumes, and standardizing interview questions can help minimize bias.

The Recruitment Process in Your Organization

Would you like to review and further refine the recruitment process in your organization? Feel free to contact one of our consultants. They can answer questions about the recruitment process and help you implement it effectively.

body:
A competency is something you bring to the table in terms of knowledge, experience, personality, skills, or communication abilities. Being a leader means that someone is capable of leveraging available opportunities to advance the process and is also willing to continue developing themselves. Competencies can also be focused on specific areas. Consider, for example, competencies focused on education or healthcare.

The Three Pillars of Competencies

Competencies consist of a combination of three core components that together determine how effectively someone can perform:
Component Description Example
Knowledge Facts, information, and understanding Knowledge of project management methodologies
Skills Practical application of knowledge Creating schedules and monitoring deadlines
Attitude Attitude and motivation Proactive and results-oriented thinking

Development of competencies

Every person has talents. The key is to recognize, develop, and utilize them. In addition, education helps develop knowledge, and membership in an organization, a group of friends, family, and other activities helps people learn new skills. It quickly becomes apparent whether someone has leadership qualities, what this might entail, and whether that person is capable of putting those qualities to use. The environment often determines whether an innate leadership quality will become a competency. Much depends on the opportunities and support people receive. This is certainly true in the workplace. The key question is always whether talent is recognized and its development encouraged—or not.

The 70-20-10 Rule for Competency Development

Research shows that competency development is most effective when it follows this breakdown:
70% On-the-job learning: Practical experience, challenging assignments, new projects 20% Social learning: Coaching, mentoring, feedback from colleagues 10% Formal learning: Training sessions, courses, certifications
 

Development Cycle

A development cycle that is clear to everyone can support this process. By identifying a new colleague’s capabilities starting with the introductory interview, you can make the most of them. A good competency model helps build on this foundation. This can be achieved through internal training, by offering specialized courses and programs, but also by giving people opportunities to further develop within the workplace. Within a clear HRM cycle, two things are very important: giving and demonstrating trust, and transparent policies. Employees who feel challenged to grow and supported in that process perform better. It really is that simple.

Step-by-Step Plan for Effective Competency Development

Step Action Result
1. Assessment Identify current competencies Competency profile for each employee
2. Gap Analysis Difference between current and desired levels Identifying development needs
3. Development plan Formulate specific actions and goals Personal Development Plan (PDP)
4. Implementation Carry out development activities Developing new competencies
5. Evaluation Measuring progress and making adjustments Continuous improvement
 

Competency model

The question, of course, is which model works best. Before you start implementing all kinds of models, it might be better to identify everything that is still unknown. A first step could be a workshop with employees, during which they are specifically asked for suggestions for improvement. Two things often derail this process: first, the fact that the boss leads the workshop, and second, PowerPoint presentations. The first makes people hesitant. The second means they’re already bored before the actual work begins. There’s another way, and embracing a new competency model can be the key to that change—provided it isn’t simply imposed, but rather approached collaboratively from the moment it’s brought up. Encouraging one another to keep improving.

Different Types of Competency Models

Organizations can choose from different approaches, depending on their objectives:
Model type Focus Suitable for
Function-oriented Specific skills per role Specialized roles
Organization-focused Core values and culture All employees
Leadership-oriented Management Skills Managers
Behavior-Focused Observable behaviors Performance Management

Success Factors for Competency Management

These elements are crucial for an effective competency system:
Management commitment: Visible support and participation from leadership Clear communication: Transparency regarding goals and expectations Practical application: Directly linked to daily work Continuous evaluation: Regular updates and improvements
 

Stay Curious

If you stand still, you’ll miss the train to the future. New developments are coming at a rapid pace. As a manager, it’s important that you remain curious about innovation. Ask questions, seek answers—where possible, together with your employees and the HRM team.
  1. What would you like to change yourself? What does that require?
  2. How can you gather as much useful information as possible from the team?
  3. What role can each employee play in a potential change?
Those who continue to develop themselves and dare to embrace new competencies will gain a firm grasp on these kinds of processes and will benefit greatly from them. It makes the work a lot easier and more enjoyable for both you and your team.

Future-Oriented Skills

The job market is changing rapidly. These skills are becoming increasingly important:

Top 5 future-oriented skills:

1. Digital literacy: Working with new technologies and data 2. Ability to learn: Quickly acquiring new knowledge and skills 3. Emotional intelligence: Understanding your own and others’ emotions 4. Critical thinking: Analyzing information and making informed decisions 5. Flexibility: Adapting to changing circumstances

Frequently Asked Questions About Competencies

How often should a competency profile be updated? Competency profiles should be reviewed annually, with interim updates as needed in response to job changes and new industry developments.
What if an employee shows no interest in competency development? Investigate the cause: lack of time, unclear added value, or the wrong approach. Link development to personal goals and career aspirations.
How do you measure the ROI of competency development? Monitor performance indicators such as productivity, quality, employee satisfaction, and career progression. Compare these metrics before and after development interventions.
```
