body:
Red represents strength, blue represents calm, and yellow represents creativity. The Caluwé test translates this symbolism into a powerful tool that maps out your personality and work style. This test uses six different colors to determine how you think, act, and collaborate within organizations.

Imagine that your colleague always starts new projects full of energy (yellow thinking), while you prefer to work out all the details first before you begin (blue thinking). These differences often cause friction, but the Caluwé Colors Test shows that you complement each other perfectly. By knowing your personality color, you’ll not only understand yourself better but also learn how to collaborate most effectively with others.

What you’ll learn in this article

  • The six colors and what they mean for your personality
  • How the test works and what it measures
  • Practical applications in work and personal life
  • Differences from other personality tests
  • Tips for getting the most out of your color profile
 

What exactly is the Caluwé color model?

Professor Léon de Caluwé developed this test to measure how people think about change and collaboration. The test is based on the belief that every person has one or two dominant “thinking patterns,” which can be translated into colors.

The test doesn’t measure what you can do or what you know. It examines how your brain processes information and makes decisions. For example, do you think logically first (blue), or do you jump right in (red)? This preference determines your color profile.

What makes this method unique is that there are no right or wrong answers. Each color has valuable qualities that organizations and teams need. A successful team combines different colors to effectively address all aspects of a project.

The test was developed based on years of research into change processes in companies. De Caluwé discovered that conflicts often arise because people put on different “lenses” when looking at problems. By making these lenses visible through colors, teams can collaborate more effectively.

Discover our color test

The six colors explained

 

Blue Thinking

People with a blue thinking style value structure and logic. You analyze thoroughly before making decisions. Details are important to you, and you want to understand how systems work.

A blue thinker first examines all available data. You ask critical questions and look for proven methods. In meetings, you’re the one who asks, “Have we researched this?” or “What are the risks?”

This thorough approach has major advantages. Projects you lead usually have a solid foundation. You prevent costly mistakes by thinking things through in advance. Colleagues appreciate your reliability and expertise.

The downside is that you sometimes wait too long to take action. While you’re still researching, the opportunity may have already passed. Other colors can help you act more quickly when the situation calls for it.

Yellow Thinking

Yellow thinking stands for creativity and innovation. You see opportunities everywhere and enjoy coming up with new solutions. Brainstorming energizes you, and you’re willing to take risks to achieve a breakthrough.

As a yellow thinker, you’re often the first to ask, “Why don’t we do it differently?” You dislike routines and are constantly looking for ways to improve. You inspire others with your enthusiasm for new ideas.

This trait makes you valuable in situations that require change. You see opportunities that others miss and aren’t afraid to experiment. Startups and innovation projects desperately need your way of thinking.

The challenge for yellow thinkers is completing projects. You quickly get excited about the next idea before the current one is finished. Collaborating with blue or green thinkers helps you actually carry out your ideas.

Red Thinking

Red stands for action and results. You tackle problems head-on and prefer concrete solutions. Long discussions frustrate you because you want to see progress.

Red thinkers are natural leaders in crisis situations. You make decisions quickly and motivate others to take action. “Let’s just do it” is your motto. This attitude ensures that projects actually get completed.

Your strength lies in turning plans into results. While others are still talking, you’ve already gotten started. This pragmatic approach often yields quick successes.

The risk is that you’ll act too quickly without fully considering all the consequences. Collaborating with blue thinkers helps you avoid overlooking important details. Thorough preparation prevents you from wasting time later on solving avoidable problems.

Green Thinking

Green thinking focuses on people and collaboration. You pay attention to the team’s atmosphere and make sure everyone feels heard. Harmony and consensus are important to you.

As a green thinker, you see the person behind the employee. You understand that good results come only when people feel engaged. In conflicts, you look for solutions that are acceptable to everyone.

This people-oriented approach builds strong teams. Your colleagues feel safe to make mistakes and share ideas. This leads to greater creativity and engagement within the organization.

The downside is that you sometimes compromise too much. Not every situation allows for endless discussions about everyone’s opinion. Learning from “red thinkers” helps you make difficult decisions when necessary.

White Thinking

White thinking stands for neutrality and a broad perspective. You view situations from a bird’s-eye view and help others see different perspectives. Objectivity is your strength.

White thinkers are natural coaches and advisors. You ask the right questions, enabling others to arrive at insights on their own. In complex situations, you help bring structure to the process without taking sides.

This skill makes you valuable in change processes. You can weigh different interests against one another without becoming emotionally involved. Teams rely on your objectivity to make better decisions.

The downside is that you sometimes come across as too distant. People also want to know what your own opinion is. Learning to take a stand at the right moment strengthens your influence.

Pessimistic Thinking

Pessimistic thinking analyzes what could go wrong. You spot risks and problems before others notice them. This critical perspective protects organizations from costly mistakes.

Pessimists ask the tough questions that others prefer to avoid. “What happens if this fails?” or “Have we really thought this through?” Your skepticism leads to better decisions.

This trait is indispensable for important projects. You prevent teams from sailing blindly on a wave of optimism. By identifying problems early on, solutions can be devised before it’s too late.

The challenge is not just to point out problems, but also to contribute to finding solutions. Pure criticism without alternatives demotivates teams. Combine your realism with constructive suggestions.

Discover our color test

How does the color test work?

The test consists of various statements, and you’ll be asked to indicate to what extent you agree with each one. There are no time limits, because the test measures your natural preference, not your speed.

A typical question is: “When solving problems, I start by gathering all available information.” You indicate whether this is completely true, somewhat true, or doesn’t apply to you at all.

The questions are designed to measure your automatic responses. It’s not about what you think is right, but about what you do spontaneously. That’s why honesty is crucial for a reliable result.

After completing the test, you’ll receive a color profile. This shows your primary color (usually 30–40% of your profile) and your secondary colors. Most people have two dominant colors that together define their work style.

Discover our color test

Practical Application

 

Working in a team

Teams work better when they understand their color distribution. A project team consisting solely of yellow thinkers generates many ideas but achieves little. A team consisting solely of blue thinkers analyzes thoroughly but lacks creativity.

The ideal composition combines different colors: yellow for innovation, blue for analysis, red for execution, and green for collaboration. Each team member contributes based on their strengths.

Conflicts often arise from color differences. The yellow thinker wants to experiment, while the blue thinker wants more research. By recognizing this as a color difference rather than a personal conflict, teams can discuss issues more constructively.

Project leaders can assign tasks based on color preferences. Let the blue thinker conduct the risk analysis and the red thinker oversee the schedule. This improves both quality and satisfaction.

Leadership Style

Your color profile determines your natural leadership style. Red leaders make quick decisions and expect immediate results. Green leaders involve everyone in decisions and ensure consensus.

Both styles have their place, depending on the situation. In crisis situations, red leadership works better; during complex changes, green leadership is more effective. By knowing your profile, you can consciously switch between styles.

Also learn from other colors. A natural red leader can learn to put on the green glasses sometimes. Involve your team more in decisions when support is important. This increases your effectiveness as a leader.

Guiding Personal Development

The test reveals where your natural talents lie, but also where you can grow. Perhaps you’re strong in analysis (blue), but you can learn to act more quickly (red).

Development doesn’t mean changing your personality. It’s about expanding your repertoire. Stay true to your strong colors, but also practice other patterns for situations that call for them.

Consciously choose situations that challenge your weaker colors. As a blue thinker, occasionally participate in brainstorming sessions (yellow). As a yellow thinker, push yourself to see plans through to completion (red). This practice will make you more versatile.

Making Career Choices

Different professions suit different color profiles. Financial analysts often have a lot of blue, creative directors a lot of yellow, and project managers a lot of red. But these aren’t hard and fast rules.

Look at the core tasks of a position and compare them to your profile. Does the job require a lot of creativity while you’re primarily analytical? Then the work will be more exhausting than if it matched your profile.

Look for roles that leverage your strong colors but also challenge your weaker ones. This fosters growth without burnout. A job that’s a perfect fit for you can become boring after a while.

Discover our color test

Differences from Other Personality Tests

The Caluwé Colors Test distinguishes itself from tests like the MBTI or DISC through its focus on change and collaboration. While the MBTI measures personality types, the Colors Test examines thought patterns within organizations.

DISC measures behavior in social situations. The color test goes deeper by examining how you process information and make decisions. This makes it more specifically applicable to work-related situations.

Another difference is flexibility. MBTI is based on fixed personality types. The color test recognizes that people can develop different patterns. Your profile can change through training and experience.

The test is also less categorical. Instead of placing you in a single box, you receive percentages for each color. This provides a more nuanced picture of your personality.

Discover our color test

Scientific Basis and Reliability

Professor de Caluwé based his theory on extensive research into change processes in organizations. He analyzed hundreds of cases to identify patterns in how people respond to change.

The test has been validated across various cultures and organizations. Studies show that the results are stable over time, yet sensitive enough to measure development.

Universities use the test in their management programs. Major consulting firms apply it in organizational development. This widespread acceptance demonstrates its scientific rigor.

A word of caution: no personality test can perfectly predict behavior. The color test provides insights, not absolute truths. Use the results as a starting point for development, not as an unchangeable judgment.

Discover our color test

Common Mistakes and Misconceptions

 

“My color determines what I’m capable of”

This is a dangerous misconception. Your color profile reveals your preferences, not your limitations. A blue thinker can learn to be more creative, and a yellow thinker can become more structured.

“I need to improve my weak colors”

Development doesn’t mean eliminating weaknesses. Focus first on further developing your strong colors. These give you the most return and energy.

"All yellow thinkers are the same"

There is enormous variation within each color. Two yellow thinkers can be very different. The test provides general guidelines, not a detailed portrait.

"The test tells me what kind of work I should do"

The test provides guidance, not rules. Successful people in every role have different color profiles. Much depends on how you apply your colors.

Discover our color test

Making the Most of Your Color Profile

Start by accepting your natural profile. Don’t fight your dominant colors—learn to use them consciously. Know when you need analytical blue and when action-oriented red works better.

Develop an awareness of situations that require different colors. An important presentation might call for more red (decisiveness) even if you’re naturally green (consensus-oriented). Practice this flexibility.

Seek out complementary partners. If you’re strong in yellow (creativity), work with people who excel at blue (analysis) or red (execution). This will increase your collective effectiveness.

Use the language of colors to communicate more effectively. Instead of saying, “You’re too slow,” say, “This calls for more red thinking.” This makes feedback less personal and more constructive.

The Caluwé Colors test offers a powerful way to better understand yourself and others. By knowing your profile, you can make more conscious choices in your work and collaborations. The secret lies not in having the “right” colors, but in cleverly combining different thinking patterns.

The benefit of this insight extends beyond just work. In personal relationships, it helps you understand why people react differently. A red person wants to act immediately, while a green person wants to talk first. Both approaches have value.

By appreciating and combining different colors, we create stronger teams and achieve better results. The test shows that diversity in ways of thinking is an asset, not a problem to be solved.

Discover our color test

Frequently Asked Questions

 

Can my color profile change over time?

Yes, your profile can gradually shift through experience and conscious development. Your dominant colors usually remain stable, but the proportions may change. Retaking the test every few years can provide new insights.

Are some colors better than others?

No, every color has unique value. Successful organizations need all colors. It’s not about better or worse, but about the right mindset for the right situation.

How long does the test take?

The average test time is between 15 and 30 minutes. There is no time limit, so take your time to answer honestly. Rushed answers lead to less reliable results.

Can I use the test for recruitment?

Yes, but use it as part of a broader selection process. The test reveals thinking preferences, not competencies or experience. Combine the results with other selection methods to get a complete picture.

Discover your personality now with our personality test and learn how to use your unique thinking patterns to achieve greater success in work and life.

Discover our color test

Competencies in Education

The new competency requirements replace those from 2006. That was the year the Act on Professions in Education (the BIO Act) went into effect. Substantive improvements have been made, making the competency requirements unambiguous, concrete, and more easily assessable. The seven competencies are grouped under the main themes: subject-specific knowledge, subject-specific pedagogy, and general pedagogy. This has made them more recognizable. The competency requirements focus on student learning and the core of the teaching profession. Through their knowledge and skills related to these competencies, teachers demonstrate that they can perform their work as educators—and as members of the professional educational community they form together with their colleagues—in a professionally effective and responsible manner. Competencies and the development of teachers’ competencies are crucial to the quality of education. Developing competencies is only possible if you know where you stand; that is why we have developed a questionnaire that provides insight into this. Read more about the SBL competencies in education in our knowledge center.

Personality Questionnaire

Hrmforce Education has adapted the online personality questionnaire into a specific questionnaire with a report on the following seven educational competencies:
  1. Interpersonal Competence
  2. Pedagogical competence
  3. Subject-matter and pedagogical competence
  4. Organizational Competence
  5. Competent in collaborating with colleagues
  6. Competent in collaborating with the community
  7. Competent in reflection and professional development
After this assessment, you will have a clear picture of both the strengths and areas for development, both individually and within the team. In addition, gaining insight into these competencies contributes to the quality of the school’s education: fewer mismatches between individuals and their roles, greater satisfaction among the teaching staff, and increased motivation for teachers to continue their professional development. Motivated and satisfied teachers have a positive impact on students’ motivation and performance! In addition to the online assessment, we also offer supplementary tools such as in-depth interviews, role-playing exercises, and (nonverbal) assessments. Ask one of our consultants about the options.  

Employee Participation Training

This equips members with knowledge of all aspects of employee participation and fosters a valuable partner for the competent authority, where support for educational development is central. More information about the Employee Participation Training can be found here.

This is according to the ruling of the National Dispute Resolution Committee for Employee Participation on February 25, 2019. The ruling means that MR members who wish to purchase this service do not need to ask their board for permission. Cost Savings Currently, many schools still use service packages individually from different providers. With multiple schools in a foundation, the costs of this are often unnecessarily high. Hrmforce Education is the only provider in the Netherlands to offer this service at the supra-school level.  The benefits then apply to all affiliated schools and school boards. body:
You want to understand people better, help teams work together, and foster leadership. Many organizations turn to the MBTI for this. The question is what this test really tells you and where its limitations lie in HR decision-making.

In short

  • The MBTI is popular as a conversation starter in teams and coaching
  • The model works with preferences and types, not with continuous scores on a scale
  • MBTI is not a solid basis for selection and evaluation
  • When retaken, people’s results often vary
  • For data-driven HR, a Big Five-style approach is more suitable

 

What is MBTI and where does it come from?

MBTI stands for Myers-Briggs Type Indicator. It is a questionnaire that classifies you into one of sixteen “types.” These types are derived from four pairs of preferences:
  • sensing versus intuition
  • extraversion versus introversion
  • thinking versus feeling
  • and judging versus perceiving.
Its roots lie with Carl Jung . In 1921, Jung described psychological preferences as a way to explain differences between people. The MBTI is not a direct copy of Jung’s work. It is a later adaptation into a practical tool, developed by Katharine Cook Briggs and her daughter Isabel Briggs Myers. They wanted a model that would help people articulate differences in preference, particularly in collaboration and decision-making. Source: Wikipedia Important detail: The MBTI is a self-report assessment. You choose the option that best fits you each time. The result therefore says more about how you see yourself and how you perceive your preferences. That makes it useful for self-reflection. It makes it less suitable for making firm decisions, because self-image, context, and the moment in time all play a role.

What exactly does the MBTI measure?

The MBTI measures preferences. Think about where your attention often goes, how you like to process information, and how you usually make choices. It does not measure skills, performance, or any “truth” about behavior. In the workplace, there’s often a difference between preferences and behavior. Someone can be an introvert and still give many presentations. That might be due to experience, job requirements, or training. The MBTI can help start that conversation. The MBTI cannot prove that someone is or isn’t suitable based on this alone.

Why is the MBTI so popular in organizations?

The MBTI provides recognition and a common language. Teams recognize patterns and find it easier to discuss communication, collaboration, and irritations. The labels serve as a framework. This helps during team-building days, onboarding, or coaching. There’s also a risk in that success. Labels stick. Then you get statements like, “You’re just a P, so planning doesn’t work for you.” This locks behavior into place, even though behavior can often be developed in practice.

How reliable is the MBTI if you take it again?

With the MBTI, you often see shifts when someone takes the questionnaire again later. This is partly due to the structure involving preference pairs. Many people don’t fall on one extreme or the other. In such cases, even a small shift in answers can result in a different label. This is an important consideration for HR. If a result changes, you should be cautious about drawing conclusions. Therefore, use the MBTI as a starting point for discussion. Do not use it as a decision-making rule.

Can you use the MBTI for selection or evaluation?

For recruitment, promotion, or performance evaluation, the MBTI is a weak foundation. It does not provide a reliable prediction of job performance. Nor does it offer a stable comparison between candidates, because the model does not use a scale that allows you to accurately place someone’s score within a relevant normative group. There’s another factor to consider. In recruitment, you want to be able to explain why you’re making a choice. This works better with tools explicitly designed for HR decisions. Then you can focus on competencies, behavior, and potential for development.

What often goes wrong with the MBTI in HR?

Here are four common mistakes I often see.
  • The type becomes a label instead of a conversation starter
  • It’s used as proof, when it’s really meant to facilitate reflection
  • Teams start making excuses instead of agreeing on what they’ll do differently
  • No connection is made to observable behavior in the workplace

 

MBTI versus the Big Five. Why HR Often Shifts Its Focus

Big Five models describe personality as dimensions. For example, you score higher or lower on extraversion, conscientiousness, and emotional stability. This aligns better with how personality is typically approached in research. You don’t get an “on/off” label, but a nuanced profile. This is useful for HR because it makes it easier to make the connection to behavior and competencies. You can also make better comparisons within a relevant reference group, provided the tool uses norm groups.

How can you use the MBTI effectively?

Use the MBTI in situations where you primarily want to focus on language and reflection. Think of team communication, collaboration, and coaching. Make it practical by establishing agreements on behavior. What will you do differently in meetings? Who will take on which role? How will you give feedback in a way that resonates? If you want to make decisions regarding hiring, promotion, or development, you’ll need assessment tools explicitly designed for those purposes. In that case, you’ll want to consider not only personality but also motivation, cognitive ability, and real-world feedback.

The connection with hrmforce

At hrmforce, it’s all about behavioral insights that you can translate into actions in recruitment and development. You combine information from assessments and feedback so you don’t rely on a single label. This provides a solid foundation for discussions with candidates, employees, and managers. MBTI can serve as a starting point for establishing a common language within a team. For HR decisions, however, you’ll want to take a broader view. Consider personality data with reference groups, supplemented by 360-degree feedback and competency assessments. This gives you a well-founded picture that you can link to job requirements and development steps.

FAQ

Is the MBTI suitable for recruitment? No. It’s best not to use the MBTI for recruitment, promotion, or performance evaluations. It is primarily intended for self-insight and discussion. Why does my type change when I retake the MBTI? Many people fall around the middle of a preference pair. Small differences in answers, context, or self-perception can then lead to a different label. Does that mean the MBTI is worthless? No. In team development, it can help make differences open to discussion. It only becomes a problem when you use it as a decision-making rule. What’s a better alternative for HR decisions? Look for tools that work with dimensions and normative groups, and combine that with feedback and performance data. Can the MBTI help with leadership? It can help as a reflection tool. It says little about leadership success, because preference isn’t the same as leadership behavior. How do I prevent pigeonholing in a team? Link every result to behavior. Agree on what you do want to see in collaboration. Repeat that in evaluations and feedback.

Here’s how to approach it

If you want to use the MBTI in HR, stick to reflection and team communication. If you want to make decisions about hiring, career development, or role fit, use assessments designed for HR decisions and combine multiple data sources. Three steps you can take today. Choose one collaboration theme for your team, translate that into two concrete behavioral agreements, and after four weeks, use brief feedback to assess what has changed.
title: MBTI in HR. What does it measure—and what doesn't it measure?

body:
In the modern workplace, employees continue to learn and develop—both professionally and personally, with a focus on their behavior and competencies. We were already aware of the importance of this, and the COVID-19 crisis has significantly reinforced this understanding. Yet implementation often stalls when it comes to putting these ideas into practice on the job. This is despite the fact that encouraging learning and development—or even behavioral change—among employees is entirely possible. We’ve listed seven closely interrelated success factors.

From Wanting to Actually Doing

Many employers and employees are now aware of the benefits. When employees remain actively engaged in learning and their professional development, it leads to greater job satisfaction, job security, and career opportunities. Numerous studies also show that these employees are more loyal, motivated, and productive. Moreover, it is a key prerequisite for, for example, increasing sustainable employability. Research from Tilburg University also shows that it encourages older employees to continue working longer in a way that is enjoyable for them. Awareness of the benefits and necessity has grown significantly since the COVID-19 crisis, including among employers. Worldwide, a substantial majority of CEOs (70 percent) now recognize the value of lifelong learning. Before the COVID-19 crisis, this figure was alarmingly low (29 percent), as shown by this international study. So the willingness is there, but creating a “learning organization” does not always prove easy in practice. Often, high workloads act as a barrier, preventing employees from “ever getting around to” a learning program, or they are not sufficiently encouraged and supported to continue developing. How can this be achieved? These success factors can provide immediate help.

  1. Enhance and facilitate self-direction

In practice, fostering self-direction among employees has proven to be the crucial factor for companies that have successfully become learning organizations. However, this arises from an interaction between employer and employee. It’s not just a matter of placing responsibility on employees, but also of effectively facilitating them. This often begins with raising awareness, establishing a good cycle of dialogue, and ensuring accessible and appropriate development opportunities. So it takes more than just launching an “Online Academy.” Ensure clear awareness and communication from the employees’ perspective. What’s in it for them? Consider not only their current role but also career advancement opportunities, job satisfaction, or more personal motivations and drivers. This shifts the perception of learning and development from a sense of “having to” to a desire to do so.

  1. Strengthen self-awareness

Employers can effectively facilitate employees’ awareness and self-direction with practical, accessible tools. In addition to providing greater self-awareness of their current situation, online tools can, for example, offer a clearer picture of an employee’s long-term development path—and what’s needed to get there. Most organizations now use online assessments to support the development needs of employees or teams.

  1. Consider 360-Degree Feedback

A concrete example of a powerful tool for increasing self-awareness is leveraging 360-Degree Feedback. After all, good feedback is extremely valuable for greater self-awareness and employee development. It’s not just their own insights that matter, but also those of relevant people in their environment. Think of colleagues, a manager, or, for example, (internal) clients. By drawing more broadly on employees’ professional circles, performance and development opportunities come into focus in a meaningful and accessible way. The “360 degrees” represent the perspectives from which feedback is received regarding, for example, skills, personality, abilities, and motivation. The questionnaires can be tailored to different competency levels and are often used to foster a productive dialogue between employees and managers or to facilitate a modern, customized performance review cycle.

  1. Watch out for fear of failure!

When organizational changes require different learning or development behaviors, it’s important to be aware of a major pitfall. It lies within our brains. At first, changes often immediately encounter resistance in people. This is because, when we experience change, the same parts of our brain are activated as when we think about death. “A change—even a positive one—is primarily viewed by our brains as a loss. That triggers thoughts of mortality, because death is the ultimate loss,” says American researcher Professor James R. Bailey of George Washington University. “When thoughts of death are subconsciously triggered, a whole series of defense mechanisms kicks in to protect our identity, routines, and competencies.” But you can also leverage these principles, for example, by informing and preparing employees in a timely manner. This underscores the importance of good communication—in this case, to allow people to acclimate safely first. Then the brain can adapt flexibly, because, in fact, the brain is constantly changing. The key is to influence this process positively. This can be achieved by connecting changes to employees’ deepest essence and motivations (the “WHY” from Simon Sinek’s Golden Circle model). Beyond WHAT someone does and HOW they do it, what ultimately matters most is WHY someone truly does something. With that awareness, people can consciously work on their development, and their brain structure is positively influenced. HR can facilitate this by seeking methods that help employees and managers consciously reflect on this core question.

  1. Adapt to the Different Types of Conversations

To facilitate effective conversations between employees and managers during times of change or throughout learning and development processes, it’s important to keep the various conversation cycles in mind. After all, in a complete conversation cycle, they engage in different types of conversations (such as Bila+ and development or annual reviews), each at different times and with a different purpose. A (digital) development cycle can facilitate individual or team development. The starting point is usually the job classification system and the job profiles within an organization. The principles of the conversation cycle are built around these. Objectively designed questionnaires can help bring the conversations up to the right level quickly and in a well-founded manner. Read more about the different feedback cycles here.

  1. Provide Appropriate Learning Opportunities

It may sound logical at first, but you must also provide appropriate learning opportunities when learning and development actually need to be facilitated. Across an entire organization, this often involves a diverse range of options, tailored to each target group and to what individual employees want to learn. After all, different people learn in different ways. Not every learning path is suitable for everyone. Therefore, give careful consideration to the learning methods and formats offered. In some cases, an accessible e-learning course may suffice, while in other situations, frontline workers may prefer to learn together in a classroom setting. Discuss this and tailor the learning offerings carefully to the various learning needs. In an online learning environment, assessments can also be offered to increase self-awareness and self-direction. Don’t forget the potential of internal knowledge sharing among colleagues. Don’t underestimate how much knowledge, experience, and expertise exists within your organization. This can be shared through, for example, internal webinars, training sessions, or knowledge-sharing sessions. Or choose a format that addresses frequently asked questions. This can relate to learning and development or simply to the substantive knowledge and experience available internally.

  1. Give employees a meaningful purpose

In a thriving “learning organization,” many of the success factors just mentioned—if done right—are closely intertwined. After all, there can be no self-direction without self-awareness. And there can be no enriching learning journey without appropriate learning opportunities. An important underlying success factor is that employees are given a clear goal to work toward. To achieve this, align the organization’s goal with an employee’s professional—and ideally also personal—goals. Often, the organization’s goal and strategy are clear, but sometimes they need to be better communicated to employees. Employees themselves are often initially a bit unsure about their own goals. To address this, assess the extent to which their talents, motivations, and interests can be aligned with the goals of the organization or their team. Here, too, 360-Degree Feedback can likely be very useful.
title: 7 Tips for Encouraging Employee Learning and Development

For talent development in education.

Hrmforce Education offers an online tool for structured HR policy. This reduces the risk of a mismatch between employees and their roles and increases job satisfaction—and, consequently, performance. A motivated and satisfied teacher has a positive impact on students’ motivation and performance. Explore the following options: - Choosing a Field of Study - Selection of Teachers and School Leaders - Matching Career Changers - Competency Framework with 360-Degree Feedback - Employee Participation

Choosing a Field of Study

A career choice test is a test used to help students choose their next educational path or career. The test evaluates the student’s interests, skills, and personality and then provides recommendations on which programs are the best fit for them. There are various types of college selection tests available, such as online tests, consultations with a career counselor, and personality tests.

Selection of Teachers and School Leaders

Selecting the right teacher can be very challenging. Sometimes the interview goes very well, but the teacher falls short in practice—or vice versa. By using multiple tools to gather data, the risk of a mismatch is significantly reduced. Using objective tests to measure competencies and matching them to a competency profile you’ve created in advance further minimizes the chance of a mismatch. That’s why hrmforce allows you to use multiple tools (tests, reference checks, structured interview questions) simultaneously without having to engage an assessment firm. This saves a lot of time—and therefore money!

Matching Career Changers

There is a high demand for teachers in primary and secondary education. One way to address this shortage is by recruiting and selecting career changers in education. To assess candidates’ competencies, the qualification requirements have been translated into personality questionnaires. By assessing a candidate’s personality, you gain valuable insight into their strengths and areas for improvement. This allows you to use the questionnaire to select career changers based on their teaching qualities. This reduces mismatches and ensures you select only those with the potential to become effective teachers. It is also possible to use these questionnaires to design a coaching program that helps develop any missing qualities.

Competency-Based Assessment with 360-Degree Feedback

Competencies and the development of teachers’ competencies are crucial to the quality of education. Hrmforce Education has adapted the online personality questionnaire into a specific questionnaire that provides reports on the following seven teaching competencies:

  1. Interpersonal Competence
  2. Pedagogical competence
  3. Subject-matter and pedagogical competence
  4. Organizational competence
  5. Competent in collaborating with colleagues
  6. Competent in collaborating with the community
  7. Competent in reflection and professional development

This assessment provides a clear picture of both strong competencies and areas for development, both individually and within the team. In addition, providing insight into these competencies contributes to the quality of the school’s education: fewer mismatches between individuals and their roles, greater satisfaction among the teaching staff, and increased motivation for teachers to continue their professional development. Motivated and satisfied teachers have a positive influence on students’ motivation and performance.

Employee Participation Training

In addition to the personality questionnaire, we have also developed training programs specifically for the education sector. Drawing on our knowledge and experience in the field of staff participation, we create a customized training program for each school or educational institution that effectively contributes to the development of a professional staff participation body within the organization. This equips members with knowledge of all aspects of employee participation and establishes a valuable partner for the competent authority, where support for educational development is central.

body:
Screening employees means verifying whether a job applicant is trustworthy and suitable for a position. When people hear the word “screening,” they often immediately think of an (online) background check on the person in question. But did you know that other screening methods are much more valuable? With assessments, you can determine not only whether someone is trustworthy, but also whether their talents and personality are a good fit for your organization.

What you’ll learn in this article

  • Why screening is more than just a background check.
  • How assessments work as a screening tool.
  • What other screening methods are available.
  • Practical tips for a smart screening process.

Why screening candidates is becoming increasingly important

The job market is changing. Candidates often present themselves better on paper than in practice. In addition, the risks are increasing: think of confidential data, financial responsibility, or customer contact. A wrong choice costs not only money, but also energy and reputation. Screening helps prevent this by evaluating facts, skills, and behavior.

Screening through assessments

An assessment is a test or questionnaire that objectively measures how someone scores on competencies, personality, and cognitive skills. While a Certificate of Good Conduct (VOG) only indicates whether someone has committed any criminal offenses, an assessment provides insight into future performance and behavioral tendencies.

Examples of assessments

Hrmforce offers various screening modules that you can use during recruitment and selection: → Personality questionnaires : measure behavior, motivations, and work style. These help you determine whether someone is a good fit for your company culture. → Aptitude tests : provide insight into analytical ability, problem-solving skills, and learning ability. → Integrity tests : focus on reliability, sense of ethics, and the risk of inappropriate behavior. → 360-degree feedback : provides a picture of how others perceive someone in practice. By combining these assessments, you gain a comprehensive and objective picture of the candidate, significantly increasing the likelihood of a good match .

Other Forms of Employee Screening

In addition to assessments, there are traditional forms of screening. These remain valuable but have limitations.
  • Reference check: useful for supplementary information, but often subjective.
  • Degree and resume verification: useful for factual verification, but says nothing about behavior.
  • Certificate of Good Conduct (VOG): an official document, but only reflects past behavior, not future risk.
  • Social media check: provides insight into behavior, but carries legal risks.
  • Credit check: relevant for financial positions, but privacy-sensitive.

Legal Rules for Employee Screening

The GDPR (privacy legislation) always applies to screening. This means:
  1. Screening should only be conducted if it is relevant to the position.
  2. Inform the candidate and request consent.
  3. Process results securely and delete them in a timely manner.
Assessments offer an advantage here: they are objective, transparent, and less privacy-sensitive than, for example, a credit check.

Smart Candidate Screening in 2026

A smart approach combines traditional checks with modern assessments. This gives you certainty about both reliability and talent. Tips: → Start with a job profile : determine which competencies and behavioral traits are required. → Choose appropriate assessments : for example, an aptitude test for an analytical role. → Combine checks : A Certificate of Good Conduct (VOG) plus an assessment provides a broader picture than a single method. → Work with a screening partner : such as hrmforce, which offers proven tools and guidance.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are assessments mandatory during screening? No, but they offer objective insights that traditional checks do not provide. How long does an assessment take? From 20 minutes (aptitude test) to several hours for comprehensive personality assessments. Are assessments GDPR-compliant? Yes, provided you process the results securely and use them only for the specific hiring process. What is the average cost of assessments? It depends on the depth: ranging from a few dozen euros per test to packages for complete selection processes.

Conclusion: Screening = Certainty and Looking Ahead

Screening employees in 2026 isn’t just about the past—it’s primarily about future behavior and performance. With assessments, you can identify who truly fits your organization and avoid making the wrong choices. Would you like to know how Hrmforce assessments can help you evaluate candidates more effectively? Request a free demo, check out all our assessments, or visit our matching & selection page.
title: Screening Employees? Here’s How to Do It the Smart Way

body:
Christmas is almost here: a great time for organizations to look back on the past year and make plans for 2023. Many employees also use their days off around Christmas to reflect on their work. Are they still in the right role? As an employer or HR manager, it’s wise to address this now—so that your team remains motivated to work for you in the new year. Take a moment to consider: what was the situation like for your employees around this time last year? You might find it hard to imagine now, but in December 2021, the Netherlands was in lockdown. A significant portion of the workforce was working daily from their attic rooms or at their kitchen tables. Teachers spent months teaching via Teams or Zoom—and not always willingly. Healthcare professionals, security guards, and other essential workers who did have to leave the house did so after taking the necessary precautions. Their workdays were more stressful, and they faced a higher risk of contracting the coronavirus. At the slightest cough, they, too, had to stay home.  

Many are still uncertain

Although the days of lockdowns and face masks seem to be behind us, thankfully, the aftereffects of the COVID-19 crisis on the job market are still very much evident. The pandemic caused many people to reflect: Where am I actually headed in life? Am I still in the right place? Does my job make me happy? This led to career doubts among about 30 percent of employees, NU.nl reported. Such career doubts are resurfacing for many people as the end of the year approaches. The dark days around Christmas encourage reflection. Of course, as an employer, you want to prevent your employees from returning after the holidays to announce that they’re leaving. But how do you go about it? Good news: you can take action right now.  

Those on the Brink

Let’s first take a closer look at those who are having second thoughts. Not all of them will simply quit their jobs, but that doesn’t mean you can rest easy. An international trend seems to have made its way into the Dutch labor market: “quiet quitting.” Have you noticed that your employees haven’t been very eager to do more than the bare minimum lately? If so, they’ve become “quiet quitters.” The term first appeared in a TikTok video that received nearly 500,000 likes and was shared more than 40,000 times. “Quiet quitting” means doing only what’s strictly necessary at work. So these employees do remain on the payroll and perform the tasks outlined in their job descriptions, but they’ll never go the extra mile. At five o’clock sharp, they shut down their work laptop. They don’t work overtime, don’t assist with colleagues’ projects, and organizing the company outing? No way. In short: they show up physically, but mentally they’ve checked out. Interestingly, “quiet quitting” occurs across different generations. Some are older employees who are simply biding their time until retirement. Another group of “quitters” consists of younger employees. Generation Z in particular—those born in 1997 or later—values a good work-life balance. They’re not willing to go to the same lengths for an employer as the generation before them, the millennials.  

Don’t Judge

As an employer or HR manager, the term “quiet quitter” probably sounds like a nightmare scenario to you. Experts say you shouldn’t judge this behavior, but rather see it as a warning sign. After all: what are the working conditions causing employees to mentally disengage? And what role do you play in this as an employer? It’s important to understand what drives people to become “quiet quitters.” It has everything to do with high work pressure—caused by the historic labor shortage. Turnover is particularly high in healthcare and education. Hybrid work is also cited as a cause. As a result, the focus of work has shifted more toward productivity and efficiency, and less toward job satisfaction, loyalty, and team spirit. Yet these are precisely the factors that keep employees engaged and motivated.  

Here’s what you can do

Organizations that manage to retain employees long-term and keep them enthusiastic consciously invest in job satisfaction, encourage employees to relax sufficiently, and ensure autonomy in the workplace. Fortunately, job satisfaction and team spirit are also factors that you, as an employer, can influence! So give your employees a great start to 2023. Organize a generous New Year’s reception if you haven’t already, and go ahead and plan a team outing for the spring. Also, think about how you can pamper employees personally, for example with a “Happy New Year” surprise on their desks. But above all, make sure you pay attention to their work throughout the year. Check in with them regularly, reward them for their efforts, and give them compliments. In short, let them know you’re happy to have them! Of course, employees also bear some responsibility for their own job satisfaction. As media mogul Arianna Huffington wrote in a critical article: “Quiet quitting isn’t just about quitting your job; it’s a step toward quitting life.” It’s a shame, she argues, to stay in a place that doesn’t energize you. Huffington introduces an alternative term, as a counterpoint to “quiet quitting”: “joyful joining.” In other words: joining in with joy.  

New Year’s Meeting

How do you get your people to “joyfully join in” in 2023? The most important thing is to start the conversation early. Ask employees, on a personal level, if they’re still in the right place. Do this in a quiet one-on-one setting: that increases the likelihood that someone will feel safe enough to be open and honest. Also ask employees about their plans for the new year. What would they like to achieve? What tasks or projects do they most enjoy taking on? What knowledge and skills do they want to develop? And are there perhaps things they’d rather do less of—or not at all? Offer to help them shape these ideas together. For example, through a coaching program or a personal development plan.

Assessment as a Tool

Do you want to discover together how an employee can best thrive? Then an assessment is a useful tool. A development assessment is specifically designed for employees who no longer feel they’re in the right place and are looking for something different. You can think of such an assessment as a baseline evaluation. It provides insight into what your employees are capable of, where their talents lie, and in which direction they want to grow. Armed with that knowledge, you’ll be ready for the next step in 2023: working together to find a role within your organization that’s a perfect fit for them. That way, your employee will be sitting under the Christmas tree next year feeling completely satisfied. Want to learn more about assessments? Get in touch! We offer digital assessments at locations throughout the Netherlands. We welcome your employees warmly and give them personalized attention so they feel completely at ease. Check out the Lamark or hrmforce websites to explore the options.
title: From "Quiet Quitting" to "Joyful Joining": Here's How to Make It Happen in 2023

body:
The Good Conversation

To create a more modern feedback cycle, many organizations and HR professionals are encouraging “the good conversation.” No more conversations as “mandatory obligations,” but rather genuine, open (developmental) dialogues between employees and managers. Positive, concrete, and results-oriented to ensure better performance and higher engagement. A key success factor here is to keep in mind the different types of conversations that take place.  

What Is “The Good Conversation” in HRM?

The term “the good conversation” has been used more and more frequently in recent years in the fields of organizational development and HRM. At first glance, it may sound a bit “vague,” but in fact, it refers to a very concrete process. In this process, people in organizations engage in purposeful conversations about their talents and development. Often, this is a dialogue between an employee and a manager, coach, or HR professional. But these conversations can also take place among colleagues. In fact, the “good conversation” (also known as the “continuous dialogue”) is the backbone of the performance review cycle. Traditionally, this cycle was centered around performance reviews and evaluations. That traditional approach is often perceived as uninspiring or even demotivating. As a result, more and more organizations are now striving for a more modern, customized conversation cycle that transforms the counterproductive routine of the traditional conversation cycle into a constructive dialogue. This involves more flexible and accessible conversations that are more tailored to individual needs and based on equality. Such a conversation is primarily conducted collaboratively and at appropriate times. It has a clear focus on goals and making (better) use of talents. And to that end, you determine the specific actions together.  

Characteristics of a Good Discussion

A modern development conversation is primarily about employee development, with personal attention as a key success factor. It’s a two-way process: initiated by both employees and managers. It can take the form of an ongoing dialogue, but the conversations should take place at least several times a year. At least four times a year, but preferably even more often in an accessible manner. This keeps (personal) development and engagement front and center and allows for timely adjustments when needed. In fact, it’s not necessarily about having more conversations, but rather different ones. Not mandatory conversations, but open discussions that truly contribute to improving performance, job satisfaction, and employee engagement. So much for the theory. How do you put this into daily practice within an organization?  

How does this work in practice?

Using a (digital) development cycle, individual and team development can be facilitated through the intended types of conversations. The starting point is usually the job classification system and the job profiles within an organization. The principles of the conversation cycle are built around these. Objectively designed questionnaires can help bring the conversations up to the right level quickly and with solid support. An important consideration is effectively facilitating the various types of discussions that are needed. In addition to in-person meetings, this often involves shorter remote digital interactions. A digital discussion cycle can also serve as a solid foundation for the approach, to which in-person meetings are then added. Also keep in mind the various conversation cycles that are needed: at different times and for different purposes. Consider, for example, these conversation formats and their characteristics:
  • Bila: The daily to-do list with specific work agreements established during a one-on-one meeting. This can take place between a manager and an employee, but also between colleagues. In addition to general notes, it’s helpful to document for each agreement who will carry out what and when.
  • Bila+: For the basic development cycle of (often operational) employees. They and their managers want to be able to initiate these discussions themselves to provide input on topics such as: Work, Learning & Development, Health & Fitness, Collaboration & Leadership, and Family & Social Contacts. With this input, a concrete action list can be established. It is also valuable if the history and progress can be documented immediately.
  • Development Meeting: As part of an agile development cycle, it is helpful to be able to schedule development meetings based on individual needs. For trainees, for example, every two weeks; for a senior employee with extensive experience, perhaps once a year or every six months. Key components of a development meeting include: Education & Training, Documents, Job Profile (hard & soft skills), 360-degree feedback, and the Development Plan (by competency and result area).
  • Annual Review: For a development cycle in which an annual review is conducted to evaluate performance and set development goals. In addition to these components, employee well-being can also be assessed. The performance agreements and competencies can then be assessed separately. Afterward, a single development plan is created. It is beneficial if each annual review can be digitally signed by both the employee and the manager.
  • Annual Cycle: The traditional review cycle consists of a planning, performance, and evaluation meeting. All components from the four cycles just described are included in the Annual Cycle. This can be supplemented with additional open-ended questions for each phase, for both the employee and the manager. In this way, the entire traditional cycle is digitized. As a result, the Annual Cycle becomes a very comprehensive and complete form of evaluation and development.
Streamlining a (digital) meeting cycle that includes one or more of these components requires a robust development platform (such as hrmforce, which supports all the components mentioned). A well-thought-out performance review cycle and an (online) platform that supports it form the foundation for truly effective development discussions.  

From Good to Better Conversations

The actual discussions can then take place in all the different formats that are valuable to employees, managers, and the organization—with the previously mentioned characteristics of a good discussion as essential elements. HRMforce can also assist as a strategic implementation partner in effectively utilizing the right conversation techniques during the actual discussions. In this context, asking follow-up questions is important to elicit the right input and feedback during the conversation. For example, by asking about personality-related topics. How is someone feeling? What gives him or her energy? What, on the other hand, drains their energy? What does someone want to focus more attention on? And consider questions about their current and future role. How is someone currently fulfilling their role? Which talents does someone want to utilize more? What knowledge and skills are needed for that? These types of questions definitely come up when meaningful conversations take place. And above all, make sure to start with open-ended questions, driven by genuine interest and curiosity—without making assumptions or thinking in terms of “right” or “wrong.” Working with the previously mentioned objective questionnaires can make the conversations even more impactful, ensuring that these meaningful conversations continue to improve.
title: That’s how “the good conversation” gets even better!

body:
Many HR teams focus on strategy, roles, and processes, while day-to-day behavior tells a different story. That discrepancy lies in organizational cultures and corporate culture . By making culture measurable, you can gain a better understanding of collaboration, leadership, and employee turnover. Source: wetalent

In short

  • Organizational culture drives daily behavior, decision-making, and collaboration
  • Corporate culture is the visible result of values, norms, and unwritten rules
  • Culture can be measured using targeted questionnaires and behavioral assessments
  • Models are only helpful if you translate them into concrete behavior
  • Differences between the current and desired cultures explain many HR problems
  • Measuring culture makes it possible to discuss it without relying on assumptions

What is organizational culture, and what do we mean by corporate culture?

Organizational culture describes the shared patterns of thought and behavior within an organization. Corporate culture is how those patterns manifest in day-to-day work—how decisions are made, how people deal with mistakes, and how managers provide guidance and feedback. In many organizations, values are displayed on posters or websites. Yet employees experience something different in practice. This discrepancy arises because culture consists primarily of unwritten rules : what is rewarded, what is ignored, and what brings status. This is relevant for HR. Behavior determines performance, collaboration, and engagement. Those who do not measure culture are primarily managing based on assumptions. Source: Sociable

What types of organizational cultures exist?

There are several models for describing organizational cultures. They help identify patterns, not to pigeonhole people. A commonly used distinction looks at the organization’s focus:
  • Internally focused versus externally focused
  • Stability versus change
  • Process-oriented versus results-oriented
These classifications clarify why teams operate differently than intended. For example, an organization may communicate in a results-oriented manner, while its systems primarily reward cautious behavior. It’s important to note that culture is never a single type. You usually see a mix, with variations by team, location, or job category.

What is the difference between organizational culture and work climate?

These terms are often used interchangeably, but they mean different things. Organizational culture is about deeper patterns: norms, beliefs, and unspoken assumptions. Workplace climate describes how employees experience their current work situation: workload, trust, collaboration, and communication. You can have a positive work environment within a culture that is unsustainable in the long term—and vice versa. That’s why it’s important to know what you’re measuring. Work environment surveys provide indicators; culture surveys reveal underlying causes.

How does corporate culture influence behavior and performance?

Culture determines what behavior feels natural. Employees adapt without this being explicitly stated. This is reflected in:
  • How quickly decisions are made
  • Who takes the lead in discussions
  • How safe it feels to discuss mistakes
  • How feedback is given and received
When desired behavior doesn’t align with the culture, tension arises. HR sees this reflected in high turnover, friction within teams, and difficult change processes. Culture often explains why interventions don’t work. Training sessions, new processes, and leadership programs stall when they clash with existing norms.

What cultural models are used in HR?

Models help put culture into words. They are not an end in themselves. A well-known framework is the idea that culture consists of multiple layers: observable behavior and symbols; conscious values; and deeper assumptions that are rarely articulated. It is precisely this last layer that drives behavior. Other models focus on practices. For example, the extent to which an organization is open to feedback, how decisions are made, and how strictly rules are followed. This makes culture more concrete and easier to discuss. The risk with models lies in oversimplification. They only work if you link them to measurable behavior. Source: Beaks

How can you measure organizational culture?

Measuring culture starts with a clear question. Do you want insight into collaboration? Leadership? Change behavior? Or alignment with strategy? Effective culture measurements focus on:
  • Current situation versus desired situation
  • Differences between teams and departments
  • Concrete behaviors rather than abstract values
This can be done using culture questionnaires, pulse surveys, or team analyses. It’s important that employees understand why you’re measuring. Without context, confusion or socially desirable behavior can arise. Measuring alone isn’t enough. Interpretation and discussion determine the value.

What benefits does measuring corporate culture offer HR?

Culture assessments provide HR with a solid foundation for decision-making. You gain insight into patterns that were previously invisible. Specifically, this yields:
  • Informed discussions about collaboration and leadership
  • Targeted development initiatives for each team
  • Fewer assumptions during change initiatives
  • Better alignment between strategy and behavior
For managers, this provides clarity. Not because numbers explain everything, but because they make it possible to discuss behavior without judgment.

How do you use culture data in the HR cycle?

Culture only becomes valuable when you link it to existing HR processes. During onboarding, culture data helps clarify expectations. In leadership development, it shows which behaviors are reinforced or discouraged. In team development, it highlights differences that were previously viewed as personal issues. Culture also plays a role in the performance review cycle. Feedback becomes more focused when it’s clear which behaviors align with the desired way of working.

Why does cultural change fail so often?

Many organizations begin cultural change with communication—new values, slogans, and meetings. However, employees see different behaviors being rewarded every day. Culture only changes when:
  • Managers consistently model exemplary behavior
  • Systems and goals support the desired behavior
  • Teams are given the space to discuss differences
Metrics help keep this in focus. They reveal where behavior deviates from intent.

How do you deal with subcultures within a single organization?

Subcultures are normal. They arise from expertise, team goals, and leadership. Problems only arise when subcultures work against each other. By measuring culture on a team-by-team basis, you can see:
  • Where norms differ
  • Which expectations clash
  • Where collaboration breaks down
This enables targeted interventions without lumping the entire organization together.

Frequently Asked Questions About Organizational Cultures and Corporate Culture

What is organizational culture in simple terms? The shared way in which people think, make decisions, and act within an organization. What is corporate culture? The visible manifestation of organizational culture in daily behavior, communication, and collaboration. Can you really measure culture? Yes, by systematically surveying and comparing behavior, preferences, and perceived norms. Click here for more information . How often should you measure culture? That depends on the goal. Large-scale assessments annually. Shorter pulse surveys more frequently. What is the difference between culture and engagement? Engagement is an outcome. Culture is a cause. Who do you involve in culture assessments? Preferably all employees, with analysis by team or job category. Is cultural change measurable? Yes, by comparing the current situation with the desired situation and repeating this periodically.

How to Start Measuring and Discussing Culture

If you want to leverage organizational cultures and corporate culture strategically within HR, start small and be specific.
  1. Determine which behaviors you want to understand or change
  2. Measure the current and desired situations for each team
  3. Discuss the results without judgment
  4. Link actions to day-to-day work
  5. Repeat the process and track patterns over time
Culture only becomes a tool for change when you make it visible and open to discussion. That starts with measurement. Click here for an organizational culture scan
