body:
The 360-degree feedback method is a powerful tool for better harnessing employees’ potential and improving their performance. Individual performance is assessed in an accessible way. Employees and their managers can then work together to gain a clear understanding of their talents and identify valuable areas for development. This approach motivates employees to realize their potential and increase their contribution to the team. This article outlines the possibilities of 360-degree feedback. This way, you’ll know exactly what the pros and cons are and when it’s best to use this method in a company or organization. In this article:
  • What Is 360-Degree Feedback?
  • Characteristics of 360-degree feedback
  • When should you use the 360-degree feedback method?
  • When is it better not to use the 360-degree feedback method?
  • Using 360-degree feedback with your own competency framework
  • How does 360-degree feedback work in practice?
  • Tools to Simplify the Process
  • What are the benefits of 360-degree feedback?
  • Does the method also have any drawbacks?
  • Tips for implementing 360-degree feedback within your organization
  • Conclusion

What is 360-degree feedback?

[ps2id id='360-versus' target=''/] With 360-degree feedback, employee performance is evaluated by multiple people they interact with, such as their manager, colleagues, suppliers, or customers. There are various ways to provide feedback to employees. This can be one-way (one-dimensional feedback) or take the form of a conversation in which the employee is also given the opportunity to provide their own input (180-degree feedback). In 360-degree feedback, more than two people provide input about the employee. This allows the employee to receive feedback from different perspectives, creating a more complete picture of the employee and their performance in the workplace.

The Characteristics of 360-Degree Feedback

[ps2id id='360-kenmerken' target=''/] The most striking characteristic of 360-degree feedback is the involvement of multiple people in this method. This allows multiple individuals with different perspectives to paint a complete picture . The employee is not a passive participant in this process either. He or she also has the opportunity to articulate and defend their performance . By comparing this perspective with the views of others, a learning process is set in motion. This gives the employee a clear picture of their strengths and areas for improvement. As a result, this is a motivational method that focuses not on weaknesses, but rather on an employee’s opportunities and potential. Image: cognology.com.au

When should you use the 360-degree feedback method?

[ps2id id='wanneer-gebruiken' target=''/] This feedback method is valuable for developing a modern cycle of dialogue between employees and managers, as well as for objectifying and preparing substantive performance or evaluation reviews. In many organizations, these discussions take place only once a year. To fully leverage the potential of 360-degree feedback, it’s recommended to schedule sessions several times a year . For example, once a quarter or even once a month. This can also be done through shorter—and often more informal—conversations. This keeps employees engaged and motivated to continue developing themselves. The method is also well-suited for peer review or for pre- and post-assessments in training programs.

Using 360-Degree Feedback with Your Own Competency Language

[ps2id id='competency-language' target=''/] Unambiguous competency language is a valuable tool for conducting effective (competency-based) conversations. It ensures everyone speaks the same language and helps prevent misunderstandings. Competency terminology clearly defines which definitions of competencies you use and what behaviors correspond to them. This is also valuable when using the 360-degree feedback method. At hrmforce, we create fully customized competency language for many organizations so that it aligns perfectly with their internal language and terminology. Organizations can develop or adopt a competency lexicon themselves, as standard lexicons are also available. Those who use hrmforce’s tools can utilize a standard competency lexicon (with a competency handbook) in addition to their own organizational language. This framework consists of approximately 50 competencies (based on the Big50) that make behavior measurable and discussable.

When is it better not to use 360-degree feedback?

[ps2id id='when-not-to-use' target=''/] Sometimes this feedback method is also used in recruitment or selection processes. However, that is not its intended purpose. What is essential is feedback from people who are close to an employee, work with them frequently, and therefore know them well. This makes the method unsuitable for new evaluation situations, such as the recruitment or selection process. The method is also not intended as a “psychological test.” Of course, a psychological test can be used independently of the 360-degree feedback method.

How does 360-degree feedback work in practice?

[ps2id id='in-de-praktijk' target=''/] There are various ways to implement 360-degree feedback in practice. For example, by collecting feedback via a (digital) questionnaire or in a face-to-face conversation. The latter option is called a roundtable discussion. Both methods have advantages and disadvantages. Feedback is always a standard part of the process.

The (digital) questionnaire

The simplest and most accessible way to implement this method is with a 360-degree feedback questionnaire. You can choose between a digital or a paper questionnaire. The questionnaire can address general (work) performance or a specific aspect of job performance. The questionnaire is completed by the employee and a selected group of people who know the employee well and work closely with them. A drawback of this method is that a manager must wait for the results and then set aside time to review them.

The Roundtable Discussion

Some employers prefer a roundtable discussion in which feedback on an employee’s (work) performance is provided in a structured manner. In this format, everyone sits together at a table and provides direct feedback. This can be confrontational and stressful for some employees. Completing a (digital) 360-degree feedback questionnaire prevents this situation. The advantage of this method is that you have everyone together in one location. This allows for interaction among participants. Uncertainties can be clarified, and viewpoints can be discussed. Additionally, you spend less time collecting and processing the results.

The Feedback

After the feedback is collected, an employee’s results are compared with those of the feedback providers. This allows the employee to see where the similarities and differences lie. He can then work with his manager to set one or more goals to improve his performance or take it to the next level. A personal goal helps employees to (continue to) improve themselves    

Tools to simplify the process

[ps2id id='simplify-process' target=''/] Fortunately, you don’t have to create the questionnaires yourself. Once you’ve determined the topic of the questionnaire, there are standard online questionnaires available that you can use right away. There are also companies that focus entirely on developing software to simplify the process for you as a manager. You can choose to use this software and/or these services to save time. Of course, you’ll need to weigh the costs of such a service against the benefits, but it’s always a good idea to explore the options for outsourcing the logistical aspects of the 360-degree feedback method.

What are the benefits of 360-degree feedback?

[ps2id id='benefits-360' target=''/] The biggest advantage of 360-degree feedback is that an employee receives feedback from people they work with on a daily basis—not just from the manager who (often only partially) interacts with the employee. This shifts the focus away from numerical results and toward talents, development, and opportunities. Through this feedback method, an employee can identify their own talents and weaknesses and develop themselves in specific, targeted ways in certain areas. Because it provides a broader perspective, 360-degree feedback has also proven to be a reliable method. Studies show that the results are accurate. Furthermore, it is an accessible and constructive method. It fosters a positive atmosphere by focusing on improvement rather than “downgrading” a colleague. As such, it is also a process from which every participant can learn.

Does 360-degree feedback also have disadvantages?

[ps2id id='disadvantages-360' target=''/] The success of the 360-degree feedback method depends entirely on the reliability of the people in the feedback group. It is important that these people provide honest feedback and do not act out of self-interest or excessive caution. Research has shown that the use of 360-degree feedback yields reliable results under these conditions. However, there may also be situations in which this method is not recommended. For example, a work environment that is highly competitive or hostile. Similarly, a department where a culture of fear prevails does not provide a suitable foundation for 360-degree feedback. The method works best in a work environment where people work as a team to bring out the best in themselves and in each other. And in a work environment where people want to develop talents to utilize them within the team.

Three tips for implementing the 360-degree feedback method within your organization

[ps2id id='tips-360' target=''/] Now that you know more about how this feedback method works, you may want to implement it within your organization. However, its implementation does require some preparation. It’s important to establish the method firmly right from the start. Next, it’s essential to thoroughly prepare the substance of the process. Finally, it’s important to approach the process with a positive attitude. These three tips are explained in detail below.

  1. Introduce the method carefully and decisively

Changes are often difficult for employees and are initially perceived as “unnecessary.” People are initially inclined to want to keep things as they are and are therefore negative toward a new method from the outset. For employees who have been with the organization for some time, this may seem like “yet another new idea” being introduced. It is therefore important to proceed decisively during the introduction. Formulate the plans clearly, communicate openly about the method, and convince employees of the benefits—including those for them. After all, this approach benefits not only managers but certainly employees as well! Once they understand how the 360-degree feedback method supports their personal development, they’ll be more motivated to participate in the process.

  1. Set goals for the feedback and select the right feedback providers

Clearly define for yourself and for employees which aspects of (work) performance you want to assess. You can then link these aspects to employee goals and company objectives. For example, if you want to assess the extent to which an employee collaborates with others, focus the questions solely on that aspect of their performance. Next, select feedback providers for each employee and for each feedback objective. The aspect of (work) performance you want to gain insight into helps determine who you choose as feedback providers. It’s important that these are people who work closely with the employee and are therefore familiar with their work style. Selecting reliable and effective feedback providers is essential for obtaining a reliable result.

  1. Approach the process with a positive mindset

When comparing the feedback group’s findings with an employee’s performance, it’s important not to focus on problems, but rather on possibilities and opportunities. Approach differences in perspective between the employee and the feedback providers in a positive light. Look for ways to improve the weaknesses of a specific employee or the team. In addition, you want to give talented employees the opportunity to develop as much as possible. Foster a culture of improvement within the team where everyone strives to bring out the best in themselves and in one another. Always lead by example.

Conclusion

[ps2id id='conclusion-360' target=''/] When a manager evaluates an employee in a one-on-one meeting (using one-dimensional or 180-degree feedback), a one-sided view of the employee’s performance emerges. The manager usually doesn’t know the employee as well as colleagues who work with them on a daily basis. As a result, in a performance or evaluation meeting, the focus may end up being primarily on the results rather than on the process through which those results were achieved. By using 360-degree feedback, a more comprehensive picture of employees’ strengths and areas for improvement emerges. After all, you receive information about the employee’s performance from colleagues and managers who work directly with them. You can even involve a coach, suppliers, or customers in the process. By responding to the information obtained, you can make much better use of employees’ potential. The 360-degree feedback method is a powerful tool that allows you to bring out the best in your employees. This benefits not only the development of individual employees but also the team and, consequently, the company’s bottom line. Want to implement 360-degree feedback in your organization? Start the free demo here.

body:
Due to high inflation and rising energy and raw material prices, companies will be paying extra attention to their expenses in 2023. At the same time, effective employee selection and development remain essential. Those who use HR tools such as online tests and questionnaires can potentially work more efficiently by consolidating them on a single platform. This allows you to maintain quality and continue doing the same work with less money—or accomplish more with the same budget. Be sure to keep these five points in mind.

How Are Companies Saving Money?

Due to rising costs, approximately 60 percent of companies are looking for ways to save money this year, according to this survey by HR service provider Acerta, which polled 1,200 employers. Energy costs, in particular, are being closely monitored (41 percent), and consumption is being cut back where necessary. Labor costs are also being scrutinized (18 percent), but employers are proceeding cautiously in this area because such cuts could directly undermine their competitiveness in the labor market. Meanwhile, labor shortages—even during and after this “headwind”—remain significant in many sectors, primarily due to the ongoing exodus of older workers in the coming years. Furthermore, 90 percent of companies indicate that cost savings on energy, other raw materials, and labor costs are “not possible.” As a result, a large majority expects to implement price increases, but only 13 percent expect this to cover their rising costs, according to this study by Van Lanschot Bank. The study also shows that companies are not going to cut back on innovation because they actually need it more than ever.

Saving Money and Growing Through Digitalization

Digitalization and other innovations are also crucial for working more efficiently and effectively and for increasing productivity. This approach enabled Shell to save billions over three years. But this is also achievable on a smaller scale. The digital transformation was initiated for good reason. Central to this is the digitization and optimization of work processes. In fact, we’re talking about the Fourth Industrial Revolution (also known as Industry 4.0), which is currently underway and is having a major (positive) impact on businesses and organizations. It enables significant cost savings, as well as greater sustainability and productivity. This is because technology, sustainability, and efficiency go hand in hand, and that is transforming companies’ work and production processes at their very core. That is why it is called a new industrial revolution. And it offers major opportunities that companies are not willing to pass up. And the COVID-19 pandemic has already provided a significant source of savings. Because we’ve shifted to a more hybrid way of working—both in the office and more often from home—but now because we choose to—substantial savings are being realized. For example, companies are saving an average of €10,000 per employee. This study by the auditors at PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) also shows that the benefits of working from home more often are substantial. “Employers are saving primarily on office rent. For employees, the main savings come from reduced commuting costs,” according to PwC. And less commuting also leads to fewer traffic jams, lower CO2 emissions, fewer accidents, and reduced investment in infrastructure. So there are opportunities there as well. However, hybrid work also requires a different management approach.

Greater Efficiency Through Consolidated Procurement

If we look at other areas where organizations can realize savings (and gain other benefits), a key step is consolidating procurement packages. This leads to greater efficiency and effectiveness, according to the “House of Control” knowledge base from the consulting firm Improven. In the areas of HRM and online tools—again, innovation driven by digitization—there are significant opportunities. So what should you keep in mind? Here are five key points to consider.

Digital Performance Review Cycle

Do you already have a digital performance review cycle? This is an important tool for fostering meaningful, substantive discussions between employees and managers—for example, to promote the development of employees and teams through tailored approaches. But it’s also a valuable solution for efficient discussions between managers and employees.

What kind of integrated solution do you need?

In practice, it’s common for online HR tools, tests, and questionnaires to be purchased from various sources. This approach has simply evolved over the years. However, consolidating these tools on a single central platform (such as hrmforce) can often be more powerful and cost-effective. So take a close look at which online tools you need and where they’re being procured. If your approach is still highly fragmented, this may be a good time to opt for a consolidated solution. Often, a combination of tools and questionnaires is needed for 1) selecting the best candidates and 2) developing existing employees. This helps employers place employees in the right roles, make the most of existing competencies, and better retain and engage employees. At the same time, employees also get to know themselves better and maintain an ongoing dialogue with their managers about their development. Because that, too, remains just as important. Another financially attractive aspect of using a single provider is the option to purchase unlimited access to tools for both job applicants and current employees for a fixed fee (this is possible with hrmforce).

Consider the various types of development discussions

There are various types of development discussions. Make sure to choose a single provider that effectively facilitates them all. An important consideration is setting up workflows for the various development cycles that organizations use—from the daily to-do list (Bila) and a basic development cycle to development and annual reviews, as well as organizing and monitoring the annual cycle. All these variations of the review cycle are supported by hrmforce’s software for the digital review cycle.

Don’t forget about employee satisfaction

Don’t forget about employee satisfaction in the pursuit of efficiency. This remains a key priority for ensuring strong performance and engagement, as well as for retaining employees and offering them new challenges when necessary. This is especially true given the previously mentioned structural labor shortage. We’ll need to take this into account in an increasing number of sectors through at least 2040. In employee satisfaction surveys, factors such as culture, career development, loyalty, work processes, management, and working conditions are key areas of focus. This is especially important for keeping track of changes and new needs, and for making timely adjustments where necessary.

Other Important Insights

The beauty of having online HR tools on a single platform is that it enhances measurability and can yield many more valuable insights. This is crucial for continuing to develop a competent workforce in a cost-effective manner. Which specific insights are important often varies by organization. Whatever your priorities may be, HR Analytics allows you to gain detailed insights into the talents, pitfalls, and performance of employees and teams. Features such as the 9-box grid can also be valuable for effectively assessing employees, for example, for your strategic workforce planning. In this “box” or “grid,” employees’ potential is plotted against their performance. This makes it possible to quickly gain a clear picture of the entire organization or specific units. You’ll also find these tools on the hrmforce online platform.

body:
Increasing sustainable employability is an increasingly important goal for organizations and employees. Employers also have growing ambitions in this area, but putting these into practice on the job often falls short. Giving employees sufficient insight into their own performance, talents, and development opportunities is invaluable for taking concrete steps forward. In this regard, 360-degree feedback is extremely valuable because it fosters broader self-awareness and facilitates more productive conversations between employees and managers.

Go directly to:

  • What is sustainable employability?
  • Who takes the lead?
  • Sustainable employability with 360-degree feedback
  • Why use 360-degree feedback?
  • A single competency framework for sustainable employability
  • Sustainable employability is changing
  • Ensure consistency
 

What Is Sustainable Employability?

[ps2id id='1' target=''/] In recent years, there has been a growing awareness that employees must continuously work on their development—not only in terms of professional expertise but also in terms of their behavior and competencies in the workplace. This often refers to sustainable employability. In fact, this is a somewhat broad and popular term for a concept that has many different definitions. Collectively, they primarily concern: adaptability, talent development, productivity, personal growth, mobility, vitality, motivation, and health. And they concern the ability of employees to be—and remain—“relevant.” Due to its great importance to employers and the growth of the workforce, many organizations now have ambitions in this area. However, when it comes to translating these into concrete personnel policies and taking decisive action in practice, progress often stalls. Almost all collective bargaining agreements now include provisions on sustainable employability. According to the National Survey on Sustainable Employability (2019), the issue is now on the “strategic agenda” at 68 percent of companies and organizations. In particular, the practical translation of sustainable employability into HR policy and workplace practices often falls short. Employees do regularly participate in training, but this is still primarily focused on their current roles. For sustainable employability, however, you need to look a bit further ahead.

Who takes the lead?

[ps2id id='2' target=''/] When it comes to putting this into practice, the key question is usually: who is responsible for employees’ sustainable employability? According to employers, employees themselves should take the lead in managing their own careers. But they’ll only do so once they’re sufficiently aware of the importance and necessity of this—and once they’re given the right tools to do so. Exactly which tools those should be varies depending on the type of organization, the people who work there, and their development goals. One of the key steps is increasing self-awareness and clarifying one’s own long-term development path. Practical tools can contribute significantly to this. In addition, meaningful conversations between employees and their managers are, of course, important—preferably as part of a modern performance management cycle.

Sustainable Employability with 360-Degree Feedback

[ps2id id='3' target=''/] To give employees greater insight into their own performance, talents, and development opportunities, a Sustainable Employability Scan can be helpful. But 360-degree feedback can also help employees and managers truly put development goals into practice. It is a simple and accessible way to assess employees’ (work) performance. And it’s a powerful tool for better leveraging employees’ potential and improving their performance—not only by supporting productive development discussions between employees and managers, but also by providing the insight needed to foster greater sustainable employability. Employees and managers can jointly identify talents and determine what areas still offer valuable opportunities for development. Looking toward the future, this can also be linked to anticipated organizational developments or, for example, strategic workforce planning (SPP).

Why use 360-degree feedback?

[ps2id id='4' target=''/] With the 360-degree feedback method, employee performance is assessed not only by a manager but by multiple people with whom the employee interacts. These may include, for example, colleagues, suppliers, a coach, or even customers. This can be tailored differently for each employee or development goal. As a result, an individual receives feedback from various perspectives, creating a more complete picture of how they perform in the workplace. As part of the modern performance cycle—which involves multiple short check-ins rather than the traditional performance review or appraisal—360-degree feedback can also help maintain a continuous focus on sustainable employability. Fortunately, organizations do not have to create 360-degree feedback questionnaires on their own. Standard questionnaires are available online, and users of hrmforce can utilize the 360-degree feedback questionnaire. You can read about how the method is used in practice in this article, which includes practical tips. To measure the sustainable employability of employees within organizations, the Sustainable Employability Index (DIX) has also been developed by the research organization TNO. This index provides insight into key areas such as health and energy, knowledge and skills, motivation and engagement, and employees’ work-life balance. However, this is a somewhat complex tool for organizations to implement.

A Single Competency Language for Sustainable Employability

[ps2id id='5' target=''/] Discussions about sustainable employability quickly turn to competencies. In this context, a clear and consistent competency vocabulary is valuable. After all, what exactly do you mean when you talk about competencies such as “customer focus,” “leadership,” or “self-management”? With a standardized competency framework, everyone speaks the same language, and you prevent misunderstandings from arising. A competency framework defines what each competency entails and describes the behaviors associated with it. Organizations can develop or adopt a competency framework on their own. Standard frameworks are readily available online, and those who use hrmforce tools can utilize a standard competency framework in addition to their own organizational framework. At hrmforce, we often create fully customized competency frameworks for organizations so that they align perfectly with the language and terminology used internally. Our standard competency framework (complete with a competency handbook) consists of approximately 50 competencies (based on the Big50) that make behavior measurable and discussable. This is certainly valuable when using 360-degree feedback and the development discussions that follow.

Sustainable employability is changing

[ps2id id='6' target=''/] The focus on sustainable employability originally began primarily as learning and development programs in “emergency situations,” such as layoffs or reorganizations. Due to the challenges of our current economy and labor market for organizations and workers, early and continuous development programs have become increasingly common in recent years. In this context, adding value for both the employer and the employee has become increasingly central. For example, there has also been a growing focus on “lifelong learning and development.” In our modern society—characterized by ever-increasing dynamism, a tighter labor market, globalization, new technologies (automation and robotization), greater flexibility, and faster job changes—both employers and employees must remain vital and adaptable. This increasingly determines their (job) opportunities and success. And because people are working into later and later ages, it is important that they also remain energetic and “up to date.” After all, the nature of existing jobs is changing at an ever-faster pace. As a result, existing knowledge becomes outdated more quickly.

Ensure coherence

[ps2id id='7' target=''/] In addition to supporting employees in their career development, organizations face another challenge when translating their ambitions for sustainable employability from policy into practice: ensuring coherence among the various existing initiatives. This coherence for sustainable employability is often lacking. A logical growth process might be to first build buy-in among managers and employees (using practical tools) to work together on sustainable employability. Then, step by step, programs can be integrated into the approach. As soon as the first results become visible, examples can be shared, and in this way, “the movement” grows. My advice: always start with a structured approach and by increasing self-management and self-awareness. Then determine which tools and resources are needed for employees and managers. 360-degree feedback may also make a valuable contribution here, especially by providing a much broader perspective on one’s own performance.
title: Enhance Long-Term Employability with 360-Degree Feedback

body:
To make recruitment processes better and more efficient, companies are increasingly using psychometric tests. That’s a fancy term for using recruitment questionnaires to measure and objectively assess candidates’ personalities, motivations, and competencies. In addition to cost savings and higher-quality matching, this can also significantly contribute, in the long term, to greater diversity, lower turnover, and a more balanced workforce.

The Future of Recruitment

Questionnaires are already being used more and more frequently to improve recruitment processes and make them more objective. This measurability is expected to become an increasingly important foundation for the recruitment of the future (and HRM in general). Because by recruiting and selecting more objectively, you no longer have to rely on a gut “click” with candidates, but can actually select them based on relevant characteristics and competencies. This requires, above all, well-designed questionnaires and interview techniques that ensure more objective selection interviews. In the past, it was quite complicated to actually conduct these interviews in this way, mainly due to classic pitfalls and (unconscious) human subjectivity. Such as relying too heavily on a candidate’s “first impression” or acting on preconceptions or stereotypes. Another classic pitfall is placing too much emphasis on a single positive trait when evaluating candidates (the halo effect). Fortunately, these days, well-designed questionnaires can help ensure the most objective and balanced assessment.

Three Types of Tests

Psychometric testing in recruitment is best understood as the use of tests and instruments that measure a candidate’s suitability for a position or organization. The various tests available cover different areas of focus and topics. The three main groups are the tests for these key areas:
  1. Personality
Measuring personality traits is invaluable for identifying candidates’ behavioral patterns. The Personality Test (Big50) is often used for this purpose. This is the most widely used (and researched) personality theory in organizational settings.
  1. Motivators
A motivation test is valuable for understanding what increases or decreases candidates’ motivation. After all, motivation is one of the essential components of success, productivity, and job satisfaction. A commonly used questionnaire from hrmforce to measure this is the Motivation Test. This test takes about 20 minutes to complete.
  1. Competencies
Does someone possess the right skills to perform a job well? And where are there still opportunities for development? To gain a clear and quick understanding of candidates’ competencies, there are competency tests such as the Competency Check. In just 20 minutes, this provides much greater insight into strengths, weaknesses, and potential areas for development. Exactly which questionnaires are relevant and important for a recruitment process can vary depending on the organization or the position and role within your organization. In addition to the tests mentioned above, which are widely used in recruitment, an intelligence test (also known as a cognitive ability test) or a selection assessment is also frequently used. This assessment is a testing method that evaluates applicants’ suitability for a specific position. It is also used to gain insight into individual qualities and to provide, for example, education and training recommendations. Such a suitability assessment significantly increases the success rate of recruitment and selection processes.

Benefits of Recruitment Questionnaires

Since the 1980s, various studies have shown that using questionnaires in recruitment and selection offers major benefits for both organizations and candidates. With the rise of online questionnaires, testing has also become much simpler and more accessible. International studies confirm that this allows selection processes to proceed much more quickly and significantly reduces candidate mismatches (research results vary, showing a reduction ranging from at least 40 to at least 50 percent). Furthermore, a good match leads to better employee performance, with an average 43 percent increase in revenue, according to research by the consulting firm Hay Group. This alone results in significant savings in time and money and a strong “Return on Investment” (ROI). Furthermore, a better match also enables organizations to retain new employees longer and to develop their skills more effectively and in a more targeted manner. After all, thorough testing allows you to assess an individual’s long-term potential by evaluating their personality type, behaviors, and cognitive abilities. This is valuable not only for the organization but also for candidates and employees themselves. For HR, using questionnaires can also help streamline the recruitment process.

Diversity and Inclusion

In addition to the benefits mentioned, the growing focus on inclusive business practices and diversity within organizations is another important reason to start using questionnaires in the recruitment and selection of candidates. On the one hand, this allows for more objective recruitment and selection based on the actual competencies and relevant characteristics of candidates. In addition, tests can also help current employees and managers foster a more inclusive organization. Inclusive leadership, for example, is a key success factor in this regard. You can cultivate this by clearly identifying development opportunities for employees and managers.
title: Questionnaires Make Recruitment Better, More Efficient, and More Inclusive

body:
At many companies, the hiring process involves several steps. An initial meeting is followed by a selection interview. During this interview, the candidate’s skills and competencies are explored in greater depth. The goal is to provide as objective an assessment of candidates as possible, so that the most suitable candidate can be selected. In this article, you’ll learn more about conducting a selection interview.  

The Difference Between a Selection Interview and an Introductory Interview

A selection interview differs from an introductory interview in that more people from the company will be present, which means there’s a chance that certain points will be repeated. For example, in addition to the HR manager, the head of the department where the candidate will be working may also be present. Questions on specific topics are now probed more deeply, and real-world examples are discussed. While an HR manager primarily focuses on the person and their profile, a department head can delve more deeply into the substance. The candidate’s skills and knowledge are critically evaluated and tested, making it more difficult to “pass” the selection process.  

The STARR Method as an Interview Guide

However, maintaining objectivity is not always easy, which is why the STARR method is a tool used by many HR managers. It serves as a kind of interview guide aimed at assessing a candidate’s experience and knowledge. The HR manager asks questions about past events in which the candidate had to apply certain skills or knowledge. It is important to ask follow-up questions so that a clear picture can be painted of the situation and how the candidate would respond to it. STARR is an acronym for Situation, Task, Action, and Result (sometimes with an extra R for Reflection):
  1. Situation - What is the situation or context?
  2. Task—What was the task the candidate undertook?
  3. Action—What actions did the candidate take?
  4. Result—What was the response to this, and was the final result satisfactory?
 

Employment Terms During the Job Interview

An important point to mention during the job interview is the terms of employment. Although these are not discussed in detail, an indication of the terms will be provided. This also gives the candidate in question greater clarity. Selecting a suitable employee is no easy task. That’s why a thorough, focused interview is essential to understand exactly what you, as an employer, are dealing with, so you can get the most out of your staff!  

What happens after the selection interview?

The selection interview is normally the final interview, but this depends on the size of the company and the procedures it follows. Sometimes as many as 8 different interview stages are held to assess candidates, especially at large multinational corporations. For small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs/SMEs)—and often for larger companies as well—two interviews are usually the norm. It’s also becoming increasingly common to ask candidates to complete an assessment before they’re officially hired. This phase usually takes place after the job interview and applies only to the very best candidates (partly because it’s an expensive process). During such an assessment, the candidate’s competencies are tested based on situations that might arise in the job responsibilities. If, after the final interview, there are still two candidates remaining, they are often invited back together for a final interview.
title: Job Interview: Tips and Strategies for Successful Hiring

body:
The 4Gs of Feedback is a proven and simple method for providing clear, honest, and constructive feedback. The model helps you make conversations less personal, less emotional, and, above all, much more concrete. The 4Gs stand for Incident – Behavior – Feeling – Consequence , and are used in evaluations, performance reviews, team communication, and 360-degree feedback. Would you like to collect feedback in a more professional and structured way? Then check out hrmforce’s 360-degree feedback assessment.

What are the 4Gs of feedback?

The 4G method helps make feedback concrete and respectful. You move step by step from factual observation to impact and desired behavior. The four components are:
  • Event – What actually happened? (without judgment)
  • Behavior – What specific behavior did you observe?
  • Feeling – How did that make you or others feel?
  • Consequence – What is the impact on work, results, or the team?
By breaking down the feedback into smaller parts, you create less resistance and more understanding.

Why does the 4G feedback method work so well?

Many people find feedback nerve-wracking, precisely because it can quickly feel personal. The 4G model prevents this by:
  • starting objectively (Event)
  • staying specific (Behavior)
  • adding empathy (Feeling)
  • identifying the business impact (Consequence)
This creates a conversation that feels clear and safe. People better understand exactly what is meant and how they can use that information.

The 4Gs Explained Step by Step

1. Event – what actually happened?

This is the objective starting point. You stick to the facts, without emotion or interpretation. Examples:
  • “During Monday’s meeting, the report wasn’t ready.”
  • “Yesterday, you joined the client call 20 minutes late.”
  • “Last week, three deadlines were missed.”

2. Behavior – What specific behavior did you observe?

Here, you specifically describe what someone did or failed to do. No labels, no character assessments—just behavior. Examples:
  • "You didn’t provide an update on the status of the assignment."
  • "You interrupted your colleague several times during the meeting."
  • "You didn’t get in touch to let us know you’d be late."

3. Feeling – how did that make you or others feel?

By describing your feelings, the feedback becomes more human. It shows why it’s important. Examples:
  • "That made me feel stressed about the schedule."
  • "I didn’t feel taken seriously."
  • "The team became uncertain because it wasn’t clear who was doing what."

4. Consequence – what impact does the behavior have?

This step clarifies why the feedback matters and why change is necessary. Examples:
  • "If reports are missing, we can’t make decisions on time."
  • "Interruptions make colleagues afraid to share their ideas."
  • "As a result, the customer perceives us as unreliable."

Example: 4G feedback in one sentence

Example 1 – Late Delivery : “During last week’s presentation (Event), you hadn’t finished the slides yet (Behavior), which made me feel anxious about the client (Feeling), and we didn’t come across as professional in the presentation (Consequence).” Example 2 – Interrupting a colleague : “In Tuesday’s meeting (Event), you interrupted a colleague twice (Behavior). That made the team feel unsafe (Feeling), causing people to be less willing to share their ideas (Consequence).” Example 3 – Positive Feedback "During the sprint review (Event), you took the lead in answering customer questions (Behavior), which gave everyone confidence (Feeling) and created a very professional impression (Consequence)."   https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wtl5UrrgU8c&pp=ygUMNGdzIGZlZWRiYWNr

Complete 4G Feedback Questionnaire

Below is a set of questions that you or your colleagues can use to provide concrete feedback using the 4G method.

Questions About the Event

  • When did you first notice something?
  • What exactly happened?
  • When and where did it take place?

Questions about behavior

  • What exactly did the coworker do?
  • What specific behavior caught your attention?
  • What was said or done?

Questions about feelings

  • How did this make you feel?
  • What did you feel or experience as a result of that behavior?
  • How did others react to that?

Questions about consequences

  • What was the impact on the outcome?
  • How did it affect the team or the client?
  • Why is it important to discuss this behavior?

4G Feedback: Do’s and Don’ts

Do’s

  • Describe only behavior, not character.
  • Keep feedback brief and specific.
  • Always ask for the other person’s response.
  • Use the 4Gs for positive feedback as well.

Don’ts

  • Don’t use labels (“You’re always so…”).
  • Don’t bring up old frustrations.
  • Don’t make assumptions (“You must have meant…”).
  • Don’t make assumptions about intentions.

Applying 4G Feedback in Organizations

The 4G method works in:
  • performance reviews
  • POP meetings
  • team feedback
  • performance reviews
  • 360-degree feedback
  • Daily collaboration
Using this method organization-wide fosters a culture of openness, clarity, and constructive improvement discussions.

Do you want to organize feedback more professionally?

The 4Gs of feedback provide a strong foundation, but for deeper behavioral insights, development advice, and objective reports, you can use a professional tool. Check out hrmforce’s 360-degree feedback assessment here for a comprehensive feedback experience, including behavioral indicators and reports.
title: The 4Gs of Feedback: Explanation and Examples

body:
Committed, happy, and enterprising people make up the organization—or rather, they are the organization.

…..“Good people make great business”…..

 

Nothing new under the sun

Focusing on how people function within organizations is nothing new. In a 2004 article, I came across twelve questions—which I consider simple—that still come up daily in my consulting practice:

The 12 Fundamental Questions for Employee Engagement:

  1. Do I know what is expected of me at work?
  2. Do I have all the resources I need to do my job well?
  3. Does my job give me the opportunity to do what I do best every day?
  4. Have I received recognition or praise over the past seven days for something I did well?
  5. Does my immediate supervisor—or someone else at work—care about me as a person?
  6. Is there someone at work who encourages my continued growth?
  7. Does my opinion matter at work?
  8. Do my organization’s vision and mission make me feel that my work is important?
  9. Do my coworkers strive to deliver high-quality work?
  10. Do I consider anyone at work a “good friend”?
  11. Has anyone talked to me about my performance over the past six months?
  12. Have I had the opportunity to learn new things and grow personally over the past year?

Source: Buckingham, M. and Coffman, C., *Break All the Rules*, Simon & Schuster, 1999, in: *Sigma* No. 6, December 2004

Developments

Of course, new insights are constantly being gained, and thinking about performance is constantly evolving. For example, over the past two years, many organizations have moved away from a practice that had become quite established: performance and evaluation interviews.
❌ Old paradigm ✅ New Paradigm
The performance review works terribly The Good Conversation
A quarter of employees cry after a performance review The 10 most important rules for a good conversation
Old-Style Annual Review A weekly incentive to work from the heart

Core principle: People want to learn and grow

For me, the format is less important than the twelve questions mentioned earlier. For me, the core is the belief in the intrinsic motivation of (most) people to learn, improve, achieve something, see results, and feel appreciated.

🌱 What truly motivates people:

  • 📈 Growth: Continuous development and new challenges
  • 🏆 Results: A visible impact from their work
  • 👥 Connection: Meaningful collaboration with others
  • 💝 Appreciation: Recognition for contributions and efforts
  • 🎯 Ownership: Autonomy and responsibility
An organization that pays attention to these aspects and facilitates development is generally a pleasant place to work. Organizational results improve when individuals feel a sense of ownership, collaborate with others, feel valued, and are continually challenged and given the opportunity to further develop themselves (Investors in People ).

Integrating Learning and Performance

To prevent training from becoming too detached from work, focused attention is needed on integrating learning and performance. The image below lists elements that I regularly encounter in organizations. Central to this approach is working with a personal plan that combines job agreements with a personal plan or development plan (the well-known PDP). Individuals take ownership of that plan and are 100% involved in its creation.     Each organization can adapt these elements to align with its own practices. I’ll explain three specific situations here.

Three Practical Examples

1. Work Agreements at an Online Clothing Company

An online clothing company has used online assessments to determine each person’s personality and, based on that, to estimate whether it will be easier or more difficult for them to develop specific competencies.

📊 Results:

  • 100% participation: All employees volunteered to participate
  • Increased self-awareness: Insight into one’s own strengths and weaknesses
  • Better collaboration: Teams capitalized on each other’s strengths
  • Clear agreements: KPIs linked to personal development

2. Reflection Report and Feedback at an Engineering Firm

An engineering firm that works with self-managing teams asked everyone to write a reflection report: to write a one-page A4 document about themselves and send it to their immediate colleagues or via 360-degree feedback.

💡 Powerful reflection questions:

Looking back:
  • What motivates me in my work?
  • Which activity gave me energy?
  • What do I find less interesting?
  • What growth do I see in myself?
  • What was disappointing?
 Looking Ahead:
  • What is my added value?
  • What opportunities do I see?
  • What do I want to learn, and why?
  • What’s my next step?
  • How do I build on my successes?

3. Choosing Drive, Passion, and Interest

A highly experienced tax specialist at a large accounting firm is widely respected by colleagues and clients alike. His revenue is on target. His work-life balance is excellent. And yet, at some point, he finds himself sitting at home, feeling burned out.
Previous Situation Transformation Result
Burned Out Despite Success A Choice for Professional Passion In "flow" and full of energy
Unspoken expectations Saying Goodbye to Tasks That Don’t Fit Authentic leadership
Commercial pressure Focus on knowledge sharing Increased impact and revenue

The secret to personal development

Successful personal development requires more than just good intentions. It requires a systematic approach that brings together various elements:

🔑 Key factors for success:

  1. Ownership: Employees are personally responsible for their own development
  2. Ongoing dialogue: Not just once a year, but an ongoing conversation
  3. Personalization: Every person has their own motivations and learning style
  4. Integration: Learning and work are inextricably linked
  5. Support: The organization actively facilitates and encourages

Prerequisite: Genuine interest and truly listening

We’ve already discussed “the good conversation .” To develop personal plans that truly matter—for both the organization and the individual involved—it’s essential that we have meaningful conversations. This is not an annually scheduled, recurring conversation, but an ongoing dialogue (the frequency and follow-up may vary by person) based on evolving insights. What this requires: genuine interest and listening—truly listening. Celeste Headlee explains this excellently in the TED Talk below (12 min.).
 

Start today with personal development plans that really work.

Invest in your people; invest in your future.

body:
Feeling a little stressed out by your job? Almost everyone can relate to that—and it doesn’t have to be a problem. But unfortunately, many Dutch people suffer from excessive work-related stress. Especially in healthcare and education, absenteeism due to burnout is a major problem. What can you do about this as an HR manager or employer? During Work Stress Awareness Week, we’re sharing 7 tips to prevent stress among your staff. The numbers don’t lie: work-related stress is the most common occupational illness. In 2021, a whopping 21 percent of all employee absenteeism was stress-related, according to ArboNed . Among people who have been out of work for more than six weeks, mental strain and burnout are the cause in about 30 percent of cases. All that absenteeism due to work-related stress isn’t just a nuisance—it also costs a lot of money: as much as 2.8 billion euros per year , according to calculations by TNO and Statistics Netherlands (CBS). Those are figures worth taking a moment to let sink in. Yet stress isn’t necessarily a bad thing. In fact, a little bit of work pressure is actually necessary to perform well. The problem only arises when the pressure is consistently too high, and you don’t relax enough in between. This year, Work Stress Week (November 14–18, 2022) is centered on the theme “physically and mentally strong.” What can you do as a manager to ensure that your staff is and remains strong both physically and mentally? Here are 7 helpful tips.

1. Ask your employees what they need

You can come up with all sorts of reasons why your staff is experiencing stress. But you won’t truly know where the root of the problem lies until you ask the people themselves. That’s why having a conversation is an important first step. Make work-related stress a topic of discussion during the annual performance review cycle. Keep in mind that employees won’t necessarily open up right away. Research by the Ministry of Social Affairs shows that many people are afraid to admit they’re experiencing stress at work. Nearly half of employees (45 percent) believe this will give their employer the impression that they can’t handle their job. Admitting that you’re struggling with work-related stress can make you feel vulnerable. That’s why it’s very important for you, as an employer, to invest in a safe work environment—for example, by communicating openly about your expectations, standards, and values. And by showing vulnerability yourself. Regularly ask employees for feedback. And don’t shy away from difficult topics—bring them out into the open.

2. Get people moving

Physical activity is a great way to reduce stress. When you move, you clear your head. And you produce endorphins. This chemical makes you feel happy and also ensures that your brain produces less cortisol (the stress hormone). So it’s a win-win. Want to encourage employees to be more active? Take a walk together during your lunch break. With the Ommetje app, you can even turn it into a fun competition. Or have your company participate in a running race. You can also take a more serious approach. For example, organize boot camps or yoga classes at the office. Or take a closer look at your employee benefits and reimburse the cost of a gym membership for your staff.

3. Don’t reduce the workload; increase resilience

Burnout isn’t caused solely by employees working too hard, but mainly because they don’t recover sufficiently. So don’t focus on having people reduce their workload; instead, focus on helping them increase their resilience. Work together to identify which tasks energize employees and which ones actually drain their energy. This is different for everyone! Discuss this as a team so you can redistribute projects more effectively. Perhaps one colleague hates a certain task, while another tackles that same work with ease. Also, introduce employees to the mental “Food Guide.”

4. Foster autonomy in the workplace

Autonomy is one of the most important sources of energy in the workplace. Employees who are given the freedom to organize their own work are happier and experience less work-related stress. And that ultimately benefits the organization as well, because satisfied employees are more productive. You might find it hard to let go of control. Still, it’s important that you do so. How? Focus primarily on the results, and interfere less with how, where, and when people work. That doesn’t mean, by the way, that you should completely let your employees run wild. An employer sets safe boundaries so that employees feel supported.

5. Help people log off on time

We live in a 24-hour economy. And since the COVID-19 crisis, the boundaries between work and personal life have blurred for many employees. That’s a risk, because people who feel like they’re never truly off work don’t rest as well. So make sure that “off” in your organization really means off. Resist the temptation to call employees on their days off or during vacations. And if you notice that someone is inclined to answer emails in the evening, talk to them about it. It might seem nice to have such a diligent employee. But ultimately, such behavior causes people to burn out more quickly. And as a manager, lead by example. Telling people not to take on work tasks on their days off isn’t credible if the boss is sitting there sending emails on Sundays. Is there a workaholic culture in your organization? You can let technology lend a hand. Belgian and Luxembourgish Lidl employees do not receive internal emails between 6:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m. In this way, the company aims to give people the chance to clear their minds after work.

6. Make your staff feel that their work is meaningful and appreciated

Employees can handle a lot, as long as they feel they’re doing meaningful work. The moment they realize all their efforts are in vain, it’s such a mental blow that they instantly lose all their energy and burn out. So it’s essential that you value your people’s efforts. Be generous with compliments, send flowers to someone celebrating a long tenure, or give a bonus or gift card to teams that have completed a challenging project. Such appreciation and recognition make employees feel that they matter.

7. Build a learning organization

People experience stress when they can’t do something well. So help them develop their knowledge and skills. Does that mean you have to send the entire company to training? You can, but there’s also a lot to learn in day-to-day practice—provided your organization has the right learning environment. A company with a positive learning environment is also known as a learning organization. In such an organization, employees feel safe to make mistakes, ask questions, and suggest ideas. As a result, they continually gain new knowledge and share their experiences and insights with others.

Bonus Tip

In addition to these 7 tips, would you like to use a valuable tool to tackle work-related stress among your staff? Then have them take an assessment. Stress can also arise, for example, because an employee isn’t in the right role. Digital assessments can be administered at various locations throughout the Netherlands. Candidates are warmly welcomed there and receive personalized attention, so they feel completely at ease. Curious about the possibilities? Check out the websites of Lamark or hrmforce and book an assessment right away.
title: 7 Tips + a Bonus Tip to Prevent Work-Related Stress Among Your Employees

body:
IQ is a term that frequently comes up in discussions about talent, selection, and performance. Yet it is also often misunderstood. Many people think that IQ is a fixed number that determines how smart someone is. That perception is incorrect.

In this article

In this article, we take an in-depth look at the concept of “average IQ.” You’ll discover exactly what IQ measures, how it’s calculated, why averages vary by country, and, most importantly, how to use these figures wisely in HR and recruitment.

What exactly is IQ?

IQ stands for intelligence quotient. It’s a score that attempts to measure cognitive skills, such as logical reasoning, problem-solving ability, and memory. The concept originated in the early 20th century. The first test was developed by Alfred Binet, who wanted to measure children’s mental development. Later, William Stern introduced the formula for IQ: mental age divided by chronological age, multiplied by 100. Today, things work differently. Modern IQ tests use a norm group. The average score is set at 100, with a standard deviation of 15. That means:
Score Meaning
100 Average
85–115 Normal range
130+ Very high
<70 Well below average
Important to understand: IQ is always relative. It says something about your position relative to a group, not about absolute intelligence.

How is IQ measured?

There are several well-known tests:
  • Wechsler tests (WAIS, WISC)
  • Stanford-Binet
  • Raven’s Progressive Matrices
These measure different aspects of intelligence, such as:
  • verbal comprehension
  • working memory
  • processing speed
  • logical reasoning
Raven’s Matrices is often used because it is less dependent on language and culture. This is particularly relevant in HR. It demonstrates that intelligence is not a single, uniform trait. Someone may excel at analytical thinking but be less strong in verbal ability. In practice, it is therefore much wiser to use an up-to-date, validated test—such as a cognitive intelligence test from HRMForce—rather than outdated calculation methods.

What is the average IQ worldwide?

This is where it gets complex. In theory, the average IQ is always around 100. But that only applies within a specific normative group. As soon as you look at the global picture, differences emerge. Research shows:
Region Estimated average
East Asia ~105–107
Europe ~95–102
Africa (sub-Saharan) ~70–85
World average ~85 (weighted)
That seems like a big difference. But you have to be extremely cautious with these figures. These figures are based on datasets such as those by Lynn & Vanhanen. Those datasets have been heavily criticized for small sample sizes, non-representative groups, and estimates rather than actual measurements. In fact, scientific organizations advise against using this data without careful consideration.

Why do IQ scores vary between countries?

The key finding from the research is this:

IQ differences between countries are largely explained by environmental factors.

Consider:
  • quality of education
  • nutrition
  • health care
  • economic conditions
Studies show that improvements in these factors lead to higher IQ scores. An important phenomenon in this context is the Flynn effect. This means that IQ scores are rising worldwide, by about 3 points per generation. In other words: people aren’t born smarter, but they perform better due to improved conditions.

What does the average IQ within a country indicate?

There are also significant differences within countries. IQ is related to:
  • level of education
  • socioeconomic status
  • family situation
Research shows that each additional year of education can raise IQ by several points. In addition, men and women have, on average, roughly the same IQ, while men often show greater variation. For HR, this has an important implication: context is everything. A score means little without background information and without the broader picture of a person’s abilities.

How reliable is IQ, really?

IQ tests are useful. For example, they are fairly good at predicting academic and job performance. But they have limitations.

1. Cultural bias

Many tests were developed in a Western context. This can put people from other cultures at a disadvantage.

2. Sampling issues

National averages are often based on small or specific groups.

3. Flynn effect

Scores change over time. Comparing old data with new data can be misleading.

4. What Does IQ Actually Measure?

IQ primarily measures cognitive skills relevant to school and work, not the whole person.

IQ does not measure creativity, social intelligence, motivation, or perseverance. That makes IQ valuable, but also limited.

Why is this relevant to HR?

In HR, IQ is often used in assessments and selection. That makes sense. IQ is one of the strongest predictors of job performance. But it’s often misapplied.

Common Mistakes

  1. Viewing IQ as fixed talent
  2. Focusing only on the total score
  3. Failing to take context into account
  4. Confusing IQ with potential
Someone with an average IQ can still be very successful thanks to motivation, learning ability, discipline, and social skills. That’s why a single score is often less effective than a broader view of cognitive abilities. A tool like the Ability Scan is better suited to this.

What should you, as an HR professional, actually do?

Use IQ as part of a broader picture. Combine it with:
  • personality, such as DISC
  • motivation
  • learning ability
  • experience
Also consider potential for growth. A candidate with a slightly lower IQ but high learning ability and motivation may be more valuable in the long run than someone with a high score but no drive.

The Ethical Side of IQ

Average IQ scores by country or group are a sensitive issue. They can be misused to justify inequality. Research actually shows something else:

differences can largely be explained by circumstances, not by fixed traits.

This means:
  • IQ can be influenced
  • the environment plays a major role
  • investing in people pays off
For organizations, this means you must not only select talent but also develop it.

What does “average IQ” really mean?

The most important insight:

Average IQ is a statistical tool, not an absolute truth.

It helps you compare groups, identify patterns, and make predictions. But it doesn’t tell you how smart an individual really is, what someone can achieve, or how someone will develop.

Conclusion

IQ remains a valuable measure of cognitive abilities. It aids in selection, development, and research. But it is not the be-all and end-all. Averages by country or group provide direction, but are highly dependent on context, measurement methods, and environmental factors. For HR, the real power lies in the combination of data, context, and human insight. Do you want to better assess cognitive abilities in recruitment and selection? Then check out HRMForce’s cognitive intelligence test.

Sources

The sources listed below are cited in the Deep Research Report on which this article is based:
  • Lynn & Vanhanen (2002, 2006)
  • Wicherts et al. (2010)
  • Rindermann et al. (2011)
  • Parra & Zissimopoulos (2025)
  • Various psychometric studies on IQ, education, and standardization

Research shows that few adults have a clear and realistic view of themselves. This makes it difficult to set realistic goals and make sound plans. This can lead to poor career choices, causing you to wonder one day whether your job is still the right fit for you. Career orientation helps you (re)gain a clear understanding of your core strengths, which skills can still be developed, and which roles are a good fit in what types of organizations.

Career Orientation Process

To gain as comprehensive a picture as possible of the candidate, a personality assessment is conducted as part of the career process. Based on various questionnaires, tests, and an in-depth interview, a profile is created detailing personality, motivators and demotivators, areas of interest, and work and cognitive levels. This report forms the basis for follow-up discussions in which the candidate’s career aspirations are compared with available job opportunities, whether internal or external. Once a specific direction for career orientation has been determined, practical simulations follow. The results provide insight into the areas in which a candidate needs to develop further in order to effectively fulfill the desired job level and/or job type. The combination of objective tests, your opinion, and your ideas forms a strong foundation for your career orientation.

Career Orientation Results

Career orientation provides a comprehensive picture of competencies, development opportunities, personality, and motivation. This boosts motivation and creates a realistic outlook. It is pivotal for the rest of one’s working life and can also serve as the starting point for a training program and/or an individual coaching process. Would you like more information about career orientation? Please contact us at 088-8832188.

body:
Automated HR Information System Leads to Better Business Results

A personnel information system, also known as an HRM system, has become indispensable in a modern organization. Such a system tracks all employee personal data, such as absences and leave, as well as various allowances and benefits. The days when this data was processed manually and stored in a card index seem to be a thing of the past. In recent years, more and more companies and organizations have switched to an automated HRM system. Why is that? Below, we list four key benefits:  

1. Less manpower is wasted on administrative red tape

Both small and large companies must keep track of a great deal of personnel information. Consider, for example, employee attendance and absences, payroll administration, and tracking overtime hours. In addition, various benefits and reimbursements for expenses must be clearly documented. Processing all of this manually not only costs a lot of time and money but also manpower. Especially in companies with limited staff, it’s a shame when a lot of time and manpower are wasted on administrative red tape. By using an automated HR information system, there’s more time for other matters.

2. The risk of errors is much lower

A lot of paperwork inevitably leads to errors. If a single digit is overlooked somewhere or if recent information is accidentally left out, the consequences can be significant. For example, paying too much or too little in salary, or (unintentionally) violating legal provisions, creates extra work to correct the mistakes made. With an automated HR information system, the risk of errors is significantly lower. Although, of course, the human factor still plays a role here as well. The system itself operates flawlessly, but ultimately there is little it can do if data is entered incorrectly.

3. An automated HR information system saves time and money

When an employee is on (long-term) sick leave, on maternity leave, or taking an extended vacation, this affects productivity. In the old-fashioned card-file system, it wasn’t easy to quickly assess those consequences. With an automated system, however, you immediately receive alerts that you need to take action. After all, you have a real-time overview of all relevant information pertaining to your staff. This allows you to identify much more quickly what measures need to be taken to compensate for this absence. In this way, you save time and money.

4. Immediate alerts from the workplace

Because an automated HRM system gives you immediate insight into what’s happening within the company and lets you know exactly what’s going on on the work floor, you can manage processes much more effectively. This also ensures, for example, that you have much greater control over scheduling and the availability of your employees. The system enables you to make the best possible use of your employees, which inevitably leads to better business results.  

The possibilities for your organization

Curious about the possibilities of an HRM system for your organization? Feel free to contact one of our consultants with no obligation.
title: The 4 Benefits of a Human Resources Information System

body:
A mismatch—many an HR manager has dealt with it at some point. Hiring someone who doesn’t deliver the results expected of them. An employee who, upon closer inspection, turns out not to be a good fit for the organization at all. A new colleague who throws in the towel after just a few months. Recruitment has many pitfalls; a less-than-successful hire can happen in the blink of an eye. With all the consequences that entails, because a bad match means a poor investment and an unnecessary waste of money. What should an organization look for when recruiting staff? Is it purely about degrees and experience, or are there other factors that determine whether or not you should bring a new colleague on board?

Mismatch in the Labor Market

Organizations invest a great deal of energy in recruiting and selecting new employees. After all, every company has a strong interest in getting the right person in the right position. Yet this goes wrong surprisingly often.

📊 The hard numbers:

  • 📉 17% of new employees leave within 6 months
  • 📉 31% leave within 2 years
  • 📉 50% of organizations can’t find the right candidates
Supply and demand in the labor market often turn out to be completely out of sync. On the supply side, potential candidates often lack the required qualifications. They don’t have enough experience, or they lack the right degree. In other cases, the problem is actually an excess of degrees and experience. In addition, some employees are unable—or barely able—to keep up with developments in the labor market and the changing demands of the job. Moreover, (future) employees often turn out to have very different expectations of an organization. First and foremost, they want to feel comfortable within the company and seek work in an environment that suits their personality. When the reality falls short of what they initially anticipated, they quickly become demotivated and start looking for another employer.

Recruitment pays too little attention to potential

There are also shortcomings on the demand side. Attention to training and personal development is often neglected within many organizations. Recently, the UWV called on the business community to do more to facilitate continuing education and retraining for employees. According to the benefits agency, offering apprenticeships and entry-level jobs should also be a higher priority.
Traditional focus Modern approach Impact
Degrees & certificates Learning Ability & Adaptability Sustainable employability
Years of experience Potential & growth mindset Future-proof talent
Technical Skills Soft skills & cultural fit Higher retention
Immediate readiness Development opportunities Long-term value
  Companies are facing rapid, successive changes in technology, organizational structure, and ways of working. That is why organizations should pay much more attention to their employees’ potential. They have the right degree and experience, but to what extent are they able to function in a dynamic environment and adapt to change? How can you ensure that every talented employee can not only develop their potential but also advance in their career? Often, however, the focus is on immediately measurable skills—the so-called “hard” job requirements: degrees and experience. By doing so, organizations miss out on opportunities and pay far too little attention to the future.

Skills for the Future

The U.S.-based Institute for the Future has identified a number of skills that employees will need in the near future. Strikingly, knowledge and experience are notably absent from this list. The skills mentioned appear to be primarily focused on talent, personality, and attitude.

🚀 Essential skills for the future:

  • 🧠 Sense-making: Making sense of complex information
  • 🤝 Social intelligence: Being able to connect deeply with others
  • 💡 Innovative thinking: Coming up with out-of-the-box solutions
  • 🌍 Cross-cultural competence: Working in diverse teams
  • 📱 New media literacy: Communicating effectively online
  • 🔄 Transdisciplinarity: Combining knowledge from different fields
  • 🎯 Design mindset: Shaping and improving processes
  • 📊 Computational thinking: Translating data into insights
  • 🏢 Virtual collaboration: Working productively remotely
  • 🧘 Cognitive load management: Maintaining focus amid information overload
In summary, it can be said that in future-oriented thinking, the ability to adapt and the willingness to learn new things are more important than the knowledge and experience gained in the past.

Effective selection and greater returns require long-term thinking

Short-term solutions usually prove to be largely unsuccessful. It’s like a soccer club that thinks it can stop a string of poor results by quickly signing a few new players. That’s panic soccer. For many organizations, however, long-term thinking is still hardly a reality. As many as fifty percent of organizations do absolutely nothing in the way of strategic workforce planning.

✅ Steps toward better matches:

  1. Analyze successful employees: What makes them valuable?
  2. Define culture & values: What does your organization stand for?
  3. Look beyond resumes: Assess potential and personality
  4. Invest in onboarding: Ensure a smooth transition
  5. Monitor and evaluate: Keep the dialogue open about mutual expectations
Those who think ahead and ask themselves what talents and skills are needed for the future will recruit new employees in a much more targeted and successful manner. To prevent a mismatch, it’s important to first identify which employees within the organization turn out to be a “good match.” Are these employees performing so well because of “hard” or “soft” factors? In many cases, the conclusion will be that employees who are content and feel completely at home in the organizational culture deliver the highest return on investment.

The True Cost of a Mismatch

A wrong hire costs more than you think. In addition to direct costs such as recruitment expenses and salary, there are numerous hidden costs that add up:
Cost category Impact Estimated Costs
Recruitment costs Advertisements, recruitment agency, HR time €5,000 – €15,000
Onboarding period Training, mentoring, lower productivity 3–6 months’ salary
Team productivity Disruption, demotivation, increased workload 20–30% decline
Loss of customers Errors, poor service, damage to relationships Unpredictable
Total Per mismatch 50–200% of annual salary
Recruitment must therefore focus much more on soft skills rather than strict job requirements. Not only must the new colleague be given the space to develop and adapt to changes, but they must also be an ideal “match” for your organization’s culture, motivations, and core values.

Hrmforce Recruitment

The hrmforce matching solution was designed by experienced recruiters and psychologists to add value to your recruitment process. The solution is built on a flexible infrastructure so that it integrates seamlessly with your existing processes, workflows, and systems. This allows you to determine for yourself how to utilize the solution. In this way, your experience and knowledge can be combined with the powerful features of our recruitment solution to achieve a best-practice recruitment process and thereby (significantly) reduce the likelihood of a mismatch.
title: Avoid a mismatch when hiring new employees.
