body:
In organizational and team development, Lencioni’s model is a powerful tool for gaining better insights and more control over team performance. It starts with an assessment in which team members complete an online questionnaire. How is the team doing? To measure is to know: a perfect starting point. Then the real work begins! The team members get to work on the insights and areas for improvement. Our expert Jan-Hein Ooms explains how this works and what key points to focus on.

Model Provides Focus for Team Development

Effective team functioning is becoming increasingly important. Team development allows you to work on this in a targeted way. It starts with analyzing the team’s performance and the personalities within it. A leading model for this is Lencioni’s. At the heart of this are five characteristics that build up from the foundation (Trust) into a pyramid. The four subsequent focus areas are (constructive) Conflict, Commitment, Accountability, and Achieving Results together. “The power of this model lies in its ability to immediately identify areas for improvement and provide insights that directly guide your team development. Trust is the foundation here, as it is with so many things in life. The beauty of the pyramid is that the ‘higher’ you climb, the more you realize that you also need everything in the layers below. It may sound logical, but it’s often overlooked in team development, even though it’s very important,” says Ooms.

Applying Lencioni’s Insights

Organizations that use hrmforce’s online questionnaire for Lencioni Teamwork can also receive assistance after the scan in guiding team development and applying the insights gained. Hrmforce and Ooms work closely together on this. This guidance is an option, but certainly not a requirement. Organizations can therefore also use the questionnaire on its own and determine their own next steps. The model provides teams with insight and awareness regarding the qualities, characteristics, and pitfalls of team members. “Sometimes it can also be confrontational. For example, if team members differ significantly from the others in certain areas. That can actually be very interesting, because it may say something about their role or the functioning of the entire team. In any case, it’s a good starting point for the dialogue that follows, aimed at working together on team development.” Lencioni’s model comes from the book *The 5 Dysfunctions of a Team* by Patrick Lencioni. It’s not heavy reading and is actually very easy to get through. It’s like a novel about a CEO who has to lead an executive team that has become deeply divided. This, in turn, negatively affects the entire organization.

Five Major Team Frustrations

As you read the book, the five major frustrations that team members struggle with are highlighted. These are relatable issues for many people who work with others. Here are the five frustrations, from the bottom to the top of the pyramid:
  1. Lack of Trust
This occurs when team members do not dare to be vulnerable within a team, are unwilling to admit their mistakes, weaknesses, or needs, and do not ask for help. A certain level of comfort among team members is necessary; otherwise, the foundation for trust cannot be established.
  1. Fear of Conflict
Without trust, teams are unable to engage in unfiltered, passionate debates about important issues. This creates situations where team conflicts can easily turn into backroom discussions and gossip. In a work environment where team members do not openly express their opinions, poor decisions are the result.
  1. Lack of Engagement
Without conflict, it is difficult for team members to commit to decisions. This creates an unclear environment. The lack of direction and engagement quickly leads to employee dissatisfaction.
  1. Avoiding Responsibility
If teams do not commit to a clear approach, even the most driven employees will hesitate to call out their colleagues on behaviors and actions that are important to the team.
  1. Lack of Focus on Team Results
When responsibility for the team is neglected, team members tend to prioritize their own needs (such as career development, ego, and recognition). When a team loses focus on team results, the entire organization ultimately suffers.

Key Requirements

Anyone who gains insight into the five key areas can work on them from a positive perspective. The approach is suitable for all organizations that want to get started with team development. Ooms: “In practice, I see many commercial companies using this approach, but that’s not a requirement. Non-commercial organizations—such as those in education—can also put it to excellent use. The model is always useful and always adds value to team development.” An important prerequisite is that the organizational or team culture be conducive to it. Ooms: “There must be—or must be created—some openness and transparency to get started with this. Team members must feel safe enough to be open. If a team member is a bit skeptical at first, that’s okay. That, in turn, can yield valuable insights and action items.” In addition, buy-in is an important prerequisite. “Team members must be open to working on their growth and development. That starts with buy-in at the top. You have to really want this and take action. It starts with leading by example.”

Real-World Example: ING

Ooms himself gained extensive experience with Lencioni’s model at ING. With a background in business administration and health sciences, he worked at ING for many years. When the organization adopted a more agile way of working, Ooms spent years focusing on team development and leadership development among management teams. “As a result, I have many tools and methods at my disposal that allow teams to focus on specific areas for development. This can be done in all sorts of ways. For example, to start building mutual trust among team members, I’ve sometimes had them briefly present their own life stories using music, anecdotes, and photos. What emerged from this in such a short time was very interesting and immediately provided a lot of insight into shared norms and values. Team members quickly got to know each other better, and trust grew, allowing them to move up to the next levels in the pyramid.”

Repeating the Online Survey

The power of online questionnaires lies in the fact that, in team development, they can be completed again at regular intervals to measure progress. “After the initial assessment, you start working on interventions and areas for improvement. But ideally, it doesn’t stop there. For example, you can repeat the scan every six months or year to see if the goals are being met and how the team is developing in the meantime. In addition to improvements in results or, for example, engagement, you might also notice that trust dips slightly at certain times. Why is that? You can discuss this together to ensure you continue to steer the entire development process effectively. Team development is not a short-term project. Team development is primarily focused on the long and medium term. You can always keep working on it by looking for ways to improve things.”

Watch the Expert Session

Are you interested in improving team dynamics and achieving top results within your organization? Then don’t miss our recent expert session with Jan Hein Ooms. In this engaging video, Ooms—drawing on his expertise in health sciences and business management—shares valuable insights into the Lencioni methodology and the importance of a strong foundation in teams. This session is a must-see for managers and team leaders who seek a deeper understanding of team dynamics and the application of the Lencioni model. Click here or on the image below to watch the video.

body:
Coaching is becoming increasingly important to the success of organizations and the development of employees. That said, the proliferation of coaches in recent years does pose a challenge—especially if you want to use coaching in a targeted way that delivers demonstrable results. One key solution is to support coaching programs with objective measurement tools, such as online questionnaires. In addition, a comprehensive organizational policy on coaching can make a significant difference.

The Challenge

Many organizations, HR professionals, and managers are still figuring out how to use coaching effectively, purposefully, and in a measurable way. For example, when it comes to one-off coaching programs for teams, employees, or managers, or because they want to modernize their performance review cycle with a greater emphasis on development discussions and coaching.

A Proliferation of Coaches

Coaching can be extremely valuable for taking the (personal) development and performance of employees or teams to the next level. The problem, however, is that the measurability of the results often leaves much to be desired. And this despite the fact that there has been a veritable proliferation of coaches in recent years. Anyone can call themselves a coach in this unregulated profession. Many coaches undoubtedly begin their new “calling” with the best of intentions, but there are concerns about unclear methodologies and results that can vary widely. And that’s not all. A coach can also have a significant influence on important decisions in people’s professional or personal lives. So you really have to handle that with great care. Two-thirds of occupational physicians and psychologists seriously question whether all these coaches are sufficiently qualified and whether they actually deliver high-quality services, according to a 2019 study by the National Stress Debate. At that time, this already represented an increase of no less than 66 percent compared to five years earlier. According to the Chamber of Commerce, the number of coaches specializing in stress and burnout alone has increased more than tenfold in 20 years (to 4,484 by 2019). Many occupational physicians and psychologists refer to this as a “proliferation,” and Intermediair calculated this year that this trend has been further fueled during the COVID-19 crisis. This data again shows a fourfold increase over the past five years.

Questionnaires for measurable results

How should an organization deal with this uncontrolled growth? After all, you do want to ensure you have high-quality coaches who are a good fit for your organization’s needs. Because career or lifestyle coaching is, of course, very different from, for example, coaching for personal leadership or for stress or burnout issues. And once a coaching program is underway, you naturally want to see measurable, objective results. This doesn’t require sharing the personal details of an individual coaching program with the employer. However, measuring progress is a key part of the solution to this current challenge facing organizations and HR professionals. Therefore, start by determining what types of coaching are needed. Ask prospective coaches or coaching firms about their experience in this area. And also ask how they address the need for measurable outcomes. There are now effective (online) tools available to monitor progress, such as the online questionnaires from hrmforce. These allow users to conduct an objective baseline assessment and then monitor the effects and track changes (such as behavior). This makes it possible to objectively assess the development of employees, managers, or teams. It provides insight into the effectiveness of the coaching and gives you greater control over a goal-oriented and effective coaching approach within your organization.

Organization-wide coaching policy

In addition, it is valuable for organizations to develop a comprehensive policy in the area of coaching. Employers often already have everything well organized when it comes to absenteeism, but this is often not yet the case for coaching. “Coaching is often implemented differently depending on the employee, department, or manager,” explains Michael Gijzenberg of hrmforce. He has been active as an organizational consultant, trainer, and coach for more than twenty-five years. Gijzenberg places great value on measurability and uses hrmforce’s online questionnaires for this purpose. Gijzenberg: “In coaching, awareness is the most essential component. To accelerate this process and make it concrete, we have our own talent portal where we can provide insights to get to the heart of the matter more quickly, effectively, and efficiently.” As an organizational consultant, Gijzenberg also helps employers develop broader (coaching) policies. A key reason such policies are often still lacking appears to be the fact that coaching in the Netherlands is still primarily viewed as a “personal process.” But this seems set to change in the coming years. Gijzenberg: “In part, coaching is a personal journey between an employee and his or her coach, but you cannot view an individual employee in isolation from his or her work environment. By taking all important factors into account, coaching can be deployed in a much more powerful, concrete, and goal-oriented way.”

Choosing the Right Coach(es)

A sound coaching policy can also help clarify what kind of coaching suits your organization and the key challenges it faces. Handy search tools are now available to help find coaches with (accredited) training. It may also be wise to choose a coaching firm that employs multiple coaches. In addition to their different areas of expertise, this can be valuable for providing broader feedback to your organization. After all, this is much more difficult to achieve with multiple individual coaches or coaching firms than with a single, dedicated coaching partner. When searching for the right partner(s), you’ll quickly come across various (English) terms for the different types of coaching available. Here are some common terms with brief explanations:
  • Business coaching: for developing business-related aspects.
  • Corporate coaching: focused on the entire organization.
  • Counseling: more focused on emotional aspects and finding meaning.
  • Executive coaching: focused on the development of top managers.
  • Career coaching: focused on career development, hiring, and turnover.
  • Mediation: for facilitating the resolution of disputes and conflicts.
  • Performance coaching: for behavioral, competency, and mental development.
  • Personal/Life coaching: for personal matters such as work-life balance.
  • Team coaching: focused on coaching teams or departments.
It is also common for coaches to provide coaching in multiple areas. This can also be a valuable consideration. And once you seem to have found the right coaching provider, be sure to pay close attention to measurability. This provides insight into the value and concrete results of the coaching and offers input for further developing your coaching policy.
title: More Effective Coaching in Organizations Using Objective Measurement Tools

body:
Objective interviews are essential for selecting the best candidates during the hiring process. However, actually conducting them is not so simple due to various classic pitfalls and often unconscious human subjectivity. Fortunately, well-designed questionnaires and the right interview techniques help ensure that the most objective and balanced assessment is made.

The Importance of Objective Selection Interviews

Objectivity doesn’t exist. But you can strive for it. This allows you to recruit the best and most suitable candidates for your organization and to offer candidates fair opportunities. Effective selection is a skill in itself. Ideally, you do this by evaluating candidates as objectively as possible. Objective recruitment and selection means not relying on a “click” but rather selecting candidates based on their relevant characteristics and competencies. The selection interview is a crucial moment in the recruitment process. It differs from an introductory interview in that more people from your organization are often present. This can also make it more difficult to conduct the interview as objectively as possible. Many employers and HR departments therefore wonder which selection methods can help them and which will yield the best results. We’ve listed a number of key points to consider.

Common Pitfalls in Selection Interviews

During selection interviews, there are various pitfalls that you can fall into—usually without realizing it. These include relying too heavily on a candidate’s first impression or acting on preconceptions and stereotypes. The latter can unfairly rule out much better candidates right from the start. Another major pitfall is placing too much emphasis on a single positive aspect of a candidate during the evaluation. This is also known as the “halo effect.” Based on this, you unconsciously assume that a candidate’s other qualities “must be just as good” if this one trait is so strong. Like a “halo,” this positive trait then casts its light onto the other traits, and you become blind to other aspects. The opposite effect can also occur. In that case, too much weight is placed on a single negative aspect. This is also known as the “Horn effect.” Unconsciously, biases always play a role in recruitment and selection—whether we want them to or not. This is due to our ancient instincts, which cause us to “flinch” when something deviates from what we’re used to. In this alert mode, we then assess whether someone is a “friend or foe.” The more homogeneous the group in which you grew up, the greater the chance that you’ll unconsciously slip into that alarm mode. This is due to the oldest part of our brain—the reptilian brain—which has had the longest time to evolve and is therefore the most powerful. As a result, we often make 95 percent of our decisions unconsciously using this part of our brain. So if you’re not careful, you’ll quickly end up making more primitive choices than we, as developed, civilized beings, often realize.

Questionnaires and interview techniques help

So how can we conduct a selection interview that’s as objective as possible, without falling into these sometimes ancient pitfalls? Two tools are particularly important here: well-designed questionnaires that objectively assess candidates’ characteristics and effective interview techniques to gather the right information. This allows you to evaluate different candidates using the same criteria. Which questionnaires are important for a recruitment process can vary depending on the organization and the specific position or role within your organization. Commonly used questionnaires include, for example, the Motivation Test, a Personality Test (Big50), or an Intelligence Test (also known as a cognitive ability test). Questionnaires are also valuable for conducting competency-based selection interviews, thereby providing clear insight into candidates’ competencies. A Selection Assessment is also a valuable tool. This is a testing method used in recruitment and selection procedures to evaluate applicants’ suitability for a specific position. The assessment is also used to gain insight into individual qualities and to determine, for example, education and training recommendations. Such a suitability assessment significantly increases the success rate of recruitment and selection processes.

Structured Interview Techniques

Conducting well-structured interviews with candidates is essential for carrying out better and more objective selection interviews. In this process, the interviewer carefully evaluates the criteria against which an applicant is assessed for the relevant job profile. This allows for a more accurate evaluation of qualities such as knowledge, expertise, and professional competence, as well as important soft skills. Standards and scores are then established for all questions. This prevents misunderstandings or skewed comparisons regarding who receives a positive or less positive evaluation. Candidates are thus assessed more fairly based on the same questions, criteria, and standards. This significantly reduces the likelihood that subjective judgments—such as first impressions, the halo effect, or the Horn effect—will play a decisive role in selecting the most suitable candidate. As a result, the reliability of a structured interview is much higher than that of unstructured interviews, making it a better method for predicting job performance. This is also confirmed by the study “Personnel Selection in the Netherlands,” conducted by the staffing agency Yacht in collaboration with the University of Amsterdam.

STARR Interview Technique

A good method for conducting structured interviews is the STARR method. This is a widely used tool among HR managers. It serves as a kind of interview guide aimed at assessing candidates’ experience and knowledge. The interviewer asks questions about past events in which a candidate had to apply certain skills or knowledge. The focus is on various fixed aspects of that event, summarized by the acronym STARR. It stands for: Situation, Task, Action, and Result (and possibly an additional R for Reflection): Situation – What is the situation or context? Task – What was the task the candidate undertook? Action – What actions did the candidate take? Result – What was the response to this, and was the final result satisfactory? It is important to ask follow-up questions during the interview to gain a clear picture of the situation and how a candidate responds. The starting point of the STARR method is a specific trait of an individual—for example, “leadership” if this is a key competency for the position in question. The STARR method makes these sometimes somewhat abstract traits concrete and links them to practical work situations.
title: Questionnaires and Interview Techniques Are Crucial for More Objective Hiring Interviews

body:
An intelligence test for adults measures your cognitive skills, such as logical thinking, memory, and problem-solving ability. These tests are increasingly used in job applications, career counseling, and personal development. Maybe you’re wondering if you’re smart enough for that new job, or you just want to know how you measure up against others. Intelligence tests answer these questions and help you discover your strengths.

What will we cover in this article?

• The different types of intelligence tests for adults • When you should consider taking an IQ test • How to best prepare • Where to find reliable tests • Practical tips for better results

What is an intelligence test, and why would you take one?

An intelligence test is a standardized tool that measures various aspects of your intelligence. The test consists of tasks that assess your verbal skills, spatial reasoning, working memory, and processing speed. Most adults take an intelligence test for professional reasons. Employers are increasingly using these tests during the hiring process because they provide an objective picture of your cognitive abilities. Career counselors also use intelligence tests to help you make the right choice of major or career change. In addition, some people take an IQ test out of curiosity. They want to know how they score and where their talents lie. This can be valuable for personal development and self-awareness.

Discover Intelligence Tests

The main types of intelligence tests for adults

Different types of tests each measure different aspects of your intelligence and have their own advantages and disadvantages.

WAIS-IV: the gold standard

The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale-IV is considered the most reliable intelligence test for adults. Psychologists worldwide use this test for diagnosis and research. The WAIS-IV takes about 90 minutes and measures four main areas: verbal comprehension, perceptual reasoning, working memory, and processing speed. You’ll be presented with various types of tasks. For example, vocabulary exercises, memorizing number sequences, solving block puzzles, and identifying patterns. Each task tests a different aspect of your intelligence. The advantage of the WAIS-IV is its scientific basis. The disadvantages are the high cost and the requirement to see a licensed psychologist. A full test typically costs between 300 and 500 euros.

Raven’s Progressive Matrices: Culture-Free Testing

This test uses only visual patterns, without words or numbers. You’re shown incomplete patterns and must choose which figure completes the pattern. Raven’s test is popular because cultural background and language proficiency have less of an impact on your score. The test consists of various difficulty levels, ranging from simple patterns to complex logical puzzles. Many companies use a version of this test during the hiring process because it is quick and objective.

Ability Scan: Modern Cognitive Assessment

The Ability Scan combines intelligence assessments with practical applications for your career. This assessment not only tests your cognitive skills but also shows how they align with various roles and work environments. The advantage of the Ability Scan is that it gives you immediate insight into which professions best match your cognitive profile. You’ll receive a comprehensive report with concrete advice for your career development. The test takes about 45 minutes and is more affordable than traditional psychological assessments.

Discover intelligence tests

When should you consider taking an intelligence test?

The right time for an intelligence test depends on your personal or professional situation.

For your career

More and more employers are using cognitive tests during the hiring process. These tests have become standard, especially in sectors such as IT, consulting, and financial services. By taking a professional test in advance, you’ll know what to expect and where your strengths lie. An Ability Scan can help you gain insight into your cognitive skills and how they align with different job roles. These modern assessments not only reflect your IQ level but also provide recommendations on suitable career paths.

If you have learning difficulties or trouble concentrating

Do you struggle with certain tasks at work, or do you find that you’re slower than your colleagues? An intelligence test can reveal whether you have specific weaknesses or, conversely, hidden talents. Sometimes, people with ADHD or dyslexia turn out to be above-average in certain areas.

For personal development

Self-awareness is valuable for your continued growth and development. By understanding your cognitive profile, you can make more informed choices in both your professional and personal life. You might discover that you excel at spatial reasoning, which could open up new career opportunities in architecture or engineering.

Discover the intelligence test

How do you prepare for an intelligence test?

Proper preparation can improve your test performance.

Physical Preparation

Make sure you’re well-rested before taking the test. Lack of sleep has a direct negative effect on your performance on cognitive tasks. Eat a light meal beforehand—not too much, but don’t go in on an empty stomach either. Caffeine can help with concentration, but don’t overdo it.

Mental preparation

Practice with online puzzles and logic problems to keep your mind sharp. Sudoku, crossword puzzles, and brain teasers train your thinking skills. Note: You can’t really “study” for an intelligence test, but you can get used to the types of questions. Stay calm during the test. Stress negatively affects your performance. Breathe calmly and take your time with each question. On most tests, you won’t lose points for wrong answers, so feel free to guess if you’re unsure.

Different test formats and what to expect

Each test has its own structure and measurement method, but here’s a general idea of what to expect:

Verbal intelligence

These sections test your vocabulary, reading comprehension, and ability to make verbal connections. You’ll be asked questions such as: “What is the similarity between…?” You may also be asked to explain the meaning of words or draw analogies.

Numerical intelligence

This section focuses on arithmetic skills and logical thinking with numbers. Examples include arithmetic sequences, percentage calculations, and math puzzles. These sections often predict how well you’ll perform in analytical roles.

Spatial intelligence

These tests measure your ability to work with shapes, patterns, and spatial relationships. For example, you might have to mentally rotate figures or recognize patterns. Architects, engineers, and designers usually score high here.

What Does Your IQ Score Actually Mean?

Your IQ score provides an indication of your cognitive abilities, but its interpretation has limitations. An average IQ score is around 100 points. About 68% of people score between 85 and 115 points. Scores above 130 are considered above average, while scores below 70 are considered below average. Important to know: your IQ score isn’t a fixed number. Factors such as stress, fatigue, and motivation can affect your performance. Also, each test measures different aspects of intelligence, so you may get different scores on different tests. Furthermore, your IQ score says nothing about creativity, emotional intelligence, or practical skills. These aspects are just as important for success in work and life.

Where can you find reliable intelligence tests?

The choice of test provider largely determines the reliability of your results.

Professional HR Assessments

For practical applications, HR assessments such as the Ability Scan offer the best balance between reliability and usability. This test provides concrete recommendations for your further development.

Psychologists and Diagnostics

For the most accurate results, consult a licensed psychologist. They use validated instruments such as the WAIS-IV and can professionally interpret your results. However, the costs are higher.

Common Misconceptions About IQ Tests

There are several myths surrounding intelligence tests that lead to false expectations. People often think that intelligence is fixed and doesn’t change. This isn’t true. Your brain continues to develop, and you can train your cognitive skills. Solving puzzles, learning new languages, and reading challenging books keep your mind sharp. Another misconception is that a high IQ automatically guarantees success. Emotional intelligence, perseverance, and social skills are just as important. Some people with an average IQ perform better than highly gifted individuals because they work harder and collaborate better with others. It’s also often thought that IQ tests are discriminatory. Modern tests try to avoid cultural bias by using a variety of task types. Still, factors such as education and social background can still have an impact.

Tips for Better Test Performance

Start with the easy questions to build confidence. Most tests begin simply and gradually get more difficult. By quickly answering the simple questions first, you build confidence and save time for the more challenging sections. Read each question carefully. Rushing leads to unnecessary mistakes. Take the time to understand what’s being asked before you answer. With multiple-choice questions, you can sometimes eliminate answers by thinking logically. Use your time wisely. On timed tests, it’s better to try to answer all the questions than to give perfect answers to only half of them. If in doubt, take a guess; you usually won’t lose points for incorrect answers. Stay focused but relax between sections. Stress significantly impairs your performance. Breathe calmly and think positively. You’re already doing well by taking the test seriously.

How do you interpret your test results?

Interpreting your scores correctly helps you make the most of the results. Your test results usually come in the form of different scores for different domains. Don’t just look at your total score; also look at the distribution. Perhaps you excel at verbal tasks but are average at numerical tasks. Compare your results with relevant reference groups. A score of 110 is above average in the general population, but perhaps average among college graduates. Context is important when interpreting results. Use your results constructively. You can further develop your strengths and apply them in your work. You don’t have to avoid your weaker areas, but you can take them into account when making important decisions. Remember that a single test doesn’t tell the whole story about your abilities. Different tests can yield different results, depending on what they measure and how you were feeling that day.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I increase my IQ? You can improve your performance on intelligence tests through training and practice. Your underlying intelligence doesn’t change easily, but cognitive skills can be trained. At what age are adult tests reliable? You can take adult tests starting around age 16. Most tests are standardized for people aged 16 to 90. How often can I take an intelligence test ? For reliable results, wait at least six months between tests. Otherwise, you might score better due to repetition, not because of increased intelligence. Are online IQ tests reliable? Free online tests provide, at best, a rough indication. Professional online tests can be reliable, but always check the scientific basis. Want to know what an intelligence test can mean for your career? Then consider the Ability Scan, which maps your cognitive skills and directly links them to concrete career opportunities. This way, you’ll not only discover your IQ but also how to best apply your talents in your work and life.

Discover the intelligence test

Organizations that want to take a targeted approach to their team and talent development often need a simple yet effective tool to assess the potential and performance of their employees. The 9-Box Grid Model has been a widely used tool for identifying and monitoring performance, talents, and potential for many years. In this article, you’ll learn how to use this tool and what key considerations to keep in mind when introducing it to your organization.

What is the 9-Box Model?

The “9-Box” is a relatively simple yet powerful tool for identifying, retaining, and developing talented employees. This can be done at both the individual and team levels. That’s why, in addition to talent development, it’s also valuable for team development or, for example, strategic workforce planning. The model maps out employees’ potential and talent and compares them to their performance. This makes it easier to identify high performers, “future leaders,” or potential successors for specific roles within a team. It also allows you to better identify which employees’ performance may still fall short of their potential and where there may still be opportunities for growth. [caption id="attachment_20147" align="aligncenter" width="500"] source: www.aihr.com[/caption]

Origins of the Model

The 9-Box Grid Model has been around for a long time. It was developed in the 1970s by the consulting firm McKinsey. It was initially used to compare business teams with one another. This allowed companies to better determine which business units required investment. Its use gained international recognition when the American company General Electric began applying it. The famous CEO Jack Welch placed strong emphasis on improving performance by attracting and retaining the right people. The model later evolved into a well-known HR tool for measuring the performance and potential of teams and individual employees.

Using the 9-Box Matrix

Today, the model remains the most widely used performance matrix internationally. As a result, many internationally oriented companies also use it. For users of the hrmforce development platform, the 9-Box Matrix is available as a standard feature. This makes it possible to gain a clear overview of the entire organization or specific units relatively quickly. This is achieved by having managers evaluate employees according to the model along two axes: their potential and their performance. This creates a grid of nine quadrants into which employees are categorized. For each organization and team, you can specify who is authorized to assign scores and who can view the results.

In this video, you’ll see how it works:

Using the Results

The results provide a quick overview of employees’ performance, talents, and potential. This is valuable for facilitating discussions among managers using a consistent framework. It helps ensure targeted investments in areas such as talent and team development. The results can also be used to foster constructive conversations between managers and employees, such as those focused on career development.

Benefits of the 9-Box Grid Model

The 9-box grid offers several advantages for organizations that use it, including compared to other available models. Organizations that use it often cite these benefits for monitoring and facilitating talent and team development:
  • The simple model powerfully simplifies the identification of high-potential employees or potential leaders.
  • It provides a standardized way to evaluate employees in their current roles. This makes it easier to assess performance and potential consistently and to compare employees.
  • Talent identification: The 9-Box helps organizations identify high-potential employees so they can offer them the right resources and opportunities for further development.
  • The model is transparent and provides employees with an honest view of how the organization assesses their potential.
  • The model provides a valuable overview of the existing employee population at a glance. This enables organizations to optimize their talent management and make sound decisions regarding employee development and career planning.
  • The model can help organizations set quality standards for employees and evaluate performance against these standards. This enables organizations to improve performance standards and encourage employees to reach their full potential.
  • Recruit fewer new employees. With a better understanding of the existing workforce and its potential, it becomes easier to retain key talent, reducing the need to recruit them. This can help prevent high-potential employees from leaving.
A well-known drawback is that the assessment can be quite subjective, especially when a single manager assigns the scores. In such cases, objective data—such as questionnaires for 360-degree feedback or the use of motivation tests or personality assessments for talent or team development—is not utilized. However, the subjective view resulting from a one-sided assessment can be broadened by involving multiple people in assigning scores to employees.

Points to Consider When Implementing the 9-Box Grid

To get the most out of the 9-Box Grid Model as an organization, effective implementation of the approach is essential in addition to the online tool. To this end, discuss internally with teams why and how the model is used, as well as the criteria that play a role in the assessment. These criteria typically relate to both performance and behavior. Also specify what follow-up steps are taken after an employee has been placed in a particular quadrant. It should not become a “judgmental model.” Define and clarify the different quadrants of the model as well. After all, how do you define “low,” “average,” or “high” performance internally? Where possible, align these definitions with internal job or competency profiles. Keep the model up to date by regularly assessing employees’ performance and potential. Continue to adapt the model over time to the organization’s changing needs. Once all employees have received a score, it’s time to discuss the results. Managers gain valuable insight into the composition of their team in terms of performance and potential. These results provide a solid foundation for strategically advancing the team’s development and growth. After all, what does the team want to achieve in the future? The 9-Box Model can also help answer this question and provide a roadmap for achieving that goal.

What do the 9 boxes mean?

The 9-Box classification model consists of nine boxes, each representing a specific combination of performance and potential. They’re almost self-explanatory, but at their core, they have the following meanings:
  • Box 1: Low Performance/Low Potential: These employees may not have the right skills or motivation to improve their performance and reach their potential. What does this mean for the future? Can the organization still help with their development?
  • Box 2: Average Performance/Low Potential: Employees perform at an average level but show little potential for growth and development. The organization can explore ways to motivate these employees and support their development.
  • Box 3: Low Performance/Average Potential: Performance is low, but there is potential for growth and development. The organization can help these employees develop, for example through training and coaching.
  • Box 4: High Performance/Low Potential: When high performance is combined with little potential for growth and development, the organization can reward employees for their performance. However, it should also explore new ways to motivate and challenge these employees.
  • Box 5: Average performance/Average potential: This group, which is quite average in terms of performance and potential, can be supported in their development by challenging them to reach their potential.
  • Box 6: Low Performance/High Potential: There’s still plenty of room for improvement here! An organization can help these employees develop and challenge them to reach their potential.
  • Box 7: High Performance/Average Potential: The organization can reward these employees for their performance and challenge them to further develop their potential.
  • Box 8: Average Performance/High Potential: Employees perform at an average level but show great potential for growth and development. The organization can support these employees’ development and challenge them to reach their potential.
  • Box 9: High Performance/High Potential: These employees are valuable assets to the organization! They should be encouraged and rewarded to reach their potential. The organization should also look for ways to involve them in the organization’s development.
title: Work on team and talent development with the 9 Box

Due to the severe labor shortage, employers are increasingly turning to recruiting candidates from other professions. With a strong focus on their previously acquired competencies and effective guidance, this is an attractive recruitment channel. A competency test is valuable in this regard, but a motivation test and a personality test can also significantly increase the chances of success.

Shortages in an Increasing Number of Sectors

The growing shortages in the labor market—partly due to an aging population—were predicted years ago. In recent years, they have become increasingly noticeable in more and more sectors. Trains are running less frequently, Schiphol Airport can’t handle the holiday crowds, and school classes are increasingly being sent home due to the teacher shortage. And this isn’t just happening in the Netherlands, but throughout Europe. That makes the problem even more complex to solve. In the Netherlands, unemployment fell to a historic low of 3.3 percent in the first quarter of 2022. Looking at the entire eurozone, unemployment has also never been this low. In addition to the sectors that have long been struggling with structural labor shortages (such as healthcare, IT, engineering, and education), more sectors are now joining the list. Due to this shortage, the UWV’s list of high-demand occupations in early 2022 suddenly included forklift operators, train dispatchers, hotel receptionists, cleaning staff, and, for example, physical therapists. As a result, employers in an increasing number of sectors must tap into additional sources to find new employees. And this is not a temporary issue. We must expect staffing shortages in many sectors for many years to come.

More Candidates Through Career Changers

An interesting additional “pool” to draw from is that of career changers. After all, let’s not forget that there are also shrinking industries. And many people working in those sectors would like to transition to different professions and industries. Making that move is often quite feasible. Especially if employers carefully assess candidates’ competencies and match them to the competencies and tasks required within their organization. Sometimes there are also very logical connections to be made, as illustrated by the UWV’s lists of career transition options. In the Netherlands, the SER (Social and Economic Council), as an important advisory body, also advocates for a more skills-focused labor market approach. “Taking a more nuanced look at the skills people already possess and the opportunities those skills offer—whether or not through targeted training—opens up many possibilities. A breakthrough that provides a solid foundation for the developments in tomorrow’s labor market,” said then-SER Chair Mariëtte Hamer in 2021.

What is needed for successful career transitions?

Due to the increasing labor mobility across sectors in recent years, we’re gaining a clearer understanding of the conditions for successful lateral entry. This naturally starts with a focus on competencies, rather than traditional criteria such as degrees and work experience. Consequently, candidates’ previously acquired competencies must be clearly identified. In addition, the motivation and personality traits of lateral entrants also play an important role. This is also evident from an analysis by *Binnenlands Bestuur* that examined lateral entry into the engineering field. Furthermore, effective guidance and training are key success factors—ideally tailored to ensure that an educational program or training course is well-aligned with the career changer’s existing skills and those still to be developed.

Quick Insight into Competencies, Personality, and Motivation

Fortunately, convenient (online) tests are now available to quickly and effectively assess candidates’ competencies, motivation, and personal characteristics. For measuring skills, for example, there is the Competency Check from hrmforce. This provides a new or existing employee with feedback on their own behavior and competencies (also known as “zero-degree feedback”). In just twenty minutes, this provides a much clearer picture of strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities for development. In addition, a Motivation Test and a Personality Test (Big50) are also available. Motivators are also important, though not everyone is fully aware of their own. What drives a person? Is it status, independence, compensation, self-development, or creativity that matters most in their work? And does that align with the work in your organization? Furthermore, the results of a personality test can be translated into competencies, for example, based on an “ideal profile” for career changers. These tests quickly provide a clear picture of candidates and the likelihood of success for career changers in your organization.

Use of a Single Competency-Based Language

Conducting effective competency-based interviews—and productive development discussions after hiring—requires, above all, clear competency-based language. To achieve this, you can use competency-based questionnaires and, for example, the previously mentioned Competency Check. The questions can be linked to the competency profiles that are important for your organization and its roles. The characteristics from a Big50 Personality Test can also be linked to these. Unambiguous competency language is an important tool for conducting effective competency-based interviews. It ensures that everyone speaks the same language and helps prevent misunderstandings. Competency language clearly defines which competencies you are using and what behaviors correspond to them. An organization can develop its own competency framework or adopt an existing one, as there are already established frameworks available. A practical example: users of HRMForce’s HR software can create their own framework and integrate it with the tools, but a competency framework is also available that includes a comprehensive competency handbook. This framework comprises approximately 50 competencies (based on the Big50) that make behavior measurable and discussable. For each competency, a definition is provided along with examples of behaviors at various job levels, complete with selection questions, development tips, and coaching advice.

Research on Career Changers

After reviewing the tools designed to ensure the success of lateral entry and ongoing competency management, we will now examine the previously mentioned success factors in greater detail. Because there is still relatively limited knowledge and research data on lateral entry initiatives in the Netherlands, the Gak Institute (which focuses on the labor market and social security) commissioned a study in 2020. The findings regarding the chances of success for lateral entry are positive. “Organizations that link talent and value are highly successful. The success of a lateral entry initiative often hinges on effectively managing expectations and addressing the concerns of lateral entrants,” according to the study. The researchers also note that training is a key requirement for enabling career changers to successfully transition from one job to another. “Employers also want to take previously acquired competencies and skills into account,” the researchers note. However, there is also a clear demand for flexible, personalized training programs, which traditional educational providers in particular are not always able to offer effectively. In part, this is, of course, a broader societal (educational) challenge, although more and more partnerships are now emerging through which employers themselves are launching more flexible training programs (such as specialized vocational schools). These are often structured with various modules that can be tailored to each individual.

Examples of Successful Career-Changer Initiatives

Those who wish to focus more on attracting lateral entrants can now find an increasing number of examples of other initiatives. These are often organized at the regional, local, or sectoral level. In education, for example, there is the career change program offered by the Onderwijsloket, and similar initiatives exist in fields such as engineering or elder care. At the regional and local levels, there are also successful initiatives that take a more cross-sectoral approach. One interesting initiative in the Amsterdam Metropolitan Area is House of Skills, a partnership between the business community, industry associations, employee and employer organizations, knowledge institutions, educational institutions, and regional policymakers aimed at restructuring the labor market to be more competency-based. For career changers, there is, among other things, a “Transferpunt Zorg en Welzijn” (Health and Welfare Transfer Center) and an initiative for career paths in Engineering and Construction. The aforementioned study by the Gak Institute also highlights various successful initiatives and their success factors, including the “De Achthonderd” initiative. This is a regional platform where close integration takes place, bringing candidates, recruitment specialists, employers, and training providers together. By 2023, De Achthonderd aims to have secured approximately 800 sustainable job placements. Among other things, the study praises the “close collaboration within the chain.” Of course, there are an increasing number of examples where the focus is on lateral entry and prior learning. We will undoubtedly see this much more frequently in the coming years.
title: Focusing on acquired competencies makes lateral entry more effective

body:
Integrity in the workplace is an important and fundamental value for many organizations. So it makes sense that they would want to measure it. But measuring integrity can be quite challenging. As part of feedback for employees themselves, it’s not too difficult, but when it comes to broader personality assessments for recruitment and selection, things quickly become more complex. In this article, you’ll learn how to approach measuring integrity in an organization in a way that’s both valuable and responsible.

The Challenge of Measuring Integrity

Integrity is a personal trait that ensures you are honest, sincere, and consistent—and, for example, not susceptible to bribery. Employees who act honestly, reliably, and responsibly contribute to a stimulating and healthy work culture and to the achievement of business goals. Measuring integrity can therefore be valuable and insightful for organizations—including during the recruitment and selection process. After all, as an organization, you want to know what kind of people you’re bringing on board. Still, measuring integrity in the workplace is quite complex. Integrity tests can certainly be useful, but it’s important to look beyond just the numbers and test results. It also depends on the purpose of the assessment. As part of a feedback survey for employees themselves, it’s certainly a useful tool. However, when used as part of recruitment and selection processes, it becomes more complex. Why is that, exactly?

Scientific Research on Reliability

Over the past few decades, a great deal of scientific research has been conducted on the reliability of integrity assessments and the context in which these assessments take place. In these assessments—especially in recruitment and selection—the following factors often complicate matters:

  1. Social desirability

People want to present themselves in the best possible light, especially during job interviews. This can lead to socially desirable responses, causing candidates to portray themselves as more honest or ethical than their actual behavior suggests.

  1. Overestimation of One’s Own Behavior

Various studies show that people often unconsciously and sincerely overestimate their own behavior when it comes to ethics and integrity.

  1. Complexity of Behavior

Integrity is a broad concept and certainly not just black and white. What is seen as “ethical” behavior in one situation may be considered unethical in another. Moreover, it is not a fixed trait or a one-time achievement. It is something you can work on, and environmental or organizational influences (which, in turn, can change) play an important role in this process. Many studies emphasize that a high integrity score does not automatically mean that someone actually behaves with integrity. This is partly due to the risk of socially desirable responses, as this 1993 American study already demonstrated. However, reliability does appear to increase when questions focus on behavior in a specific context, as this study and other research have shown. For example, integrity surveys among students proved to be more reliable when questions focused on their behavior in a specific situation, such as “at school” or “at the university.”

How can you make effective use of integrity surveys?

For a broad integrity policy within an organization, it is valuable to make integrity a regular topic of discussion. Not only during recruitment and selection, but also, for example, at regular intervals within the standard review cycle. Take the context of behavior into account and invest in a culture of openness where employees feel involved in promoting ethical behavior. When it comes to providing employees with feedback on their self-awareness, performance, or development opportunities (such as 360-degree feedback), these assessments are definitely useful. For other personality assessments, we at hrmforce recommend exercising caution with these measurements. If you do wish to use them for recruitment and selection, you must be sure to thoroughly discuss and explain the results. Otherwise, it can become a sensitive issue that may be misinterpreted. An important point to consider is the difference between a person’s personality—which relates to aptitude and potential—and behavior that is actually observable. You cannot conclude, based on the measured results, whether someone is or is not a person of integrity. It does, however, say something about their potential for development. And keep the previously mentioned context in mind. If an integrity score comes out somewhat “lower,” you can also ask about specific past (work) situations during interviews. How did the person handle those situations? You can find more specific interview questions in the hrmforce competency handbook.

What else can your organization do to promote integrity?

In addition to making integrity a recurring topic of discussion and fostering an open culture, paying attention to the context of behavior is a key focus area. In addition to testing behavior or personality traits, you can therefore also develop tests (or conduct interviews) that focus on the specific context in which the behavior occurs. This can be done, for example, using scenarios in which candidates or participants describe how they would act in certain situations. Furthermore, organizations can invest in structured behavioral observation and, for example, feedback methods such as 360-degree feedback. This can certainly yield valuable information for the intended purpose.

Integrity and Organizing Leadership

In the field of leadership development, integrity is a key focus area—for example, when facilitating and developing organizational leadership. Among all the leadership styles that exist—and the many hybrid forms thereof—this one has been gaining significant traction in recent years. In addition to greater self-awareness across different levels of the organization, a clear Leadership Operating System (LOS) can also significantly increase and accelerate the impact of organizational leadership. It serves as a framework for discussions, shared protocols, and communication and decision-making flows that enable leaders to “steer” the organization in the right direction.
title: Measuring integrity is valuable, but be cautious during recruitment and selection

The rapid advancement of Natural Language Processing (NLP) technologies has created new opportunities for companies to optimize their recruitment and employee development processes. By leveraging NLP, companies can streamline their talent acquisition, improve job-candidate matching, and enhance employee training and development. In this article, we discuss how NLP can revolutionize employee recruitment and development, ultimately leading to a more efficient and successful workforce.

Streamlining Talent Acquisition

Traditional recruitment methods often involve manually screening a large number of resumes and cover letters, which can be time-consuming and prone to human error. NLP can help automate this process by extracting relevant information from candidates’ documents, such as skills, experience, and education. This data can then be analyzed and matched against job requirements, enabling recruiters to quickly and accurately identify the most suitable candidates. In addition, NLP can be used to analyze job descriptions and job postings to ensure they are clear and concise and do not contain gender or cultural biases. This not only helps attract a diverse group of applicants but also promotes a more inclusive work environment.

Improving Job Matching

One of the challenges in recruitment is accurately matching candidates with the right job openings. NLP can address this issue by analyzing and comparing the language used in resumes and job descriptions. By identifying patterns and similarities, NLP algorithms can suggest suitable job openings to candidates, thereby improving the overall efficiency of the recruitment process. Furthermore, NLP can be used to analyze the language used in online professional profiles and social media posts, giving recruiters better insight into a candidate’s personality, interests, and values. This information can be crucial in determining whether a candidate is a good fit for the company culture.

Improving Employee Training and Development

NLP is not only valuable during the recruitment phase but also plays a crucial role in employee development. Companies can use NLP to create personalized training programs based on employees’ individual needs. By analyzing employees’ written communication, such as emails or reports, NLP algorithms can identify areas for improvement and suggest relevant training resources. This targeted approach to employee development ensures that resources are used efficiently and that employees receive the support they need to grow within the organization.

Conclusion

Natural Language Processing has the potential to significantly transform the landscape of employee recruitment and development. By automating the talent recruitment process, improving job matching, and providing employees with personalized training and support, NLP can lead to a more efficient and successful workforce.
title: Using Natural Language Processing for Efficient Employee Recruitment and Development

body:
Conflicts at work occur in almost every team. Sometimes they’re about the substance of the work, sometimes about the division of tasks, and sometimes about behavior or communication. Many organizations don’t realize until it’s too late what lies beneath a conflict: differences in motivations, communication styles, or stress responses. By better understanding how people react in conflict situations, you can prevent escalation and help teams work together more effectively.

Key Points

  • Conflicts often arise from differences in communication styles or expectations
  • Team members react differently to tension, depending on their personality
  • Recognizing early warning signs helps keep situations manageable
  • Objective tools such as DISC or personality assessments provide insight into patterns
  • Constructive conversations usually resolve issues more effectively than rigid procedures

What causes conflicts at work?

Conflicts are rarely the result of a single incident. Tension usually arises from a combination of factors such as a heavy workload, unclear roles, miscommunication, or clashing work styles. In teams where things are rarely discussed openly, small irritations build up into a larger clash. In many cases, personal preferences play a role. One person seeks clarity and structure, while another wants the freedom to make their own choices. When these differences go unaddressed, frustrations arise that lead to conflict behavior.

How can personality influence conflicts?

Everyone reacts in their own way when tension rises. That behavior often stems from underlying personality traits and motivations. By understanding these patterns, you can respond much more effectively in conversations or mediation. One model that many organizations use to highlight behavioral differences is the DISC methodology. It clearly illustrates how someone communicates, makes decisions, and reacts under pressure. This is based on colors. Would you like to objectively identify such behavioral preferences? Then consider the DISC test. It helps you understand why certain colleagues are more likely to seek confrontation while others are more likely to back down. For a broader picture of personality, you can use a comprehensive assessment such as the Big Fifty. It shows how someone scores on aspects such as dominance, empathy, conscientiousness, flexibility, and stress sensitivity. These insights help you understand which situations cause tension and which approach works to reduce conflicts.

How do you recognize a conflict before it escalates?

Conflicts usually don’t escalate overnight. There are almost always warning signs. Consider:
  • Withdrawn or, conversely, conspicuously direct behavior
  • Misunderstandings that occur more and more frequently
  • Declining motivation or negative comments
  • Team members avoiding each other instead of seeking each other out
  • Minor irritations that linger
If you recognize these patterns early on, you can initiate a conversation before emotions get the better of you.

What approach actually works for workplace conflicts?

A good approach starts with clarity about the real problem. Not the form—the angry email or the sharp remark—but the underlying need or frustration. Teams that get straight to the heart of the matter often resolve conflicts without much intervention. These steps help keep a conversation constructive:
  1. Ask about their experience—How does the other person perceive the situation?
  2. Focus on specific behavior—What exactly happened?
  3. Explore motives—What need was driving the behavior?
  4. Identify shared goals—Where do you want to go together?
  5. Agree on what needs to change—clear, small, and actionable.
Personality assessments such as DISC or a broad assessment model can help put into words the behaviors that emerge during conflicts. This makes conversations less personal and more focused on collaboration.

How do you prevent recurring conflicts?

Many teams aren’t bothered by the conflict itself, but by patterns that keep recurring. Think of clashes between structure-seekers and improvisers, or between colleagues who want to move quickly and those who want to process information first. Teams that understand these differences usually work together more harmoniously. It helps to regularly reflect on questions such as:
  • What does each team member need to work comfortably?
  • How do we respond when we feel tension?
  • Who takes the lead in difficult situations?
  • What agreements help prevent misunderstandings?

FAQ – Frequently Asked Questions About Workplace Conflicts

1. Is every conflict negative? No. A conflict can lead to better decisions, clarity, and new ideas when it’s discussed carefully. 2. When should HR intervene? When discussions reach an impasse, when safety is at risk, or when the conflict affects performance. 3. Does a DISC profile help with conflict management? It can help you understand behavior and put differences into words. That reduces tension and opens up conversations. 4. What if two coworkers consistently avoid each other? Then there’s a good chance there’s an underlying pattern at play. A facilitated conversation may be necessary to identify the real problem. 5. Can you learn to prevent conflicts? Yes. By understanding communication styles, expectations, and triggers, teams can recognize tension more quickly and bring it up for discussion. 6. What are the benefits of understanding personality? It provides language, understanding, and clarity. As a result, a conflict becomes less personal and more focused on collaboration.

Finally: What can you do right away?

  1. Identify differences in communication styles
  2. Use a tool such as DISC or a broad personality model
  3. Have conversations as soon as you notice the first signs
  4. Agree on communication guidelines and expectations
  5. Regularly discuss how the collaboration is going
title: Conflict at Work: Causes and Solutions

Preparing for an Assessment

What can you expect before, during, and after an assessment at hrmforce? If you still have questions after reading this page, feel free to contact one of our advisors or use the chat feature on the website. Would you like to practice a bit before taking the assessment? We’ve developed a special practice assessment so you can get a feel for how it works and be perfectly prepared. Good luck! TAKE THE PRACTICE ASSESSMENTAfter completing an assessment, you’ll gain insight into your talents, what motivates you in your work, and where your potential for growth lies. An assessment provides you with a nuanced understanding of your qualities. Assessments can consist of online tests and questionnaires. An assessment provides greater certainty about a candidate’s qualities and development potential through a nuanced understanding. In this way, clients receive a clear and comprehensive description of the participant. Assessments can be used in various phases and departments within organizations, including for selection, onboarding, and career advancement. Hrmforce offers various types of assessments. For example, you can turn to us for selection, development, and career assessments, as well as for team assessments or group analyses that provide insight into a team’s strengths and areas for development. The advantage of an online assessment is that it can be taken virtually anytime and anywhere. Assessments can be completed either at home or on-site, and this can be customized according to the client’s preferences. First, the candidate receives an email with an invitation to take the assessment. This email contains both practical information and personal login credentials. It also includes a link that directs you to a secure online environment where you can complete the assessment. If a client prefers that you take the assessment in a supervised environment, they can suggest a location within their organization. You can practice for assessments in advance—in fact, this is highly recommended. By taking practice tests beforehand, you’ll gain a clearer understanding of the assessments you’ll need to complete. You’ll also learn to manage time pressure and know what kinds of questions to expect. This will allow you to start the actual assessment better prepared and more relaxed. Here you’ll find a practice test for the aptitude test. First and foremost, it’s important that you understand the purpose of the assessment and know what it covers. For many assessments, it’s possible to practice in advance or to read up on the material. Next, it’s important that you’re well-rested and can take the assessment in a quiet environment where you won’t be disturbed by (external) factors. Cognitive ability tests fall under the category of intelligence tests and are the most effective predictors of success in the workplace. These tests often consist of analytical insight (number sequences, figure sequences), logical reasoning, spatial insight, and mathematical and/or linguistic abilities. A cognitive ability test, also known as an “Ability Analysis assessment,” measures how quickly a person can understand problems, form an opinion, and/or learn new things.A personality questionnaire examines the candidate’s personality. There are no right or wrong answers in this type of assessment. The test is based on the five key personality factors that influence behavior in work situations: Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness.Please use a recent browser. Internet Explorer 9 or earlier is no longer supported by Microsoft, and there is therefore no guarantee that these browsers are compatible with the assessments. The assessments can also be taken on Mac computers, laptops, and the Safari web browser. While the assessments and tests can generally be taken on most tablets, this cannot be guaranteed. Due to the wide variety of tablets available, it is impossible to say with certainty whether the assessments and tests will work on every model. We therefore recommend taking assessments or tests on a desktop computer or a laptop—this is certainly possible. Just make sure you have a stable internet connection. If you’ve been invited to an assessment day, you’re expected to arrive at the specified location in the morning. Throughout the day, you’ll undergo various assessments, interviews, and (simulated) conversations. The purpose of this full day is to gain a clear picture of the candidate in terms of development, ambition, motivations, and aspirations. The duration of the assessment varies and can range from 4 to 8 hours. You will always receive information about the length of the day before it begins. The exact schedule for the day depends on the client’s preferences and will always be communicated in advance. The time required may vary by assessment. At the start of each assessment, you will always be informed of its duration. Assessments you can take at home last no longer than an hour and a half. To prepare for an assessment interview, it’s especially important that you know who you are and how to demonstrate this. Required competencies: provide concrete examples that show you possess these competencies. Make sure you have a clear overview of your ambitions and motivation. Be honest about your strengths and weaknesses. If applicable, you can discuss the common thread running through your career and your professional development. It is recommended that you practice for an assessment interview in advance. This varies by interview. In a selection assessment, the focus is (primarily) on job-related competencies. Ambition and motivation are also discussed, and you’ll be asked about your strengths and weaknesses. In development assessments, the focus is (primarily) on career opportunities and development potential. Here, options within the client’s organization are explored. Ambition, motivation, and career goals are also discussed. In assessments focused on career development, the emphasis is (primarily) on motivation and driving factors. Linked to the candidate’s ambitions, the assessment explores a suitable next step, which may be either within or outside the current organization.During a practical simulation, a real-life situation is reenacted. In this simulation, your conversation partner is usually an actor who plays his or her role realistically. By simulating a real-life situation, it is possible to observe how someone reacts in a specific (work) situation. The results of the practical simulation are combined with the results from the interview assessment, the personality questionnaires, and any other assessments. During a practical simulation, the candidate’s social and communication skills are evaluated. The candidate’s behavior and conversation techniques are observed.It is recommended that you dress as you would for your future job or as you do for your current job. It is important that the dress code fits the environment where you will be working or for which you are taking the assessments.
  1. Be yourself. This is the easiest approach and provides the best insights for both you and the manager/assessor.
  2. Make sure you’re well-rested and arrive on time. Plan ahead accordingly.
  3. Check in advance where you’re expected to go and the best way to get there. Leave early and allow for possible traffic jams or delays. If you factor in potential delays, you’ll feel more at ease.
  4. Familiarize yourself in advance with the assessments you’ll need to complete and take any relevant practice tests.
  5. Never complete assessments at the last minute. This ensures you’ll be able to finish them on time. If something does go wrong, you’ll still have enough time to resolve the issue and complete the assessment.
  6. Always take assessments in a quiet environment where you won’t be disturbed.
  7. Assessments provide a clear picture of the candidate. Answer the questions honestly and use the results to get to know yourself even better.
  8. If you’ve been invited to an assessment day, be sure to prepare thoroughly for the following:
    1. Know your own strengths and weaknesses and be able to describe them using examples.
    2. Identify your areas for development.
    3. Make sure you can clearly articulate your ambition and motivation.
