A thorough reference check significantly reduces the risk of making a hiring mistake. It provides valuable insights that go beyond resumes and job interviews. By systematically checking references, you gain a more complete picture of your potential new employee. This article offers a practical guide to effective reference checks that are both legally and ethically sound.

Why Reference Checks Are Important

Research shows that 40% of resumes contain inaccuracies. Reference checks help uncover these and provide insight into soft skills that are difficult to assess during interviews. They are an indispensable part of the selection process.
What to Verify? Why is this important? Red flags
Work History Confirms experience and stability Unexplained gaps, inconsistent dates
Position & Responsibilities Validates competencies Exaggerations, inconsistencies
Achievements & results Predicts future success Vague answers, contradictions
Collaboration & culture Determines team fit Conflicts, communication problems
Reason for leaving Reveals motivation and integrity Evasive answers, termination

Legal framework: consent is important

The GDPR imposes strict requirements on the processing of personal data. Follow these steps to conduct a lawful reference check:

✓ Legal requirements:

  • Obtain written consent from the candidate
  • Specify which references you will contact
  • Explain what information you will be requesting
  • Carefully document all information obtained
  • Do not retain data longer than necessary
  • Respect the NVP recruitment code
A refusal to provide references may be grounds for rejection, provided this has been clearly communicated in advance.

Select references strategically

Do not blindly rely on references provided by candidates. Deliberately seek out different perspectives:
  • Immediate supervisor: For performance and development
  • Colleagues/team members: For collaboration and soft skills
  • Subordinates: For leadership style (for managerial positions)
  • Customers/suppliers: For external relationships (for relevant positions)
Pro tip: During the interview, also ask about references that the candidate did NOT provide. Their response can be revealing.

The Art of the Reference Check

A successful reference check requires preparation and technique. Use this step-by-step guide:
Phase Approach Sample Questions
Opening Introduce yourself, explain the purpose, and confirm consent "Did [name] inform you about this conversation?"
Verification Verify factual information "Can you confirm the duration of employment?" "What were the main responsibilities?"
In-Depth Analysis Assess competencies and behavior "How would you describe their work style?" "Give an example of problem-solving"
Critical questions Follow-up Questions on Areas for Development "What areas for development do you see?" "Why did the employment relationship end?"
Conclusion Summarize, thank the candidate, and ask for a final assessment "Would you hire this person again?" "Is there anything else I should know?"

Questioning: Going Beyond the Standard Questions

Avoid closed-ended questions that only elicit yes/no answers. Use these more powerful alternatives:

Smart questions that reveal more:

  • "On a scale of 1 to 10, how would you rate [competency]? Why not a 10?"
  • "Describe a situation in which [name] had to perform under pressure."
  • "What advice would you give [name] for this new role?"
  • "In what kind of work environment does [name] thrive the most?"
  • "What will colleagues miss most about [name]?"

Interpreting Cues Correctly

During reference interviews, pay attention to both verbal and nonverbal cues:
  • Positive cues: Enthusiasm, specific examples, spontaneous compliments
  • Neutral cues: Businesslike tone, factual answers, “no comment”
  • Warning signs: Hesitation, evasive answers, contradictions
Important: Silences can be meaningful. Give references time to think and continue speaking.

From Information to Decision

After gathering references, the crucial analysis phase follows:
  1. Compare sources: Look for patterns in feedback from different references
  2. Consider context: Company culture and circumstances influence performance
  3. Discuss findings: Give candidates the opportunity to respond to feedback
  4. Document carefully: Record the decision-making process transparently

Tools for reference checks

Digitization significantly streamlines the reference check process:
Traditional Digital Advantage
Follow-up calls Online questionnaires Time savings, consistency
Manual notes Structured reporting More objective, comparable
Email reminders Automated workflows Faster turnaround time
Excel reports Integrated dashboards Real-time insights

Best practices summarized

✓ Always request written consent in advance ✓ Check at least two independent references ✓ Prepare targeted, open-ended questions ✓ Listen to what isn’t being said ✓ Discuss findings with the candidate ✓ Carefully document the entire process ✓ Treat information confidentially

Improve Your Reference Checks

A professional reference check makes the difference between a good hire and an excellent one. It takes time and expertise, but prevents costly mismatches. Want to take your reference check process to the next level? Discover how hrmforce Reference Check digitizes and objectifies the process, while allowing you to maintain full control over the content and approach.
title: A Good Reference Check? Here's How to Do It.

body:
Selection of New Employees

Selection is a skill! After recruiting candidates, the selection process begins. Of course, your gut feeling plays an important role here. But wouldn’t it be helpful to objectify your instincts and back them up with a validated questionnaire? This could enrich the decision-making process. It significantly reduces the risk of a mismatch and makes it possible to select the best candidate with the highest chance of success. Hrmforce helps you make better decisions during the selection process. By utilizing relevant recruitment questionnaires—such as Personality (translated into competencies: Big Fifty Personality), Intelligence (Ability Analysis), Motivation (Motivation), and, if applicable, Leadership (Leadership), you gain insight into the candidate’s potential for development, their work and cognitive levels, their drivers, and, if applicable, their leadership styles. Based on a predefined ideal profile, the system automatically indicates, as a percentage (0% to 100%), the extent to which the candidate is a good fit for the position and organization. Additionally, it is possible to use supplementary questionnaires such as the intake form (Candidate Intake). By using this questionnaire, all necessary questions—which would normally be addressed during the first interview—are asked online and in advance. This allows you to immediately focus on any notable findings. Furthermore, the reference check (Reference Check) provides immediate insight into the candidate’s behavior at previous employers. Because we know: behavior predicts behavior! Combined with the questionnaires mentioned in the previous paragraph, you’ll immediately have a complete picture, and with the help of our competency guide, you can get the most out of the face-to-face meeting with your candidate.

Features

A happy employee is a good employee—every HR manager knows that. But how do you ensure your employees continue to enjoy their work? We’re sharing 5 helpful tips on workplace happiness during this Workplace Happiness Week. If you want a healthy and successful organization, you’d be wise to invest in your staff. After all, your people ultimately determine what you’re able to accomplish. And various studies show that happy, satisfied employees perform better. For example, researchers at the University of Warwick discovered a strong link between happiness and productivity in the workplace. Moreover, happy and motivated people take fewer sick days, cope better with stress, and stay with the same employer longer, as Professor Martijn Burger recently emphasized in the NRC newspaper . So it’s no surprise that more and more companies are actively working to increase their employees’ job satisfaction. As an employer, you obviously can’t completely control whether people are happy. But you can do a lot to contribute to your employees’ job satisfaction. These five tips will help you get off to a good start.  

Tip 1: Establish a clear vision

Employees spend a significant portion of their time at work. They therefore want to feel that the effort they put into their work is meaningful. Why does your organization do what it does? What goal are you pursuing? And what is the purpose of it all? As an employer, it’s important that you can provide clear answers to these questions. So formulate a clear vision—and, very importantly, communicate it. A shared goal motivates employees and establishes clear guidelines and expectations. Moreover, with such a narrative, you’ll attract employees who believe in you. Note: Your vision must align with reality—otherwise, you’ll lose your credibility. For example, if you’re a healthcare organization that says the client comes first, structure your operations so that employees don’t spend an unnecessary amount of time on administrative tasks and other peripheral matters.  

Tip 2: Actively Work on Your Company Culture

Colleagues and the atmosphere within a company are key determinants of employees’ job satisfaction. “Vitamin A,” is what wellness expert Hidde de Vries calls it in an interview with NRC. “People are social creatures. We need each other for our self-confidence, to feel good, and to produce the right brain chemicals,” he tells the newspaper. So think about the atmosphere you want to create, and tailor your policies accordingly. For example, when employees are given more freedom and autonomy to do their work the way they want, they experience greater job satisfaction. That can be a reason to be flexible with work hours and remote work. Also, plan regular team outings and other group activities to strengthen the bonds between colleagues. In addition, keep an eye on the workload. A consistently high workload is detrimental to job satisfaction. Take breaks seriously and send people who are working overtime home a little early. That said, too little work is also not good—it can lead to bore-out.  

Tip 3: Choose Your Managers Carefully

Various studies show that managers play a crucial role in workplace happiness. For example, the 2021 National Workplace Happiness Survey—a survey of 1,500 working Dutch people—revealed that managers can make or break employees’ workplace happiness. The authors of the Handbook on Job Satisfaction (2020) also conclude that managers play a decisive role. They must ensure that employees have enough autonomy, that the workload isn’t too high, that the atmosphere in the workplace is positive, and that the work remains challenging. It is therefore very important that your organization has capable managers and team leaders who are able to guide and coach their people. Managers with a directive or controlling style lead to lower job satisfaction among your staff. The same goes for managers who lead in a directive manner or are primarily focused on the process. Do you notice that your managers could use a little help? Training can help them further develop their leadership skills.  

Tip 4: Make sure employees feel appreciated

Appreciation is a major driver of happiness in the workplace. So let people know that you value them. Managers play a key role here as well. It’s important for them to give compliments regularly and to make room for everyone’s opinions and insights. There are many ways to show appreciation, by the way. For example, make sure employees don’t have to ask for a raise themselves—instead, take the initiative and offer one in a timely manner. Is someone home due to personal circumstances? Have some flowers delivered. And has an employee been working exceptionally hard lately? Surprise them with a personal thank-you card and a treat—such as brownies or cupcakes sent by mail. Generously filled holiday gift baskets (with a personal message from immediate supervisors) or a year-end bonus are also ways to show your appreciation. The same goes for good employee benefits: at some companies, for example, employees can claim reimbursement for their gym membership or haircuts. Or consider providing a nice lunch at the office. A daily shared moment like that immediately boosts the atmosphere!  

Tip 5: Make assessments part of your hiring process

In fact, job satisfaction begins even before someone starts working. Because if there’s no good fit between you and your new employee, nobody will be happy. People perform better when they’re in the right role. That’s why you can incorporate assessments into the hiring process. Nowadays, we’re doing this more and more online—and with great success! By having candidates take an assessment, you gain an objective picture of their personality and qualities. With that information, you can better assess whether someone is a good fit for your organization. Ultimately, this leads to people enjoying their work more. Moreover, the results of assessments help candidates get to know themselves better. They can use the test results to further their professional development. And that, in turn, contributes to their job satisfaction.  

Getting Started with Digital Assessments

Digital assessments can be administered at various locations throughout the Netherlands. Candidates receive a warm welcome and personalized attention, ensuring they feel completely at ease. Curious about the possibilities? Check out the websites of Lamark or hrmforce and book an assessment right away.
title: 5 Tips: How to Keep Your Employees Happy and Satisfied

Since August 2017, teachers in primary (PO), secondary (VO), and vocational secondary education (MBO) have been required to meet legally established competency requirements. These requirements lay the foundation for professional quality in education. They serve not only as guidelines for those who wish to become teachers, but also as a compass for experienced teachers who want to continue their professional development. The focus is on three pillars: subject matter, subject-specific teaching methods, and pedagogical practice.

A Solid Foundation for Quality in Education

The more stringent requirements clarify what is expected of a teacher. They have been translated into seven specific competencies:
  • Interpersonal competence
  • Pedagogical competence
  • Subject-matter and instructional competence
  • Organizational competence
  • Competent in collaborating with colleagues
  • Competent in collaborating with the community
  • Competent in reflection and professional development
These competencies apply to both teachers in training and teachers who have been teaching for years. In the latter case, we refer to “competency maintenance”: maintaining and further developing professional standards.

Self-analysis as a starting point for development

For teachers who want to improve—or who notice that certain skills are lagging—it’s important to start with an honest self-analysis. Where are the strengths? What still needs attention? Only once you have clarity about your own profile can you develop in a targeted way. A competency assessment is a powerful tool for this. It provides insight into where someone stands and offers practical guidance for next steps—both individually and within the team.

A profession that demands more than just knowledge

The requirements for a good teacher extend beyond subject knowledge or teaching skills. How you interact with your students, colleagues, and parents is just as crucial to success. That makes the profession multifaceted—but also demanding. Personal development is, of course, an integral part of this.

Example: Interpersonal and reflective competence

Interpersonal competence is about interacting with students in an open, respectful, and positive manner. A good teacher senses what a student needs, sets boundaries, and builds trust. Reflection is just as important: being able to learn from experiences, take feedback seriously, and act on it—that is the foundation for growth. Both competencies say a lot about how someone approaches life as a person and as a professional.

Tailored Development—Practical and Goal-Oriented

Hrmforce offers schools a practical way to map out and guide competency development. Through a personality questionnaire and assessment, the seven teaching competencies are mapped out both individually and from a team perspective. The report clearly indicates:
  • Where are the strengths?
  • In which areas is development desirable?
  • How does the profile align with the role?
This prevents mismatches, promotes team dynamics, and helps schools invest more strategically in their people. And just as important: it motivates teachers to continue working on their own development with enthusiasm.
“Motivated and satisfied teachers have a positive influence on students’ motivation and academic performance.”

Want to learn more?

Feel free to contact one of our consultants. They’d be happy to show you how a competency-based approach makes a difference—for both the teacher and the student.

With the Entrepreneurship Competence Framework, also known as EntreComp for short, the European Commission provides citizens with tools for developing entrepreneurial skills. As a competency model, EntreComp is widely applicable—for example, for identifying and developing your own entrepreneurial skills.

European Commission Maps Out Entrepreneurial Skills

In 2016, the European Commission introduced the new competency model, EntreComp. EntreComp offers everyone the opportunity to assess their entrepreneurial skills. The European Commission’s goal is for citizens to feel motivated, through the insights gained, to further develop these skills. This makes the competency model applicable not only in the informal learning environment—where lifelong learning takes place—but also in professional contexts. EntreComp is well-suited for gaining insight into and developing your entrepreneurial skills.

Context of the EntreComp Competency Model

The EntreComp competency model is the result of a study commissioned by the European Commission and conducted by the Joint Research Center. In 2006, the European Commission set a goal of promoting the knowledge society. To this end, eight competencies were formulated. The EntreComp competency model gives concrete form to the pursuit of a “sense of initiative and entrepreneurship,” making it applicable within both formal and non-formal settings. With EntreComp, the Commission has introduced a widely applicable assessment tool in the field of entrepreneurial skills. The competency model is currently one of the most popular frameworks for understanding and developing entrepreneurial skills.

The EntreComp Competency Model

The model consists of three competency areas and fifteen competencies, each listing the most important aspects. The three competency areas are “ideas and opportunities,” “resources,” and “taking action.” What makes this model unique is that the boundaries between the different competency areas and competencies are not strictly defined. The competency areas and competencies are so intertwined that it is possible to establish new connections on your own. The model not only provides insight but also offers a path to self-development as an entrepreneur. The focus here is primarily on changing behavior and developing your ability to take action, rather than on acquiring theoretical knowledge.   [caption id="attachment_10865" align="aligncenter" width="635"] source: https://ec.europa.eu/ [/caption]  

Entrepreneurship-Oriented Learning

Entrepreneurial skills can be developed by taking actions aimed at creating value for others. This involves not only bringing ideas to life and recognizing opportunities, but also the ability to create value for others in both complex and less complex situations. The EntreComp competency model maps the progression of this development across four levels, from basic to expert. Each level is further divided into sub-levels.

Four Levels of Entrepreneurship

The bottom rung of the ladder is marked by the basic level. At the basic level, individuals are able to create value for others with some outside assistance. By applying these skills with increasing independence, individuals reach an advanced level. Subsequently, by repeatedly translating ideas into concrete actions, individuals reach an advanced level of entrepreneurship. The highest level—that of the expert—is reached when actions consistently lead to above-average results.

Application of the EntreComp Competency Model

The European Commission has set itself the goal of ensuring that everyone, regardless of their role in society, can use the competency model to develop entrepreneurial skills. This aligns with the concept of lifelong learning, in which skills are acquired not only through knowledge but also through experience. Developing entrepreneurial skills is key to the development of a knowledge-based society. However, it is also an excellent model to apply within a context explicitly focused on improving entrepreneurial skills within a specific professional group. A professional learning environment is indispensable for entrepreneurs who wish to reach the expert level.

Entrepreneurial Skills for Employees

Entrepreneurial skills are not only a key competency for entrepreneurs; salaried employees who develop these competencies are also of great value within a company. For example, in numerous roles, the ability to turn ideas into value and to recognize and seize opportunities are indispensable skills. The EntreComp competency model is therefore used by many employers to assess employees’ entrepreneurial skills and develop a path to further develop these competencies. The EntreComp competency model thus serves as a guideline within the business community for employee coaching programs.

Widely Applicable

EntreComp is not only useful for assessing current entrepreneurial skills. As we mentioned earlier, it is also an excellent model for determining the learning curve. Furthermore, the EntreComp competency model is used as a guideline in the development of various courses and programs in the field of entrepreneurship-oriented learning. These courses, programs, and coaching programs are now available at the secondary and higher education levels, in both formal and non-formal settings. EntreComp has thus proven to be a widely applicable reference model for the further development of a high-level knowledge society.

Essential Professional Knowledge

The EntreComp competency model focuses primarily on the entrepreneur’s actions. Subject-specific knowledge remains somewhat underemphasized in this context. Nevertheless, we must not forget that one does not become a successful entrepreneur through behavioral change alone. Identifying opportunities and developing ideas also requires a certain degree of knowledge development. The ability to develop this knowledge and the ability to turn thoughts into action are not equally accessible to everyone. Unfortunately, developing strong entrepreneurial qualities is therefore not within everyone’s reach.

Test Your Entrepreneurial Skills Yourself

Are you curious about your entrepreneurial skills? You can easily gain insight into your entrepreneurial skills online. You can then use this knowledge to further improve your entrepreneurial qualities. The Big Fifty Personality Test maps out your personality profile. You’ll also receive an indication of opportunities to further develop various competencies. The online 360-Degree Feedback assessment provides a concrete picture of your skills, competencies, and other entrepreneurship-related traits. Insight is the first step toward progress.
title: Improve Your Entrepreneurial Skills with EntreComp

Team performance is becoming increasingly crucial. But how do you ensure that those teams actually perform well? Team development allows you to work on this in a targeted way. It starts with analyzing team performance and the personalities within the team. By taking different team styles into account, everyone can then work on specific action items.  

The Rise of Team Development

Team development has been an important topic for organizations, their teams, and HR professionals for years. In recent years, this topic has rapidly risen on organizations’ priority lists. It has now even become the most important topic, according to an international study on HRM trends conducted by Deloitte in 130 countries, including the Netherlands. This is due to various developments, such as globalization, increasing economic dynamism, and customers (and other stakeholders) who have ever-higher expectations. As a result, collaboration in general has become increasingly important for the success of companies. This applies to collaboration between organizations as well as within organizations. We also see this reflected in the rapid rise of self-managing teams, project teams, “Scrum and Agile” work methods, and the emergence of virtual teams. New technology (online collaboration) naturally plays a key facilitating role in this development.  

It doesn’t happen on its own

Within organizations, a shift is underway from the old hierarchical management models toward more (multifunctional) team-based models. This leads to better performance and is a more effective model for operating successfully in today’s dynamic, less predictable business environment. In that environment, a successful team delivers the desired results; it is more effective and achieves better performance than the mere sum of the contributions made by individual team members. There is, however, a challenge. Effective teams usually do not emerge on their own. Team development is essential for helping a team perform better and excel. Otherwise, it remains simply a group of individuals. It’s striking that fewer than 20 percent of teams consider themselves “high-performing.” That means about 80 percent do not (yet)!  

Analyzing and Improving Team Performance

Most teams can work much more effectively than they often do. And often, even small interventions can lead to significant progress. “Team development” is the key term here. In this context, team training and leadership training have proven to be important (evidence-based) interventions. But at its core, the solution largely lies in how team performance and individual characteristics are analyzed, and in giving the team responsibility for improving its own performance. Paying attention to different team styles and the roles within teams is of great importance in this regard. At hrmforce, we’ve tailored the tools organizations use for their team development analyses to address this. Quite recently, we’ve even added additional components to highlight different team styles. After all, no two teams are alike, and the same applies to the environmental factors they face at different times.  

Different Teams and Environmental Factors

Of course, there are also many theories and conceptual models regarding the most effective composition of teams. Depending on the type of team, its objectives, and environmental factors, these theories and insights can be valuable for your team development. After all, do you want to ensure the success of complex projects? Then, as this research on multinational companies shows, you should ideally assemble a large team of highly educated specialists. The downside, however, is that highly educated specialists are often less willing to learn from one another, to share information (pro)actively, and to help each other distribute the work as effectively as possible. These can be important considerations for such a team, especially if the analysis of personal and team characteristics also points in that direction. Or is this an innovation team? In that case, performance pressure can be a key concern. Research by TNO shows that innovation teams actually become risk-averse under pressure, which makes innovations more likely to fail. Their advice: create a supportive work environment in which resilient innovative behavior can flourish. HRD experts can help the team in this regard and reduce their chances of failure, according to TNO.

Balance and Phases of Team Development

Another key consideration is the relationship between individual and team performance. Through effective collaboration, team members get more out of themselves and bring out the best in one another. Within teams, you naturally have to deal with individuals who strive to get the most out of their own careers. That is perfectly healthy in itself, but the balance must also remain healthy. As soon as individual ambitions come at the expense of the team, group dynamics can actually start to backfire. Team development can address this as well, naturally within the various stages of team development, as we described earlier.  

The Role of Managers

And then, of course, there is the important role of managers. Scientific research on team performance based on “serious gaming” using an escape room (by Friesland Boeit) also provided valuable new insights. This study examined team performance at the competency level, with a strong focus on leadership. “In today’s rapidly changing world and economy, leadership and collaboration are currently crucial areas of focus,” says leadership expert Jelle Dijkstra (lecturer in Personal Leadership & Innovation at NHL University of Applied Sciences), who was involved in the study. “But those are often the weak points right now. Organizations are saying they’ll ‘work differently’ and ‘collaborate differently,’ but how exactly? That question often remains unanswered.” A notable finding from years of research in the escape room is that the most successful teams have two leaders: a dominant leader and a social leader, who can take turns. They must be able to switch flexibly between different leadership styles, depending on their team, the environment, and their assignment.  

Action Items Following the Analysis

Teams are constantly evolving. That’s why regular analysis remains valuable. And after an analysis, concrete action items are, of course, necessary. With hrmforce’s specialized questionnaires focused on teams, it’s possible to map out team development (strengths and weaknesses). Based on talent and personal characteristics, tasks and goals can then be formulated for a development plan and an action plan. The renowned Big Five personality theory (centered on the five major dimensions: extraversion, agreeableness, emotional stability, conscientiousness, and openness) is valuable for conducting analyses and determining action items for team development. Our analyses are based on this theory.
title: Team Development Is Becoming Increasingly Important, but How Do You Go About It?

body:
Improving teamwork means ensuring that all team members communicate better with one another. Teams that work well together perform up to 35% better than teams where collaboration is difficult. This happens because people can pool their talents and reinforce each other’s strengths.

What will you learn in this article?

This article covers the key elements for better teamwork: • Establishing clear communication that prevents misunderstandings • Building trust among team members • Clearly defining roles and responsibilities • Resolving conflicts constructively • Setting team goals that motivate everyone

Why Collaboration Often Goes Wrong in Teams

Teams don’t fail because of a lack of talent, but because of poor collaboration. The biggest problem arises when team members work at cross-purposes instead of with each other. This often happens because no one has taken the time to lay a solid foundation. Fictional example: A marketing team at a software company worked for months on a product launch. Everyone did their best, but the campaign flopped. It turned out later that the graphic designer thought the product was aimed at young people, while the copywriter was writing for professionals. The project leader had assumed that everyone had the same target audience in mind. Situations like these cost time, money, and cause frustration. They arise because teams skip the fundamentals of collaboration and jump right into the work. The good news is that you can prevent this.

The Foundation of Everything

Good communication is the backbone of every successful team. Without clear communication, misunderstandings, missed deadlines, and unnecessary work arise. Effective team communication goes beyond just talking; it’s about understanding and being understood.

Establish clear communication rules

Start by establishing communication guidelines that apply to everyone. Decide which communication channels to use and when. Use email for formal matters, chat for quick questions, and face-to-face conversations for important decisions. This clarity prevents confusion about where to find information. Also agree on response times. No one expects an immediate reply to every email, but they do expect clarity on when a response will be provided. Responding to emails within 24 hours and to urgent messages within 2 hours works well for many teams.

Listening Is More Important Than Talking

Active listening means truly paying attention to what a team member is saying, without already thinking about your response. Ask probing questions such as, “Can you give an example of that?” This shows interest and provides greater clarity. Regularly summarize what you’ve heard: “What I understand is that you think we need more time for the analysis because the data isn’t complete yet. Is that right?” This helps prevent misunderstandings and makes the other person feel heard.

Building Trust Among Team Members

Trust doesn’t happen on its own—it grows through consistent actions and transparent communication. Teams with high levels of mutual trust feel comfortable admitting mistakes, asking for help, and giving each other honest feedback. This leads to faster decision-making and better results.

Transparency builds trust

Share information openly with your team, even when the news isn’t always positive. Don’t hide behind vague statements; instead, explain what’s happening and why. A team leader who says, “The budget is being cut by 20% because sales figures are lower than expected,” builds more trust than someone who simply says, “We need to cut costs.” Admit when you’ve made a mistake. This might sound vulnerable, but it backfires. Team members respect leaders and colleagues who acknowledge their mistakes and learn from them. It also gives others the space to admit their own mistakes.

Keeping promises builds credibility

Only make commitments you can keep. It’s better to set a realistic deadline than an overly optimistic one you won’t meet. If you can’t deliver what you promised, communicate this as early as possible along with an alternative plan. Don’t overlook small promises either. Saying you’ll send a document on Monday and not doing so until Wednesday undermines your reliability. Team members will start to doubt your word when it comes to more important matters.

Clearly Define Roles and Responsibilities

Unclear roles lead to overlap, missed tasks, and frustration. Everyone needs to know exactly what is expected of them and where their responsibilities begin and end. This clarity prevents conflicts and ensures that all tasks are addressed.

Create a RACI matrix for each project

A RACI matrix shows who is Responsible (executing), Accountable (ultimately responsible), Consulted (consulted), and Informed (informed) for each task. This may sound formal, but it works exceptionally well for teams struggling with unclear responsibilities.
Task Responsible Accountable Consulted Informed
Create a content calendar Marketing Associate Marketing Manager Sales Manager Executive Management
Social media posts Content creator Marketing Associate - Marketing Manager
Campaign Results Data analyst Marketing Manager Marketing Associate Executive Management
This table prevents discussions about who does what and ensures that no one is left out.

Discuss overlapping responsibilities

Of course, some tasks fall between two roles. Discuss these situations openly with your team and establish clear agreements. Who takes the lead when a customer has a complaint that involves both sales and customer service? These conversations prevent conflicts down the line. Regularly review whether the division of roles still fits the current situation. Teams evolve and tasks shift. What made sense three months ago might not work anymore.

Resolving Conflicts Constructively

Conflicts are a natural part of teamwork and aren’t always a bad thing. They can lead to better ideas and stronger solutions. The problem arises when conflicts aren’t addressed or are resolved in a destructive way.

Address conflicts immediately

Don’t ignore conflicts in the hope that they’ll go away on their own. Minor irritations can escalate into major problems if they aren’t discussed. Speak with those involved individually and work together to find a solution that works for everyone. Focus on the behavior and the situation, not on the person. Say, “I’ve noticed that deadlines are regularly missed,” instead of, “You’re always late.” This makes the conversation less personal and increases the likelihood of a constructive solution.

Look for win-win solutions

The best conflict resolutions ensure that all parties are better off than before. This requires creativity and a willingness to look beyond the original positions. Ask, “What do you need to resolve this problem?” instead of insisting on one specific solution. A developer and a designer regularly had disagreements about the user interface. The developer wanted simple solutions that could be implemented quickly, while the designer aimed for visually appealing designs. The solution was to sit down together for an hour each week and align priorities before work began.

Shared Goals That Motivate the Team

Teams perform better when everyone is working toward the same goal. These goals must be specific, measurable, and relevant to all team members. Vague objectives such as “performing better” don’t motivate anyone.

SMART Goals for Teams

Formulate team goals according to the SMART criteria: Specific, Measurable, Acceptable, Realistic, and Time-bound. Instead of “generate more revenue,” use: “Increase monthly revenue from €50,000 to €60,000 within 6 months by acquiring new customers.” Involve all team members in setting goals. People are more motivated to achieve goals they’ve helped create. Ask for input and adjust goals based on feedback.

Celebrate successes together

Recognize the achievements of the team and individual members. This doesn’t have to involve big celebrations—sometimes a brief mention in the team meeting is enough. People want to feel appreciated for their contributions. Make successes visible to the entire team. A simple dashboard or a weekly update shows everyone how the team is progressing toward its goals. This transparency keeps motivation high.

Regular Evaluation and Improvement

Improving collaboration isn’t a one-time effort, but an ongoing process. Teams that regularly reflect on their work methods and are willing to make adjustments perform better than teams that cling to old habits.

Organize monthly retrospectives

Schedule a short retrospective each month where the team reflects on their collaboration. Discuss what went well, what could be improved, and what concrete steps you’ll take. Keep these meetings short—one hour is usually enough. Ask three simple questions: What should we keep doing? What should we stop doing? What should we start doing? These questions lead to concrete areas for improvement without endless discussions.

Track progress

Track how collaboration is improving using concrete metrics. These could include: the number of missed deadlines, time spent in meetings, or customer satisfaction scores. Numbers make improvement tangible and show whether your approach is working. Also, regularly ask team members for feedback on collaboration. A short survey or individual conversations provide valuable insights you might otherwise miss.

Frequently Asked Questions About Team Collaboration

How long does it take for collaboration to improve? You’ll often see initial improvements within 2–4 weeks after implementing new guidelines. Significant changes in team dynamics usually take 3–6 months. What if a team member isn’t willing to cooperate on improving teamwork? Talk to this person one-on-one to understand what’s going on. Sometimes there are underlying concerns that need to be addressed first before someone is open to change. Can collaboration improve in remote teams? Yes, remote teams can collaborate exceptionally well with the right tools and guidelines. However, it’s important to pay extra attention to communication and creating informal opportunities for interaction. How do you prevent improvements from fading away? Make new ways of working part of your standard processes. Regular evaluations and adjustments help maintain progress and build on it further. Improving collaboration in your team starts today. Let us help you with assessments that give teams greater insight, such as the Lencioni Team Dynamics or 360-degree feedback . Request your free demo now and improve your team as quickly as possible.
title: Improving Team Collaboration: Proven Methods That Work

A development assessment is a systematic method for identifying employees’ competencies, skills, and areas for development. This tool helps organizations and employees identify targeted growth opportunities and map out a clear development path. The need for development is growing in today’s job market. Employers are looking for ways to help their staff grow, while employees themselves also want to shape their own careers. A development assessment brings both parties together by providing insights into where someone stands and where he or she can grow.

What We’ll Cover in This Article

In this article, we’ll walk you through everything you need to know about development assessments: • The different types of assessments and their applications • The process, from preparation through follow-up • Practical tips for both employers and employees • Frequently asked questions about development assessments

Components of development assessments

Development assessments come in various forms, each with its own focus and method. The choice depends on your goals and the situation in which you’re using the assessment. 360-degree feedback forms the basis of many development assessments. In this process, you gather feedback from colleagues, managers, subordinates, and sometimes even customers. This broad perspective provides a comprehensive picture of a person’s performance. It helps you identify blind spots that you might not notice on your own. Competency assessments focus on specific skills relevant to a position or organization. Examples include leadership skills , communication, or problem-solving ability. This approach is practical because it allows you to immediately identify areas for improvement. Assessment centers combine multiple tasks and exercises. For example, candidates participate in role-plays, presentations, and group assignments. Trained assessors observe and evaluate their behavior. This method provides a realistic picture of how someone performs in various situations. Psychological assessments focus on personality traits and work styles. These insights help in understanding motivation and natural talents. You learn how to best collaborate with others and what kind of environment suits you best.

Why Development Assessments Are Important

Development assessments offer concrete benefits for employees and organizations. These tools create a win-win situation in which both parties benefit from the insights. For employees, an assessment means greater self-awareness. You discover what talents you have and where you can continue to grow. These proven insights help you make career choices. You’ll have a better understanding of which roles suit you and which skills you still want to develop. The assessment also provides direction for your learning process. Instead of taking courses at random, you can work specifically on developing certain competencies. This makes your development more effective and meaningful. Organizations benefit from improved workforce development. They can invest strategically in employee growth by focusing on the right competencies. This increases the return on investment for training and development programs. In addition, assessments help identify potential within the company. You discover which employees are ready for more responsibilities or a different role. This promotes internal mobility and retains talent within the organization.  

The real work begins after the assessment

The true value of a development assessment emerges afterward, when you translate the insights into concrete actions. Without follow-up and HR analytics, an assessment remains a snapshot with no lasting impact. Analyze the feedback thoroughly. What patterns do you see? Where do the assessors agree? This consistency often points to your core competencies or key areas for development. Create a development plan with concrete goals and timelines. Choose no more than three competencies to work on, otherwise your efforts will be too scattered. Set SMART goals that are measurable and achievable. Seek support from your manager or HR department. They can help you find suitable training programs, coaches, or development assignments. Colleagues can also be valuable sounding boards. Monitor your progress regularly. Schedule a midterm evaluation after three months. What’s going well? What challenges are you facing? This conscious reflection will keep your development on track.

Frequently Asked Questions About Development Assessments

How long does a development assessment take? The duration varies significantly, depending on the depth and complexity. A comprehensive assessment usually takes one to one and a half days in total, while completing the questionnaires sometimes takes as little as 15 minutes. Can I “fail” a development assessment? No, you cannot “fail” a development assessment. The goal is to learn and grow, not to be evaluated. All feedback is intended to help you move forward. Who gets to see the results? This depends on the agreements made in advance. You will usually receive a detailed report yourself. Whether your manager will also have access to the results will be communicated in advance. How often should I take an assessment? This varies by person and organization. On average, it makes sense to do one every two to three years, or at key career milestones such as a job change. A development assessment is an investment in the future of your company and in that of your employee. Take a look at the development matrix and discover how this tool can directly accelerate development.
title: Why a Development Assessment Is Important for Everyone

The quality of your service is reflected in every task your employees perform. Year-end reviews are the ideal time to look back and look ahead together. These reviews go beyond mere evaluation—they provide an opportunity for genuine dialogue about performance, ambitions, and well-being within the organization. A well-prepared year-end review helps determine the success of your business. It provides insight into employee performance and lays the foundation for future growth. But how can you turn this annual ritual into a valuable experience for both parties?

Conducting Effective Year-End Reviews

Many organizations traditionally evaluate their employees in December or January. This evaluation typically consists of a performance review, possibly supplemented by a formal assessment. The results can lead to important decisions regarding promotions, job changes, or development paths. Modern year-end reviews, however, go beyond simply looking back. They focus on development, growth, and mutual expectations. Proper preparation makes the difference between a mere formality and a valuable opportunity for growth. These five practical tips will help you transform year-end reviews into constructive dialogues that move both parties forward.

1. Start with self-reflection

A successful conversation starts with you. First, analyze your own performance as a manager before evaluating your employees. What successes have you achieved? Where did things not go as smoothly? This self-reflection helps you approach the conversation with an open mind and makes you more receptive to feedback from your employees. Take specific notes on your own strengths and areas for improvement. This preparation allows you to be authentic and vulnerable during the conversation, which enriches and deepens the dialogue.

2. Implement continuous 360-degree feedback

Don’t wait until the year-end review to share feedback. Foster a culture in which employees regularly seek and provide feedback—not only to you, but also to their colleagues. This 360-degree feedback approach ensures timely course corrections and prevents surprises during the year-end review. Continuous feedback makes the year-end review a natural continuation of previous conversations. Employees can adjust their work behavior along the way and grow throughout the year, rather than only after the annual review.
Discussion Topic Estimated Duration Focus
Opening & check-in 5–10 minutes Set the tone, align expectations
Reviewing performance 15–20 minutes Results, successes, learning moments
Development & growth 15–20 minutes Competencies, skills, ambitions
Goals for the coming year 10–15 minutes SMART goals, expectations
Agreements & Closing Remarks 5–10 minutes Specific next steps, planning

3. Support criticism with concrete examples

Vague criticism is demotivating. When discussing areas for improvement, illustrate them with specific situations and behaviors. Explain why certain behaviors impact the team or the organization. This specificity helps employees understand the feedback and actually act on it. Use the SBI method (Situation-Behavior-Impact) to clearly structure your feedback. This prevents misunderstandings and gives employees practical tools for improvement.

4. Build on previous agreements

Every year-end review has a context. Refer to reports from previous reviews and discuss progress on agreements made. This continuity demonstrates that you take agreements seriously and fosters a sense of accountability on both sides. Prepare by:
  • Reviewing previous meeting minutes
  • Taking stock of agreements made
  • Gathering concrete examples of progress
  • Identifying any obstacles

5. Foster a constructive dialogue

A successful year-end review is not a monologue but a dialogue. Start by acknowledging successes and strengths before moving on to areas for development. This positive approach fosters openness and trust. Ask open-ended questions that encourage reflection: “What are you most proud of this year?” and “What support do you need to achieve your goals?” This approach fosters ownership and engagement in one’s own development.

From Evaluation to Development

Modern year-end reviews are shifting from one-sided evaluations to collaborative development. They serve as a moment of connection in which the manager and employee jointly explore growth and potential. By carefully preparing for these conversations and approaching them with the right mindset, you can transform them from mandatory evaluations into valuable opportunities for growth. Invest in the quality of these conversations. They determine not only your employees’ motivation and performance, but also the culture and success of your entire organization. A good year-end review is an investment in the future of both the employee and the company.
title: 5 Tips for Conducting Year-End Reviews

A good workplace policy lays the foundation for a safe, productive, and pleasant work environment. It provides clarity regarding expectations, rights, and responsibilities for everyone within the organization. This document will help you draft a comprehensive workplace policy that covers all essential topics.
Legal disclaimer: This template serves as a starting point and is not a legally binding document. Always have the final policy reviewed by a legal professional to ensure it complies with all relevant laws and regulations.

Workplace Policy Overview

This workplace policy applies to all employees, interns, freelancers, vendors, and visitors. It describes the standards and procedures that contribute to a professional, safe, and respectful work environment.
Policy Section Key Points
Confidentiality Protection of company information, customer data, and NDAs
Harassment & Violence Prevention of harassment, reporting procedures, sanctions
Safety & Health Risk prevention, protective equipment, emergency procedures
Substance Use Smoking policy, alcohol- and drug-free workplace

1. Confidentiality and Data Protection

We protect personal and sensitive business information with the utmost care. This includes any information that could cause harm to the organization, employees, or business partners if disclosed without authorization.

Confidential information includes:

  • Employee records and payroll data
  • Financial reports and forecasts
  • Customer and supplier data
  • Strategic plans and innovations
  • Intellectual property and trade secrets

Your responsibilities:

✓ What you must do:
  • Always store confidential documents in locked cabinets
  • Lock your computer when you’re away
  • Use strong passwords and change them regularly
  • Share information only with authorized colleagues
  • Dispose of confidential documents using a shredder
✗ What you must not do:
  • Use company information for personal gain
  • Discuss confidential information in public areas
  • Copy documents to personal devices
  • Sharing information with third parties without permission

2. A Respectful Workplace

Everyone deserves a work environment free from harassment, discrimination, and violence. We do not tolerate any form of disrespectful behavior, regardless of intent.

What do we mean by harassment?

Harassment can take many forms, ranging from subtle to overt. Examples include:
  • Unwanted sexual advances or comments
  • Discriminatory jokes or comments
  • Spreading gossip or slander
  • Socially isolating or excluding someone
  • Verbal aggression or threats
  • Sabotaging someone’s work

Procedure for reporting incidents:

Step Action When
1 Address the person directly (for minor incidents) If you feel safe
2 Report to a supervisor In case of recurrence or serious incidents
3 Contact HR In the event of serious incidents
4 External confidential advisor If desired

3. Safety and Health

A safe workplace is a productive workplace. We invest in prevention and are prepared for emergencies.

Preventive measures:

  • Periodic risk assessments and evaluations (RI&E)
  • Mandatory safety training for all employees
  • Availability of personal protective equipment
  • Regular inspections of equipment and workstations
  • Ergonomic workstations to prevent RSI

Emergency procedures:

In case of an emergency:
  1. Stay calm and alert others
  2. Follow the evacuation plan (posted on every floor)
  3. Do not use elevators in case of fire
  4. Gather at the designated assembly point
  5. Wait for instructions from emergency response team members

4. Alcohol, Drug, and Smoking Policy

For everyone’s health and safety, we enforce strict rules regarding substance use.

Smoking policy:

Our building is completely smoke-free. Smoking is only permitted:
  • In the designated outdoor smoking area
  • At least 5 meters away from entrances
  • Cigarettes must be disposed of only in ashtrays

Alcohol and drugs:

  • Prohibited during work hours and on company premises
  • Permitted to a limited extent at official company social events
  • Zero tolerance for illegal drugs
  • Prescription medication: Report any side effects to your supervisor

Help with addiction

Are you struggling with an addiction problem? Please contact HR confidentially. We offer:
  • Access to professional counseling
  • Support throughout the recovery process
  • Adjusted work arrangements where possible
  • Complete confidentiality

Compliance and Consequences

This workplace policy is binding for everyone. Violations will result in appropriate measures, ranging from a warning to termination of employment. The severity of the sanction depends on the nature and frequency of the violation.

If you have any questions about this policy, please contact your supervisor or the HR department. Together, we’ll make our workplace an environment where everyone feels safe, respected, and valued.
title: Sample Workplace Policy

More and more companies and organizations are saying goodbye to the traditional performance review and evaluation meeting and are opting for a modern cycle of conversations. But how do you implement this? Focus on employees’ talents and development through an ongoing dialogue with their manager, using goal-oriented coaching and clear performance agreements. But what do you need to make this happen?

Are you looking for help modernizing your feedback cycle?

Discover how 360-degree feedback can improve your dialogue

From Wanting to Doing

The old performance review and appraisal meetings no longer work. Many organizations want to modernize their performance review and appraisal cycles. To do so, they’re considering ongoing coaching of employees with motivational and goal-oriented feedback to support their development. That sounds like a noble goal, but how do you make it happen? After all, the review cycle itself isn’t employees’ “core business.” But in an accessible and organic way, awareness of their own development and performance can certainly be a point of focus—one they actively engage with on a regular basis. Not because “the boss” requires it, but out of their own intrinsic motivation: because they want to do it themselves and see the value in it.

Why a modern performance review cycle?

This means that many organizations will have to make a significant shift. But why, exactly?
Problems with traditional performance reviews Consequences
Waste of time and money Inefficient HR processes
Demotivating and unfair Lower employee engagement
No positive impact on performance Stagnant development
Outdated work methods Not suitable for agile organizations
The main reason is that both employees and managers find traditional performance reviews pointless. These concerns all emerged from seven years of research at VU University Amsterdam. Researcher Kilian Wawoe wrote a book on this topic titled *The New Reward System*. In it, he advocates for the abolition of the “judgmental review.” The demotivating performance review must be replaced by ongoing coaching with motivational feedback for employees. “Because the work environment has changed dramatically. We work in flatter organizations, more agile, more in teams, and we do more complex work,” says Wawoe. Many HR professionals recognize the problem and are now looking for new approaches. The researcher (and HR instructor) advocates for a better evaluation cycle and a more modern approach to managing staff: more effective, fairer, smoother, with two-way communication in conversations, and more continuous dialogue between employees and managers.

From Performance Review to Developmental Conversation

Modernizing the appraisal cycle is closely linked to how organizations evaluate their employees. For “the new approach to performance evaluation,” they want to look at employee performance in a different way.

Traditional appraisal cycle vs. modern approach

Aspect Traditional approach Modern approach
Frequency 3 times a year (isolated) Ongoing dialogue
Focus Evaluation and Rewards Talent and development
Conversation style One-way communication Coaching and Two-Way
Duration Long and formal Shorter and more accessible
For decades, the traditional meeting cycle went something like this:
  • At the beginning of the year, goals were set jointly during a goal-setting or planning meeting.
  • Midway through the year, the goals were discussed in a progress review or performance review.
  • At the end of the year, there was a “wrap-up” with an evaluation of the goals during a performance review.
With the new approach to evaluation, the focus shifts from evaluating—or “judging,” as some prefer to call it—and rewarding to talent and (personal) development. The performance review and appraisal meeting are being replaced by development discussions between managers and employees. No longer limited to three isolated moments per year, but more frequent, shorter, more accessible, and above all, more coaching-oriented. The goal is a more continuous dialogue focused primarily on growth and development. This naturally calls for a new approach to performance evaluation.

Would you also like to conduct more coaching-oriented conversations?

360-degree feedback provides valuable input for development discussions

Solutions for a modern review cycle

Focusing on development discussions through a modern feedback cycle gives employees much more control over their own development. The review cycle encompasses all moments when managers engage with employees regarding their development. These no longer need to be strictly “formal meetings.” The dialogue can take a broader form. After all, a modern feedback cycle involves multiple touchpoints and is, above all, a flexible, customized approach for each individual. This requires an agile development cycle. Feedback questionnaires can be used to ensure truly valuable feedback—and to identify relevant discussion topics for the times when people actually speak with one another. It’s a waste of time to have to dwell on procedural “must-dos” or to first have to search for the most important topics of discussion. Fortunately, modern HR software can perfectly support the agile development and conversation cycle. This gives you a valuable tool, but organizations need to take further steps, because the software is merely a tool.

Examples

A number of our clients have already adapted their cycle. The most important question they ask is: “Can’t it be simpler?” In practice, every organization wants to incorporate everything into a single appraisal system, and that’s precisely where the pitfall lies. Our experience has shown that it makes more sense to build it up or phase it out step by step and let employees get used to a modern appraisal cycle.

BilaBasic for operational employees:

• 5 questions on fundamental core topics

• Online preparation by the employee and manager

• Facilitates a productive conversation

• Results in a concrete action plan

For example, we developed BilaBasic for a logistics organization’s operational staff. This includes, among other things, 5 questions on fundamental core topics that, based on online preparation by both the employee and manager, facilitate a productive conversation. This results in a concrete action plan. Another option is the Development Conversation. This agile development cycle was developed by hrmforce for a number of organizations that want to support professionals in their growth and development. The employee is invited to reflect on his or her own development. Step by step, employees are guided through a process. The process can be initiated at any time and is based on the employee’s role, manager, competencies, and performance areas. All development solutions can be combined with our psychometric questionnaires .

Implementing a Modern Feedback Cycle

Anyone who wants to put people first must be able to flexibly align the organization’s entire development cycle with that goal. This allows you to move from a one-sided process driven by the organization or a manager to a more collaborative process. In this process, the manager and employee jointly determine the goals and direction, and they are also jointly responsible for them.

4 Steps to a Modern Performance Review Cycle

Step Action Tools
1. Start the dialogue Discuss talents, competencies, and aspirations Feedback questionnaires, self-analysis
2. Agree on results Set specific quarterly goals SMART goals, interim check-ins
3. From evaluation to development Focus on growth rather than evaluation Coaching conversation techniques
4. The Right Tools Implement supportive systems HR software, 360-degree feedback tools
Be sure to consider these steps: 1. Start the dialogue It begins with a dialogue between the employee and the manager about his (or her) talents, competencies, and ambitions. Where does the employee want to be in three years? And how can the organization help make those ambitions a reality? And how do you give employees the insight needed to achieve that? Think about this and see how it can be incorporated into an individual’s personal development process. Also consider how feedback questionnaires can support this process. This paves the way for motivating and goal-oriented feedback. 2. Set short-term performance goals Those who opt for a modern performance review cycle aim to maintain a continuous dialogue with meaningful conversations and interactions between employees and managers. Talent and (personal) development are central, but you also set performance goals. This is an important prerequisite for the new compensation system and for ensuring that the new agile review cycle remains goal-oriented and concrete. Don’t just focus on the long term; above all, set short-term performance goals as well, for example, on a quarterly basis. 3. From Judging to Developing When evaluating performance goals, the development discussion must remain the guiding principle. Avoid creating a new performance review—or even one that feels like a “judgmental” conversation. Discuss openly and honestly what’s going well, what could be improved, and what’s needed to achieve the set goals. Don’t focus primarily on KPIs; instead, have a broad discussion about an employee’s results, competencies, and behavior. This quickly shifts the focus away from thinking in terms of “right or wrong” toward the employee’s talents and the targeted support they need. 4. What tools are needed? In addition to the resources employees need for their development, a modern performance review cycle also requires tools to ensure that the desired dialogue can be conducted effectively and flexibly. For your employees and organization, consider which tools are needed for an agile development cycle and what, for example, the added value might be of modern feedback questionnaires for the coaching dialogue between employees and managers. After all, that is the new “holy grail.”

Ready for a modern performance review cycle?

Start with 360-degree feedback for valuable input into your conversations

The perfect foundation for development-oriented conversations

For most companies, online assessments have become an indispensable part of the hiring process or a tool to support employee or team development. They can provide many valuable insights with a high degree of predictive accuracy. A careful approach yields the best results. What are the key considerations and success factors in this regard?

Why conduct an assessment?

An (online) assessment allows you to evaluate current employees or job candidates for traits that determine their success within the organization or their professional development. This may involve, for example, assessing motivations, competencies, intelligence, behavior, or personality traits. An assessment provides an objective picture of these factors and is valuable, for example, for follow-up discussions about the strengths and areas for development of employees or teams. This fosters employee growth and offers opportunities to engage and retain them or to work on, for example, job satisfaction or sustainable employability. In addition to supporting employee development or team-building efforts, the insights gained from assessments are, of course, valuable for hiring new staff. After all, recruiting, selecting, and onboarding a new employee is costly. That’s why you want to know as much as possible in advance about the likelihood of success.

Prevent “Bad Hires”

According to estimates, a “bad hire” costs at least 30 percent of the annual salary. And these failed matches occur regularly. At least three-quarters of organizations acknowledge this. According to reports, there are various underlying causes for this. For example, during a job interview, the focus was primarily on whether the candidate was a “nice person” rather than on their competencies, motivation, or driving factors (32% cite this as the cause). Or the person did not yet possess all the necessary skills, but it was assumed that he or she could learn them quickly (35%). And that is not always the case. Or perhaps the person’s skills were considered, but not their attitude (29%). Or worse yet: there were already warning signs, but they were simply ignored (25%). This is also a pitfall in an increasingly tight labor market. An assessment can prevent this and, moreover, offer many more benefits.

Benefits of Online Assessments

Assessments can be conducted in person, but these days they’re mostly held online. These online assessments (or e-assessments) save companies (and candidates!) a tremendous amount of time and money. It aligns well with the current culture of increased remote work and can significantly contribute to a positive “candidate experience,” serving as an introduction to your organization and helping to manage expectations. The use of objective assessment tools with a validated, high predictive value makes it possible to pre-screen (large groups of) applicants and increase their chances of success in the role. This also enables remote (pre)selection. You then interview only the most suitable candidates, saving a significant amount of time and money.

Convenience and time savings

Many types of tests and questionnaires are now readily available online and can therefore be completed at home or in another setting. This can also be a controlled environment when necessary. An online assessment can usually be administered more quickly, which can significantly shorten the turnaround time of a recruitment process. Furthermore, online assessments no longer require specialized experts, as was often the case in the past with offline, on-site assessments. As a result, assessments were used rather sparingly. Fortunately, these days the process is much more accessible and therefore more widely used. The results are also immediately available, making it easier to compare candidates’ performance. This can also help objectify the assessment of candidates. It prevents incorrect decisions caused by unconscious “biases” during the recruitment process. Consequently, it can also contribute to competency-based matching and to greater diversity and inclusivity in the workplace. Of course, an online portal can be available 24/7. This makes testing much easier anytime and anywhere. Online assessments are also ideal for generating conversation topics for candidates coming in for interviews. As a result, interviews can often delve deeper more quickly and in a targeted manner. This, too, yields more valuable insights about the candidates.

Success Factors for Online Assessments

An online assessment can include various components. Exactly which ones are used depends, of course, on an organization’s approach and its priorities. If an organization uses assessments frequently, a fixed base platform with multiple types of tests on a single online portal is recommended. We offer this with hrmforce for a broad suite of online assessments. This is useful if, for example, you want to use a Big Fifty personality test or a Motivator Test one time, while another time you need more insight into how quickly a person understands problems, forms an opinion, or is able to learn new things (Ability Scan). In addition to such assessments, an online intake can also be used to immediately clarify topics for an interview round. A prerequisite for using online assessments is, of course, that employees or candidates have access to a device that allows them to work online, but that’s rarely a problem these days. It is also quite possible these days to remotely verify that the person taking a test is indeed the person expected to be taking it. With certain tests, there is also a risk that participants will deliberately give incorrect answers to “do better” on the test—or to create an impression that makes them seem like a better fit for the organization. This can be effectively addressed by including smart verification questions in the test or by incorporating specific discussion topics into follow-up interviews.

Reliability of Online Assessments

Are online assessments just as reliable as traditional on-site assessments? A great deal of research has been conducted on this topic over the past 25 years. Conclusion: the value of an assessment does not depend on whether or not it is conducted online. The quality of the tests themselves is, of course, a determining factor. In addition, the context in which a test is taken can have an impact. If a candidate comes to take an assessment on-site but arrives completely stressed out due to traffic and has little time to adjust, this can negatively affect the test. And if someone takes a test remotely but experiences an unstable connection or noise from children at home, that will also have a negative impact. A test with a clear structure in a quiet testing environment always yields the best and most reliable results. A clear structure gives candidates confidence in an accurate result, which benefits the assessment results—including their reliability and the overall picture. Of course, hrmforce’s online assessments already take this into account.

Frequently Asked Questions About Online Assessments:

  • How can you ensure that online assessments are fair and unbiased in a diverse workplace?
    • It is helpful to regularly validate assessments and check them for cultural and language-related biases. Involving diverse panels during development and evaluation can also contribute to fairness.
 
  • What measures can be taken to ensure candidates’ confidentiality and data privacy during online assessments?
    • The use of encrypted platforms, access restrictions, and regular audits of security protocols are important steps to protect candidates’ privacy.
 
  • How can the results of online assessments be effectively used to promote employee development?
    • Results can be linked to personalized development plans, supplemented with targeted feedback sessions and training tailored to employees’ specific needs, as identified in the assessments.
Want to get started with an online assessment? Explore all our assessments here or request a free demo.
